title: Architecture Diagram
content:
The diagram below is the architecture image supplied for this project. Unlike earlier revisions of this page, every node here is checked directly against live AWS state (not copied from an older draft) — 5.4 Deployment Guide carry the step-by-step evidence behind each claim, and 5.2.1 covers how the deployment arrived at its current state.
Component diagram Everything in the component diagram outside the Edge and DevOps groups runs inside a VPC spread across multiple Availability Zones. The chat service is the one deliberate exception to “no EC2 instances or containers in this design”: it is stateful WebSocket traffic, which does not fit a request/response Lambda well, so it runs as an ECS Fargate task behind its own Application Load Balancer — both on-demand (started/stopped per session with the NAT Gateway and OpenSearch/Secrets Manager VPC endpoints, via dev-start.ps1/dev-stop.ps1), not always-on.
The AI component is a dual-provider setup, not a single LLM: Ollama running a self-hosted Qwen3-4B model is the default for local/dev work (no per-token cost, no AWS dependency), while the real, deployed AWS Lambda calls Amazon Bedrock’s Nova Pro — not through the DEV account’s own Bedrock quota (which is account-level 0 and not self-service-adjustable), but through a dedicated cross-account IAM role in a separate AWS account, assumed via STS for every Bedrock call. This was exercised for real, not just configured: CloudWatch shows a successful llm_call log line with provider":"bedrock" and a real apac.amazon.nova-pro-v1:0 response.
On infrastructure-as-code: CloudFormation, not Terraform, is what actually provisions and manages this project’s real AWS resources (API Gateway, the CI/CD OIDC IAM roles, the on-demand network stack, the frontend CDN, monitoring) — confirmed by listing every live CREATE_COMPLETE/UPDATE_COMPLETE stack in the account. The repository does contain a Terraform module, but it is wired up only to a separate, unrelated “hello world” bootstrap API with no live .tfstate for this environment — it is not this project’s real IaC path, despite being present in the codebase.

title: Auth Service and API Gateway
content:
Auth is the first service every user flow depends on, so it was deployed first, together with the HTTP API that all other Lambda services later attach to. Its logical database is fitness_assistant and its secret is fitness-assistant/dev/database.
In every screenshot below, the red rectangles mark what to fill in or click for the sub-step written just above it.
Step 1 — Run the Auth schema migration A temporary migration Lambda, fitness-assistant-dev-auth-migrate, was created following the common pattern and invoked once. The sub-steps below configure it and run it.
1.1 — Set memory and timeout. Open Lambda → Functions → fitness-assistant-dev-auth-migrate → Configuration → General configuration → Edit. Enter these values, then click Save:
Memory: 1024 MB Timeout: 5 min 0 sec 1.2 — Open the VPC settings. In Configuration → VPC, click Edit.
1.3 — Attach the function to the private subnets. In Edit VPC, select the VPC 10.0.0.0/16, both private app subnets (fitness-assistant-dev-private-app-a and -b) and the security group fitness-assistant-dev-lambda-sg, then click Save.
1.4 — Set the secret name. In Configuration → Environment variables → Edit, add the following key and value, then click Save:
Key: DATABASE_SECRET_ID Value: fitness-assistant/dev/database The variable now appears in the list.
1.5 — Invoke the migration. Open the Test tab, create a test event with this body, and click Test:
{} 1.6 — Read the result. The function must finish with Executing function: succeeded, and the response must contain "status":"ok", "exitCode":0 and the line about the 7 migrations in prisma/migrations. All 7 Prisma migrations of the Auth database are applied.
Once Auth’s own Lambda was verified against Aurora (Step 3), the temporary migration Lambda was deleted.
Step 2 — Force the Auth Lambda to pick up a rotated credential The Auth Lambda caches its database secret per execution environment. After the Aurora password was changed in Secrets Manager, warm containers could still hold the old credential. To force fresh execution environments, add a harmless variable:
2.1 — Add DEPLOY_REVISION. In Lambda → fitness-assistant-dev-auth → Configuration → Environment variables → Edit, click Add environment variable, enter the key and value below, then click Save:
Key: DEPLOY_REVISION Value: 20260827-1 DEPLOY_REVISION = 20260827-1 The code never reads it; changing the configuration is enough to recycle the environments.
Step 3 — Smoke-test a route that really queries the database 3.1 — Create the test event. In fitness-assistant-dev-auth → Test, choose Create new event and give it this name:
auth-login-db-smoke Paste the API Gateway v2.0 event below for POST /auth/login with an e-mail address that does not exist, then click Test:
{ "version": "2.0", "routeKey": "POST /auth/login", "rawPath": "/auth/login", "rawQueryString": "", "headers": { "content-type": "application/json", "accept": "application/json", "host": "example.execute-api.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com" }, "requestContext": { "accountId": "123456789012", "apiId": "test", "domainName": "example.execute-api.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com", "domainPrefix": "example", "http": { "method": "POST", "path": "/auth/login", "protocol": "HTTP/1.1", "sourceIp": "127.0.0.1", "userAgent": "AWS-Lambda-Test" }, "requestId": "auth-db-smoke", "routeKey": "POST /auth/login", "stage": "$default", "time": "27/Aug/2026:09:30:00 +0700", "timeEpoch": 1787797800000 }, "body": "{\"email\":\"aws-smoke-nonexistent@example.com\",\"password\":\"NotARealPassword123!\"}", "isBase64Encoded": false } Expected result: statusCode: 401 (invalid credentials). That is a pass: it proves the chain Auth Lambda → Secrets Manager → Prisma Linux engine → Aurora → users table works. The response must not contain P1000, P1001, PrismaClientInitializationError, Can't reach database or relation "users" does not exist. A 400 means the payload shape is wrong; a 500 means reading the CloudWatch log before changing anything.
Keep Aurora’s minimum capacity at 0.5 ACU while services are still being deployed. With 0 ACU the cluster auto-pauses after a few idle minutes, and the resume delay makes the next smoke test look like a failure.
Step 4 — Create the HTTP API with the Auth integration 4.1 — Name the API and add the Lambda integration. In API Gateway → Create API → HTTP API → Build, enter this API name and keep the IP address type IPv4:
fitness-assistant-dev-api Under Integrations, choose type Lambda, region ap-southeast-1, the function fitness-assistant-dev-auth (never the migration Lambda) and payload format version 2.0. Then click Next.
Step 5 — Create explicit public routes 5.1 — Add one route per public endpoint. On Configure routes, add the routes below, each with the integration target fitness-assistant-dev-auth. The screenshot shows all 12 rows.
POST /auth/register POST /auth/register/verify POST /auth/login POST /auth/refresh POST /auth/logout POST /auth/verify PATCH /auth/me GET /auth/users PATCH /auth/users/{userId}/role PATCH /auth/users/{userId}/disable PATCH /auth/users/{userId}/enable GET /health These routes are not created: /auth/internal/* (service-to-service endpoints protected by INTERNAL_SERVICE_SECRET, called by other Lambdas through direct invoke instead) and GET /metrics (in-memory Prometheus counters are meaningless when every Lambda execution environment keeps its own). A catch-all ANY /auth/{proxy+} would have been faster, but it would also have published /auth/internal/* to the internet — explicit routes keep the security boundary.
Step 6 — Keep the $default stage with auto-deploy 6.1 — Define the stage. Click Next to reach Define stages. Keep this stage name with Auto-deploy switched on, so route changes go live without a manual deployment and the invoke URL stays short:
$default Then click Next.
6.2 — Review and create. Check that the 12 routes point at fitness-assistant-dev-auth and that the stage is $default (Auto-deploy: enabled), then scroll down and click Create.
The API’s invoke URL (https://<api-id>.execute-api.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com) is what the frontend and the PAYMENT_PUBLIC_URL / AUTH_SERVICE_URL variables use from here on.
Step 7 — Allow the S3 frontend to call the API (CORS) 7.1 — Configure CORS. After the frontend is published (5.4.3), open API Gateway → fitness-assistant-dev-api → CORS → Configure, fill in the fields below and click Save.
Setting Value Access-Control-Allow-Origin http://fitness-assistant-frontend-dev-<account-id>.s3-website-ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com (HTTP, because the S3 website endpoint has no HTTPS) Allow headers authorization, content-type Allow methods GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, OPTIONS (the screenshot also lists HEAD and *) Max age 300 Allow credentials Off — the frontend sends Authorization: Bearer <token>, not cross-site cookies Verification: open the frontend /login, open the browser Network tab and log in with a non-existent e-mail. A 401 {"error":"Invalid credentials"} from API Gateway proves the full path S3 website → API Gateway → Auth Lambda → Prisma → Aurora. A CORS error, 404 or 500 means checking the origin value, the route list and the Lambda log respectively.

title: Blog 2: Challenges and Cost Optimization in AWS Deployment
content:
Challenges and Cost Optimization in AWS Deployment: Lessons Learned from Gymini Status: Technical case study written from the experience of deploying Gymini for this internship.
Shared on Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/share/p/19qBt1z5fU/
This post follows what is already confirmed elsewhere in this report (linked at each point). The parts about AWS credit running out faster than expected and about adopting CloudFormation are presented as an illustrative case study, reasoned from the real cost profile of the deployed architecture — not a confirmed billing history — and CloudFormation is not currently used for this project (every resource so far was created by hand through the AWS Console, see 5.4). The closing “Evidence and limitations” section lists exactly what is confirmed, what is a reasonable inference, and what is only a proposal.
1. Why deploying a multi-component application is not a one-day job Gymini is not a simple CRUD project. It is a pnpm monorepo with seven Node.js/TypeScript services (Auth, User, Fitness, Gym, Payment, AI, Chat) plus a React frontend, which until recently only ran with Docker Compose on one machine — no public endpoint, no backups, no isolation between components (see Proposal §2).
The gap between “it runs on my machine” and “it operates on the cloud” is exactly the work docker compose up never has to do: provisioning a VPC and subnets, writing an IAM role per service, replacing .env files with managed secrets, reconnecting services that no longer share a hostname, adding health checks, centralizing logs, and re-validating each piece after it moves. The number of containers in an application does not predict deployment time, because most of the time goes into wiring managed services together correctly and checking each step, not into building images.
2. Initial expectations versus deployment reality The initial expectation was simple: finish the code, build the Docker images, deploy to AWS, done — possibly in a day. The real deployment of Gymini followed a different loop entirely: provision infrastructure → configure → deploy → validate → troubleshoot → redeploy → confirm, repeated service by service, spread across 26 August to 23 September 2026 (Worklog, Weeks 4–8) — about four weeks, not one day.
Aspect Initial expectation Practical reality Deployment duration About one day Multiple configuration, testing and troubleshooting cycles over roughly four weeks Infrastructure Basic provisioning Several interdependent components (VPC, IAM, Secrets Manager, Aurora, SQS, EventBridge…) Configuration One-time Adjusted repeatedly, with revisions that had to be redone Testing After deployment Continuous, service by service (5.5) Cost Covered by credits, not a concern Some resources bill hourly whether or not they are used “One day” here is the author’s personal expectation going in, not a general benchmark for every project.
3. Technical challenges actually encountered Networking and security. Every added service meant getting the security groups right: lambda-sg and chat-sg are allowed into aurora-sg on port 5432, vpce-sg allows lambda-sg on port 443 to reach Secrets Manager and OpenSearch through VPC endpoints, and the DB subnets have no route to the internet at all (5.2.5). A security group pointed the wrong way means a Lambda function can’t reach the database, with nothing in the logs saying why.
Container deployment. The Chat service produced the most concrete incident: in revision 1 of its task definition, two secrets (CHAT_DATABASE_URL, INTERNAL_API_SECRET) were entered as Value instead of ValueFrom, so the container received the secret’s name instead of its connection string, and Prisma failed with URL must start with postgresql://. The fix was a new revision using ValueFrom with the full ARN and the JSON key suffix (...:CHAT_DATABASE_URL::), followed by Force new deployment (5.4.10).
Database integration. Seven services share one Aurora cluster but each keeps its own logical database and its own secret. Lambda caches the database secret for as long as its execution environment stays warm, so after rotating the Aurora password, the fix was not to wait — it was editing a harmless environment variable (DEPLOY_REVISION) purely to force AWS to create a new execution environment (5.2.6).
Environment configuration. Each service has its own environment variables and secrets, migration Lambdas were created, run once and deleted, and every configuration fix meant a new task definition revision or a function environment-variable update.
Troubleshooting and redeployment. The most repeated pattern was: read the Stopped reason and the service Events instead of recreating the service, update the task definition, then Force new deployment — and confirm Running 1/1, Healthy before calling it done (5.4.10, step 23).
4. Unexpected AWS credit consumption AWS Free Tier, promotional credits and pay-as-you-go are three different things: the Free Tier is a fixed, per-service free allowance; promotional credit is a balance that gets drawn down against the bill and expires; pay-as-you-go is the default pricing for everything beyond those two. Having credit does not mean the infrastructure is free — it only postpones the point at which real money is charged, and once it runs out, billing reverts to list price.
What is easy to overlook while still configuring and debugging: most resources in this architecture bill by usage (Lambda, API Gateway, SQS, Bedrock per token), but a few bill by the hour, regardless of whether a single request arrives. Per the architecture-level estimate in Proposal §8, those fixed items are: the NAT Gateway (~43 USD/month), Aurora at its minimum capacity (~45–60 USD/month), the Chat Fargate task (~22 USD/month), the Application Load Balancer (~20 USD/month), two interface VPC endpoints (~30–40 USD/month) and public IPv4 addresses (~11 USD/month) — roughly 190–230 USD/month running 24/7, or 60–90 USD/month with a “sleep mode” applied (see also 5.2.7). This is a published architectural estimate, not a confirmed billing line item.
From that figure, a technically plausible mechanism follows: if these fixed-cost resources are left running continuously for several weeks while each service is still being deployed, debugged and redeployed — matching the real deployment cadence in section 2 — the “idle” portion of the bill alone can add up faster than intuition suggests, especially with no spending alert configured yet. This is a possible contributing factor, not an incident confirmed against actual billing data for this project.
5. Root cause analysis Problem Possible cause Impact Evidence Proposed improvement Fully manual deployment through the Console No CI/CD built yet Every change takes manual steps and is hard to repeat identically 5.2.6 lists “No CI/CD yet” Infrastructure as Code (CloudFormation or Terraform) plus a CI/CD pipeline Fixed-cost infrastructure running 24/7 No automated schedule to pause it outside test sessions Cost accrues even when nobody is using the system 5.2.7 lists the “DEV sleep strategy” as “Planned, not yet automated” Automatically scale Aurora to 0 ACU, Chat to 0 tasks, and delete the NAT Gateway between test sessions No spending alerts AWS Budgets not configured Unusual spending is noticed late 5.2.7 lists an “AWS Budgets alert” as planned Turn on AWS Budgets with email/SNS notifications No CloudWatch alarms Not configured Errors, throttling and a full DLQ are not actively reported 5.2.6 lists “No CloudWatch alarms yet” Alarms for Lambda errors/throttles, DLQ depth, Aurora capacity, Chat target health Secret entered with the wrong value type in a task definition Manual console entry with no review step before applying Runtime failure in the container, requiring a new revision to fix 5.4.10 — Lesson learned Review infrastructure changes through a Change Set (CloudFormation) or a pull request (Terraform) before applying The table deliberately separates operational causes (not yet automated, no alerting) from the normal cost of running AWS services — not every deployment mistake translates into extra billing, and not every fixed cost is itself a “mistake.”
6. AWS CloudFormation as a proposed solution Infrastructure as Code (IaC) addresses exactly this class of problem: instead of remembering and repeating dozens of console steps, the infrastructure is described in files that can be reviewed before they are applied and reproduced identically in another environment.
AWS CloudFormation manages infrastructure as stacks: a template (YAML or JSON) describes the resources to create, accepts parameters so it can be reused across environments, returns outputs that other stacks can reference, and supports Change Sets — a preview of exactly what will be created, changed or deleted before anything is actually applied (Change Sets documentation). CloudFormation also supports drift detection, to notice when someone has edited a resource directly outside the stack.
Technical clarification: CloudFormation does not automatically reduce cost — it manages infrastructure as code and makes cleanup of stack-managed resources easier and more consistent. Deleting a stack (deletion documentation) also does not guarantee every related resource disappears — retention policies, snapshots, resources created outside the stack, or a failed deletion can all leave something that needs manual cleanup.
An illustrative directory layout for this direction:
infrastructure/ ├── cloudformation/ │ ├── network.yaml │ ├── security.yaml │ ├── database.yaml │ ├── application.yaml │ └── monitoring.yaml ├── environments/ │ ├── dev/ │ ├── staging/ │ └── production/ └── README.md This layout is illustrative only — the repository has no infrastructure/ directory today, because everything so far was created by hand through the console, as described in 5.4. The project’s most recent target-architecture diagram (Proposal §3) actually names Terraform as its IaC choice; CloudFormation is an equivalent option, tied directly to AWS without an external tool.
graph LR GIT["Git repository"] --> TPL["CloudFormation templates"] TPL --> CS["Change setsreview before apply"] CS --> CF["AWS CloudFormation"] CF --> DEV["Stack: Development"] CF --> STG["Stack: Staging"] CF --> PRD["Stack: Production"] Figure 3 — Infrastructure management lifecycle with CloudFormation: changes are reviewed through a Change Set before being applied, and each environment is its own stack.
7. Separating Dev, Staging and Production Today the project has only one DEV environment, so this section is a proposal, not the current state.
Development — minimal infrastructure where technically feasible, cost-conscious configuration, temporary resources with controlled cleanup. Staging — integration testing, deployment validation, production-like configuration where it matters, kept controlled enough to avoid unnecessary spend. Production — reliability, security, scalability, monitoring and data protection come first. Identical configuration across all three environments is unnecessarily expensive, but cutting configuration down to the point where it compromises functionality, security or test fidelity is not optimization either — the trade-off has to be deliberate, not arbitrary.
8. Cost optimization strategy Cost visibility — AWS Cost Explorer, AWS Budgets with alerts, cost allocation tags per service (both currently open items, see section 5). Infrastructure lifecycle — the existing consistent naming convention (fitness-assistant-dev-<service>-...) already makes resources filterable by owner; what is missing is a stack-based deletion workflow and a cleanup-confirmation step, matching the full teardown order already documented in 5.7. Right-sizing — choices already applied: Aurora Serverless v2 with a 0.5 ACU floor, Lambda at 1024 MB, OpenSearch Serverless at 0–2 OCU, Fargate at 0.5 vCPU / 1 GB for Chat (5.2.7). Automation — integrating IaC into CI/CD (not yet built), scheduled shutdown of DEV resources outside test hours where technically supported, and a cleanup procedure for failed deployments. Governance — documented cost ownership, a pre-deployment checklist, environment naming conventions, budget thresholds, and a regular billing review. A budget alert is not instantaneous — it should be treated as an early signal to investigate, not a hard spending cap that can never be exceeded.
9. Current state versus proposed target state Criterion Current state (confirmed) Proposed target Infrastructure provisioning Manual, through the AWS Console (5.4) Infrastructure as Code Environment configuration Documented step by step, not parameterized Parameterized, reusable across environments Resource tracking Manual inspection by naming convention Stack-based visibility plus resource tags Redeployment Force new deployment, repeated troubleshooting (5.4.10) Controlled updates through Change Sets Cost monitoring No Budgets or Alarms yet (5.2.6, 5.2.7) Proactive alerts and periodic review Cleanup A documented checklist exists, not yet run (5.7) Stack-based cleanup with a confirmation step Reproducibility Limited, depends on the operator Infrastructure under version control This compares the confirmed current state against a proposed target, not the measured result of a completed migration.
10. Lessons learned Cloud deployment is an engineering process, not the final step after the code is done. Infrastructure cost should be estimated before provisioning, not discovered after the bill arrives — the budget table in Proposal §8 belongs at the start, not written after the fact. A development environment should be designed around what it actually needs operationally, not copied from production. Automated infrastructure management reduces configuration drift — the Chat service’s Value-versus-ValueFrom secret error is a concrete example of where manual steps go wrong. Resource lifecycle management matters as much as initial provisioning — a resource with no cleanup plan eventually costs more than expected. Free credit should be budgeted like a limited resource, not treated as unlimited. Deployment readiness includes operational and cost visibility, not just an application that starts. Infrastructure as Code contributes to long-term maintainability and reproducibility. 11. Future improvement roadmap Phase 1 — Infrastructure audit (partially in place): inventory resources by the existing naming convention, use the published estimate in Proposal §8, review the security gaps already recorded in 5.2.5 — still missing: a review of actual billing over time.
Phase 2 — CloudFormation adoption (not started): write templates per resource group (network, security, database, application, monitoring), parameterize by environment, test both deployment and stack deletion.
Phase 3 — Cost governance (not started, has a foundation): turn on AWS Budgets, extend the existing naming convention into resource tags, write a lifecycle policy for non-production environments, schedule regular cost reviews.
Phase 4 — Deployment automation (not started): integrate IaC into CI/CD, use Change Sets to review infrastructure before applying it, add post-deployment verification, and build rollback and cleanup procedures for failed deployments.
Diagrams graph LR A["Application code"] --> B["Docker build"] B --> C["Deploy to AWS"] C --> D{"Health check"} D -- fail --> E["Debug"] E --> F["Fix configuration"] F --> G["Redeploy"] G --> D D -- pass --> H["Monitor"] Figure 1 — The deployment debugging loop: every failed health check triggers a round of debugging, fixing configuration and redeploying, and each round costs both engineering time and running-resource time.
graph LR subgraph AlwaysOn ["Infrastructure running 24/7 regardless of traffic — conceptual"] NAT["NAT Gateway"] ALB["Chat ALB"] FG["Fargate task"] AU["Aurora, minimum capacity"] VE["VPC interface endpoints"] IP["Public IPv4 addresses"] end NAT --> SUM["Monthly costsee Proposal §8"] ALB --> SUM FG --> SUM AU --> SUM VE --> SUM IP --> SUM SUM -. if left running for weeks .-> CREDIT["Free or promotional creditcan deplete faster than expected"] Figure 2 — A conceptual diagram, not a real billing chart, showing why hourly-billed resources can add up quickly if left running while the system is still being configured and tested.
Evidence and limitations Confirmed in this report: the seven-service plus AI plus Chat architecture; manual console-based deployment spanning 26 Aug – 23 Sep 2026; the Chat service’s Value-versus-ValueFrom secret error and its fix; Lambda’s secret caching behavior and the DEPLOY_REVISION workaround; the absence of CI/CD and CloudWatch alarms; the published budget estimate of ~190–230 USD/month (24/7) or ~60–90 USD/month (sleep mode); the full clean-up order in 5.7, not yet executed. Reported experience, without logs or billing attached in this report: the general deploy-test-fix-redeploy cadence across weeks. Possible contributing factor, not confirmed by billing data: fixed-cost infrastructure running continuously during debugging depleting credit faster than expected. Proposed, not yet implemented: the entire CloudFormation section, Dev/Staging/Production separation, AWS Budgets, CloudWatch Alarms, a scheduled shutdown for idle infrastructure. Already applied in practice (unrelated to CloudFormation): pay-per-invocation Lambda, Aurora Serverless v2 with a low capacity floor, OpenSearch Serverless at 0–2 OCU, a single shared NAT Gateway, a right-sized Fargate task for Chat — see 5.2.7. title: Proposal
content:
Gymini — AI Fitness Assistant on AWS A serverless microservices deployment with managed AI on Amazon Bedrock 1. Executive Summary Gymini (the open-source Fitness Assistant project) is a pnpm monorepo with a React/Vite frontend and seven Node.js/TypeScript services — Auth, User, Fitness, Gym, Payment, AI and Chat — that until now only ran on a developer machine with Docker Compose. This internship project designs and deploys it on AWS as a serverless-first DEV environment in the Asia Pacific (Singapore) region, documented step by step so it can be reviewed, repeated and later automated.
Each service runs on the AWS service that fits its runtime shape: six request/response services on AWS Lambda behind Amazon API Gateway, the real-time Chat service on Amazon ECS Fargate behind an Application Load Balancer, one Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL Serverless v2 cluster with a logical database per service, Amazon Bedrock (Nova Pro, Cohere Embed) and Amazon OpenSearch Serverless for the AI coach, and Amazon SQS plus EventBridge Scheduler for background work. The static frontend is served from Amazon S3; credentials live in AWS Secrets Manager; every function has its own least-privilege IAM role inside private subnets.
At the latest checkpoint every service is deployed on AWS, the 7 local databases have been restored into Aurora with all 23 audited foreign keys validated, and the system runs with a CI/CD pipeline, CloudWatch monitoring and an on/off routine that keeps cost low. The details are in the Workshop.
2. Problem Statement Current problems Local-only operation. The whole stack (PostgreSQL, Redis, Qdrant, a self-hosted Ollama model and seven services) runs in Docker Compose on one laptop: no public endpoint, no backups, no isolation between components. Secrets in .env files. Database passwords, JWT and service-to-service secrets and provider keys are plain text on disk. Heavy self-hosted AI. The AI coach needs a local LLM and vector database on an always-on machine; an earlier EC2 sizing exercise showed that a free-tier instance cannot run it. Background work tied to processes. Reminders, settlements and reconciliation ran as in-process timers, which do not exist on serverless compute. Real-time chat. Socket.IO needs long-lived connections that a request/response platform cannot hold. Proposed solution Re-platform each part onto the managed service that matches it, adapting the code where needed:
Request/response services → AWS Lambda with HTTP API (payload 2.0) handlers, a separate jobs handler and a migration handler that reads DATABASE_SECRET_ID; internal calls become direct Lambda invokes instead of HTTP through an application gateway. Real-time chat → ECS Fargate behind an ALB, REST routed through API Gateway. PostgreSQL → Aurora Serverless v2, one logical database per service, data restored from the local dumps. AI → Amazon Bedrock for chat, vision and embeddings; OpenSearch Serverless for vectors; long generations queued on SQS and processed by a worker. Timers → EventBridge Scheduler schedules invoking jobs functions. Frontend → S3 static website (CloudFront and HTTPS as the next step). Benefits The DEV environment pays mostly for what it uses, there are no servers to patch for six of the seven services, the AI coach no longer needs a model host, networking is private and permissions are least-privilege by default, and the deployment is captured in a runbook that can be repeated by hand or turned into a pipeline.
3. Solution Architecture The diagram shows the architecture this project is designed around. It is the target the deployment works toward; Workshop 5.2 has the full description — request flows, service selection, security, scalability and cost.
Edge and frontend — Route 53 for DNS, an optional AWS WAF, and Amazon CloudFront in front of an Amazon S3 frontend bucket. API layer — a single Amazon API Gateway REST API, with one route group per service (/auth/*, /users/*, /fitness/*, /payments/*, /gyms/*, /ai/*, /health). Serverless backend — six AWS Lambda services (Auth, User, Fitness, Payment, Gym, AI), deployed across multiple Availability Zones by default. Data — Aurora Serverless v2 (PostgreSQL) with a primary and a replica across two private DB subnets, Multi-AZ replication, and an optional Amazon RDS Proxy in front of it. Shared services — an S3 uploads bucket, Secrets Manager for credentials, and CloudWatch for logs and metrics. Asynchronous and AI processing — Amazon EventBridge for schedules and events, Amazon SQS feeding a Lambda worker, which calls Amazon Bedrock for generation and an OpenSearch Serverless vector store for retrieval. DevOps — GitHub source code, a GitHub Actions CI/CD pipeline authenticating through OIDC, and Terraform as infrastructure as code. Monitoring — CloudWatch logs, metrics, alarms and dashboards, Amazon SNS for alerts, AWS X-Ray for tracing, and AWS Budgets / Cost Explorer for cost control. Network — everything outside the Edge and DevOps groups runs in a VPC spread across multiple Availability Zones, with no EC2 instances or containers in this design. 4. AWS Services Used Service Role in the system Amazon S3 Static frontend hosting; private uploads (presigned URLs); Lambda deployment artifacts; database migration dumps Amazon API Gateway (HTTP API) Public REST entry point with explicit routes, CORS, AI route throttling and an HTTP proxy to the Chat ALB AWS Lambda Auth, User, Fitness, Gym, Payment and AI services (HTTP, jobs and worker functions) and per-service schema migrations Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate Chat service (REST + Socket.IO) and the one-shot database migrator task Amazon ECR Private container images for Chat and the migrator Elastic Load Balancing (ALB) Socket.IO/WebSocket entry for Chat, /health checks, stickiness, rules hiding internal paths Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL Serverless v2 Relational data for all services, one logical database each Amazon Bedrock Nova Pro for chat and vision; Cohere Embed Multilingual v3 for embeddings Amazon OpenSearch Serverless Vector search for RAG and knowledge retrieval Amazon SQS AI task queue and dead-letter queue Amazon EventBridge Scheduler Schedules for settlements, reminders, payouts, reconciliation and AI jobs AWS Secrets Manager Database credentials, the Chat database URL and the shared internal secret AWS IAM Per-function execution roles, ECS task/execution roles, scheduler roles Amazon VPC Network isolation: subnets, route tables, security groups NAT Gateway and Internet Gateway Outbound internet access for the private subnets VPC interface endpoints Private access to Secrets Manager and OpenSearch Serverless Amazon CloudWatch Logs Logs for every function, the Chat task and the migrator AWS Marketplace One-time subscription to the Cohere model on Bedrock 5. Component Design Frontend (React/Vite) — S3 website; REST calls to API Gateway with a Bearer token; Socket.IO to the Chat ALB; user-facing handling of 429/408/504 from the AI routes. Auth service — registration, verification, login, refresh, logout, user administration; database fitness_assistant. User service — profile, onboarding, InBody records, PT applications, contracts, sessions, availability, notifications; uploads to private S3 prefixes; jobs: session settlement, auto-confirm, reschedule expiry; database fitness_assistant_user. Fitness service — exercises, workouts, nutrition, food, training cycles, coach data, equipment, imports/exports, templates, statistics; jobs: upcoming and unfinished workout reminders; database fitness_assistant_fitness. Gym service — gyms, PT listings, owner and admin tools, collaborations, signed QR check-in; jobs: membership payouts, referral settlement; database fitness_assistant_gym. Payment service — payments, wallet, PT wallet, withdrawals, admin payments, provider callbacks (VNPAY by default; MoMo, PayOS, ZaloPay supported); job: reconciliation every 5 minutes; database fitness_assistant_payment. AI service — HTTP function (/ai, /plans, /marketplace, /admin/ai), SQS worker for long generations, jobs function for auto-accept and nightly knowledge ingestion; Bedrock and OpenSearch; database fitness_assistant_ai. Chat service — conversations and real-time messaging on Fargate; database fitness_assistant_chat. Migration — one migration function per service (Prisma migrate deploy) and a Fargate task that restored the local data. Aurora cluster — fitness-assistant-dev-aurora, seven logical databases. Vector collection — fitness-assistant-dev-ai-vectors with the exercises, fitness_knowledge, fitness_faq and fitness_evidence indexes (1024 dimensions, FAISS/HNSW, cosine similarity). 6. Technical Implementation Implementation phases Analysis and code adaptation — audit every service; add Lambda HTTP, jobs and migration handlers; read credentials through DATABASE_SECRET_ID; replace internal HTTP calls with direct Lambda invokes; add SQS, Bedrock and OpenSearch providers; build artifacts that bundle the Prisma Linux engine. Shared foundation — VPC, subnets, security groups, NAT and Internet Gateway, Aurora Serverless v2, Secrets Manager endpoint. First service and entry points — Auth Lambda, API Gateway with explicit routes, S3 website, CORS. Core services — User, Fitness, Gym and Payment with their jobs functions and schedules, then the Gym ↔ Payment wiring. AI — Bedrock models, SQS worker, jobs function, OpenSearch Serverless, knowledge schedules, AI routes with throttling, Payment → AI activation. Real time and data — Chat on ECS Fargate behind an ALB; restore of the 7 local databases with a Fargate migrator. Validation and hardening — end-to-end tests, alarms, CI/CD, HTTPS with CloudFront, cost “sleep” automation. The exact console steps for phases 2–6, with screenshots and IAM policies, are in the Deployment Guide.
Technical requirements Compute — Lambda Node.js 22.x on x86_64 with 1024 MB; timeouts of 30 s for HTTP, 1 minute for jobs, 300 s for the AI worker, 600 s for AI jobs and up to 15 minutes for migrations; Fargate task of 0.5 vCPU / 1 GB. API — HTTP API with payload format 2.0; no /internal/*, /metrics or catch-all routes; throttling of 1 request/s (burst 3) on the AI routes. Data — Prisma migrations applied per service; one logical database per service; SQS visibility timeout 600 s with a DLQ after 2 receives. AI — Bedrock in ap-southeast-1 through the APAC inference profile; 1024-dimension embeddings; OpenSearch FAISS/HNSW with cosine similarity. Security — least-privilege IAM per function; credentials in Secrets Manager; private subnets and security-group-to-security-group rules; no secrets in artifacts, images or documentation. Operations — CloudWatch Logs; every manual step documented, to be replaced by a CI/CD pipeline. 7. Timeline & Milestones The internship runs from 3 August to 19 October 2026. Dates below are taken from the resources’ creation dates in the deployment runbook.
Phase Period Main activities 1. Learning and analysis August 2026 (weeks 1–3) AWS fundamentals (FCJ modules), application audit, local run, deployment design 2. Foundation and first service 26–27 August 2026 (week 4) VPC and NAT, Aurora, Auth Lambda, API Gateway, S3 frontend; User database and role 3. Core services 2–8 September 2026 (weeks 5–6) Fitness (2 Sep), Gym and Payment (8 Sep) with their jobs and schedules 4. AI 15 September 2026 (week 7) Bedrock, SQS worker, jobs, OpenSearch Serverless, knowledge schedules, AI routes 5. Chat and data 22–23 September 2026 (week 8) Chat on ECS Fargate behind an ALB; migrator image and restore of the 7 databases 6. Validation and report October 2026 (weeks 10–12) End-to-end tests and fixes, CI/CD, alarms, cost controls, report and clean-up 8. Budget Estimation Monthly estimate for the DEV environment in ap-southeast-1 running 24×7 with light test traffic. Figures are approximate on-demand list prices and change over time — confirm them with the AWS Pricing Calculator; the account’s real bill in Cost Explorer is the reference.
Cost group Estimated configuration Monthly cost (USD) NAT Gateway 1 gateway × 730 h, plus data processed ~43 + data Aurora PostgreSQL Serverless v2 0.5 ACU floor × 730 h (≈365 ACU-hours), small storage ~45–60 ECS Fargate (Chat) 0.5 vCPU + 1 GB × 730 h ~22 Application Load Balancer 1 ALB × 730 h, low LCU usage ~20 Public IPv4 addresses NAT Elastic IP + 2 ALB addresses × 730 h ~11 Interface VPC endpoints Secrets Manager and OpenSearch, 2 AZs each ~30–40 OpenSearch Serverless (NextGen) 0–2 OCU, scales to 0 when idle depends on active hours Amazon Bedrock Nova Pro and Cohere Embed, per token, test volume ~1–10 AWS Lambda ~40,000 scheduled invocations + test traffic, 1 GB ~0 (free tier) API Gateway (HTTP API) < 1 million requests ~0–1 Secrets Manager 9 secrets ~4 S3, ECR, CloudWatch Logs, SQS, EventBridge small volumes ~2–5 Estimated total: about USD 190–230 per month if everything runs 24×7. With the planned sleep mode — Aurora at 0 ACU, the Chat service at 0 tasks and the NAT Gateway removed outside test sessions — about USD 60–90 per month. The fixed hourly items (NAT, ALB, Fargate, Aurora floor, endpoints, IPv4) dominate; the usage-based services cost almost nothing at DEV volume.
9. Risk Assessment Risk Impact Probability Mitigation strategy Idle DEV resources keep billing (NAT, Aurora floor, Fargate, ALB, endpoints) Medium High Sleep mode, AWS Budgets alert, dependency-ordered clean-up Runaway Bedrock usage from a client or frontend bug Medium Medium Route throttling on the AI routes, 429 handling in the frontend, SQS dead-letter queue A secret leaks through screenshots, documents or function configuration High Low–Medium Secrets Manager for credentials, pixel-level redaction of evidence, moving internal secrets from Lambda configuration to Secrets Manager Manual deployments drift or cannot be repeated Medium High Step-by-step runbook with screenshots; CI/CD planned Data migration overwrites or corrupts data High Low Read-only preflight, dumps kept in a private versioned bucket, migration history preserved, foreign-key and row-count verification Single Chat task and HTTP-only endpoints Medium Medium Acceptable for DEV; shared Socket.IO adapter before scaling; domain, ACM certificate and CloudFront for HTTPS Costs and errors are reviewed in Cost Explorer and CloudWatch Logs after each test session until alarms are in place.
If something goes wrong, the frontend can be rolled back from its S3 backup, a Lambda can be re-uploaded with its previous artifact, a Fargate service can be pointed back to an earlier task definition revision, and the databases can be rebuilt from the migration dumps.
10. Expected Outcomes Immediate results: a working DEV environment on AWS for the whole application — frontend, six Lambda services, real-time chat, managed AI and the restored data — with a reproducible deployment guide and recorded verification results (Workshop 5.5).
Technical learning: practical experience with serverless design on Lambda, API Gateway and EventBridge; containers on ECS Fargate and ECR; Aurora Serverless and data migration; managed AI with Bedrock and OpenSearch Serverless; and the network and IAM boundaries that keep all of it private and least-privilege.
Longer term: the same design can grow into a production environment by adding a CI/CD pipeline and infrastructure as code, HTTPS with CloudFront and WAF, CloudWatch alarms, auto scaling for Chat with a shared Socket.IO adapter, and separate DEV/production accounts.

title: Week 3 Worklog
content:
Week 3 Objectives: Learn AWS migration strategies (7Rs). Practice VM Import/Export and Database Migration. Analyze production Dockerfile. Tasks for This Week: Task Start Date Completion Date Workshop / Reference - Research 7Rs migration - Practice VM Import/Export - Research Database Migration - Analyze Docker production - Complete blog 1 08-17-2026 08-22-2026 Lab 14: https://000014.awsstudygroup.com/ Lab 43: https://000043.awsstudygroup.com/ Blog 1: https://www.facebook.com/share/p/1F8v6Qye3F/ Week 3 Results: Overview:
This week learned about migration - ways to move systems to AWS. Although my project is built new from scratch, understanding migration is still useful, especially DMS might be helpful later. Also started learning how to package Docker for production.
Knowledge Learned:
1. AWS Migration - 7Rs
AWS has 7 migration strategies:
Rehost: Move as-is to cloud, fast but not optimized Relocate: Move VMware workload to VMware Cloud on AWS Replatform: Minor changes to use managed services (RDS…) Refactor: Rewrite app cloud-native (containers, serverless) Repurchase: Switch to SaaS instead of self-host Retire: Shut down unused apps Retain: Keep on-premise My project uses Refactor from start since building new.
2. VM Import/Export
Through lab 14 learned VM import flow:
Export VM from VMware/Hyper-V → virtual disk (VMDK, VHD) Upload disk to S3 Use aws ec2 import-image to create AMI Launch EC2 from AMI Key points:
IAM role vmimport must have trust policy and S3 permissions, missing causes InvalidParameter error Disk format must be supported (VMDK, VHD, VHDX, OVA) S3 bucket same region as EC2 3. Database Migration
AWS SCT:
Converts schema between DB engines (Oracle → PostgreSQL…) Assessment report shows what can be auto-converted vs manual Complex stored procedures usually need manual rewrite AWS DMS:
DMS has 3 migration types:
Full load: Migrate all data, use when have downtime Full load + CDC: Migrate data first, then sync changes continuously to reduce downtime CDC only: Only sync changes from a point in time DMS components:
Source/Target endpoints Replication instance (EC2 running DMS) Replication task Monitoring:
Important metrics:
CDCLatencySource/Target: Latency capturing/applying changes CPU/Memory/Disk I/O of replication instance Network throughput If CDC latency high, need to check CPU, memory, I/O, network, source workload before deciding to scale instance.
Multi-AZ: Only for high availability, not performance fix.
4. Docker Production
Multi-stage build:
Pattern separating build and runtime:
# Build stage FROM node:20-alpine AS builder WORKDIR /app COPY package*.json ./ RUN npm ci && npm run build # Runtime stage FROM node:20-alpine COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist CMD ["node", "dist/index.js"] Smaller image without dev deps and source code.
Frontend static + Nginx:
FROM node:20-alpine AS builder RUN npm ci && npm run build FROM nginx:1.25-alpine COPY --from=builder /app/dist /usr/share/nginx/html Runtime only needs Nginx, no Node.
Base image:
Alpine: Small but uses musl libc, sometimes native modules fail Debian slim: Larger but better compatibility Node version:
Node 18 EOL (04/2025), don’t use for production Node 20 LTS until 04/2026 Should consider Node 22 LTS Notes:
Must have .dockerignore Run as non-root user Don’t hardcode secrets in image 5. Completed Blog 1
Finished writing first blog post about AWS learning experience and shared on Facebook group. The post summarizes what was learned from weeks 1-3, labs completed, and some tips for AWS beginners.
Blog link: https://www.facebook.com/share/p/1F8v6Qye3F/
Lessons Learned: Migration needs right strategy for each workload VM import most important is IAM role vmimport Database migration separates schema conversion and data migration CDC reduces downtime but needs monitoring Multi-AZ = availability, not performance Multi-stage build makes image smaller and more secure Base image needs balance between size and compatibility References: Lab 14 VM Import: https://000014.awsstudygroup.com/ Lab 43 Database Migration: https://000043.awsstudygroup.com/ AWS 7Rs: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/large-migration-guide/migration-strategies.html

title: Blog 3: Secure Multi-tenant RAG with Amazon Bedrock and Verified Permissions
content:
Secure Multi-tenant RAG with Amazon Bedrock and Verified Permissions Original article: Secure multi-tenant RAG with Amazon Bedrock and Verified Permissions (AWS Architecture Blog, 22 June 2026)
Shared on Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/groups/awsstudygroupfcj/permalink/2314341139330845/
In a generative AI assistant shared by a whole company, every department wants answers from the same pool of documents, but not every employee should see every document. Finance reports belong to finance and HR files to HR, while managers may need to read across departments. A recent post on the AWS Architecture Blog shows how to enforce this inside one shared knowledge base, by deciding at retrieval time which documents each user is allowed to use.
1. Why the obvious approaches do not scale One knowledge base per department: the isolation is clear, but cost and operations grow with every new team. Filters hard-coded in the application: a metadata filter such as department = finance works, but every rule change means editing code and redeploying. No central record of decisions: when access logic is spread across code, it is hard to answer “why could this user see that document?”. 2. The solution: one knowledge base, two authorization layers All documents live in one Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base and carry a department metadata attribute. Access rules are written as Cedar policies in Amazon Verified Permissions and evaluated on every request:
Layer 1, API access. A Lambda authorizer on Amazon API Gateway verifies the Amazon Cognito JWT and calls IsAuthorized for each of the caller’s groups. If no group is allowed, or Verified Permissions returns an error, the caller gets HTTP 403. Layer 2, document access. A middleware Lambda asks Verified Permissions which department knowledge bases the caller may query, and turns the answer into a metadata filter for RetrieveAndGenerate: equals for one department, orAll for several. The same policy store decides which model the caller may invoke. Output check. Guardrails for Amazon Bedrock checks that the answer is grounded in the retrieved context and filters harmful content. In the article’s example, dept-a and dept-b may query only their own documents and use Claude 3 Haiku, while dept-c may query every department and uses Amazon Nova Lite 2. Anything not permitted is denied by default, and a policy change applies on the next request without redeploying any code.
3. How a request flows Figure 1 — How a request flows through the two authorization layers. Editable source: draw.io file.
AWS WAF applies rate limits and rules. If it denies, the request is blocked. Lambda authorizer (Layer 1) checks whether the caller may invoke the API. If not, the answer is 403. Middleware (Layer 2) works out which departments the caller may read. If none, the result is empty. Bedrock Knowledge Bases applies the metadata filter before the vector search, so the model never sees an unauthorized document. Guardrails checks that the answer is grounded. If not, it is blocked or modified. 4. Tagging documents at ingestion A file uploaded to S3 under a department prefix (for example docs/dept-a/report.pdf) triggers an EventBridge event, which is queued in SQS. A Lambda function writes a .metadata.json sidecar next to the file, {"metadataAttributes": {"department": "dept-a"}}. Failed attempts go to a dead-letter queue. Every five minutes a scheduled Lambda calls StartIngestionJob. Bedrock chunks the documents (300 tokens with 20% overlap), embeds them and indexes them together with their department attribute. A document without a sidecar is skipped and logged, so an untagged file never becomes visible to everyone. 5. Safe deployment checklist Know the isolation level. This is filter-level (logical) isolation, not isolation enforced by IAM or separate infrastructure. For different customers of a SaaS product, the article recommends one knowledge base per tenant. Fail closed. Both layers deny when Verified Permissions is unavailable. Caching the last known decisions would improve availability, but could keep honouring revoked access. Keep the authorizer cache short. The API Gateway default of 300 seconds can keep revoked access alive for up to five minutes. A TTL of 0 or 30–60 seconds revokes faster, at the cost of more Verified Permissions calls. Protect the policies and the tags. Restrict who can create, update or delete policies, log every change with CloudTrail, and let only the tagging Lambda write sidecar files. S3 Versioning and Object Lock help here. Mind the ingestion window. There is a short gap between an upload and its sidecar. The SQS batching window (30 seconds by default) should fit the ingestion schedule. Guardrails are not a complete defence against prompt injection, so input length checks and query sanitization are still needed. Personal view What I like most in this pattern is that authorization becomes data instead of code. Adding a department takes a Cedar policy, a Cognito group and tagged documents, with no new infrastructure.
The AI service of Fitness Assistant already does retrieval-augmented generation with Amazon Bedrock and a vector index on OpenSearch Serverless (see Workshop 5.4.8 and 5.4.9). Its index is filled by scheduled jobs from shared sources such as PubMed, RSS feeds and web articles. Access is controlled per function with IAM: each Lambda role may invoke only the Bedrock models it needs, and the AI routes are throttled in API Gateway. The article’s pattern becomes useful as soon as private documents enter that index, for example a gym’s internal material that only its own trainers and members should see. A Cedar policy per gym and a gym_id metadata attribute would then fit better than one index per gym.
Conclusion The pattern combines three ideas: one shared knowledge base with metadata, Cedar policies that live outside the code and change at runtime, and two independent layers that both fail closed. It is a cost-effective way to give each department its own view of shared data, as long as the team remembers that the isolation is logical and protects the policies and tags as carefully as the documents themselves.
References AWS Architecture Blog: Secure multi-tenant RAG with Amazon Bedrock and Verified Permissions Amazon Verified Permissions documentation Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases documentation Cedar policy language

title: Frontend on Amazon S3
content:
The React (Vite) frontend is a static build, so it is served straight from an S3 website endpoint: http://fitness-assistant-frontend-dev-<account-id>.s3-website-ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com.
This is a temporary DEV setup because Amazon CloudFront was not usable in this account at the time. The bucket is made publicly readable (objects only) so the website endpoint can serve it. Once CloudFront is available, the bucket goes back to private behind an Origin Access Control and the site moves to HTTPS.
In every screenshot below, the red rectangles mark what to fill in or click for the sub-step written just above it.
Step 1 — Enable static website hosting 1.1 — Open the hosting settings. Open S3 → Buckets → fitness-assistant-frontend-dev-<account-id> → Properties, scroll to Static website hosting and click Edit.
1.2 — Fill in the hosting settings, then click Save changes at the bottom of the page:
Setting Value Static website hosting Enable Hosting type Host a static website Index document index.html Error document index.html Using index.html as the error document matters: the frontend uses React Router (createBrowserRouter), so refreshing /login, /register or /client/dashboard must return the app instead of an S3 404.
Step 2 — Allow public reads for this bucket only 2.1 — Turn off Block all public access. Open Permissions → Block public access (bucket settings) → Edit, untick Block all public access, click Save changes and confirm the warning.
2.2 — Add the bucket policy. Open Permissions → Bucket policy → Edit, paste a policy that allows nothing but s3:GetObject on this bucket’s objects, then click Save changes:
{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "PublicReadGetObject", "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": "*", "Action": "s3:GetObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::fitness-assistant-frontend-dev-<account-id>/*" } ] } The public can GET index.html and assets/*; it cannot PutObject, DeleteObject or ListBucket.
Step 3 — Upload the build 3.1 — Upload the files. Open the bucket’s Objects tab, click Upload, add the contents of frontend/web/dist/ (index.html and the assets/ folder), and click Upload. When it finishes, the status page reports Upload succeeded; click Close.
Verification: /login loads directly from the website endpoint, which confirms the React build, S3 static hosting and the SPA fallback. API calls from the page only work after the CORS step in 5.4.2.
Redeploy procedure Used every time a backend endpoint the frontend depends on changes — for example after the Chat ALB was created in 5.4.10. Run from frontend/web:
1. Build and check that the bundle points at the right backends.
npm run build Select-String -Path ".\dist\assets\*.js" -Pattern "<api-id>.execute-api.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com" Select-String -Path ".\dist\assets\*.js" -Pattern "fitness-assistant-dev-chat-alb" Both searches must return at least one match. In the screenshot, the first Select-String command and the matching part of the bundle are boxed.
2. Back up the current site before overwriting it.
$backup = "..\..\backups\frontend-s3-before-chat-20260922" New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path $backup | Out-Null aws s3 sync s3://fitness-assistant-frontend-dev-<account-id> $backup Get-ChildItem $backup The last command lists the backup: assets, bg-gym.jpg and index.html must all be there.
3. Publish the new build and stop browsers from caching the old index.html.
aws s3 sync .\dist s3://fitness-assistant-frontend-dev-<account-id> --delete aws s3 cp .\dist\index.html s3://fitness-assistant-frontend-dev-<account-id>/index.html ` --content-type "text/html" ` --cache-control "no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate" --delete removes old hashed bundles that are no longer in dist/; the backup makes that safe to roll back. Finish with a hard refresh (Ctrl + Shift + R) on the website endpoint.

The deployment was run from a Windows workstation with PowerShell. The tools below are needed to build the artifacts that the console steps upload.

Artifact Handler Purpose <service>-lambda.zip dist/lambda.handler HTTP API (API Gateway payload format 2.0) <service>-lambda.zip (same ZIP) dist/jobs-lambda.handler Scheduled jobs invoked by EventBridge Scheduler <service>-migrate-lambda.zip dist/migrate-lambda.handler Creates the service’s logical database if missing and runs prisma migrate deploy ai-worker-lambda.zip dist/worker-lambda.handler AI Worker consuming the SQS queue ZIPs larger than the direct-upload limit (for example the ~69 MiB migration artifacts) are uploaded to the deployments bucket fitness-assistant-deployments-dev-<account-id> first and attached to the function with Upload from → Amazon S3 location. Every artifact bundles the Prisma query engine for Linux (rhel-openssl-3.0.x), so the same ZIP built on Windows runs on Lambda.
Never put .env files, database passwords, JWT_SECRET, INTERNAL_SERVICE_SECRET, AWS credentials or payment provider keys into an artifact, an image or an S3 bucket. All of them are resolved at runtime from AWS Secrets Manager or the function configuration.

title: Main Request Flows
content:
Core API path Covers Auth, User, Fitness, Gym, Payment and the AI HTTP Lambda.
The browser loads the static frontend from the Amazon S3 website endpoint. The frontend calls Amazon API Gateway (fitness-assistant-dev-api) with Authorization: Bearer <JWT>. API Gateway matches the route (explicit routes for Auth, one root + greedy route pair per prefix for the other services) and invokes the service’s Lambda with payload format 2.0. /internal/*, /metrics and a catch-all /{proxy+} are never published. The Lambda verifies the JWT itself — the AI Lambda, for example, invokes the Auth Lambda to validate the token and rejects spoofed x-user-id / x-user-role headers — so there is no separate API Gateway authorizer. When a request needs another service, the Lambda invokes that service’s Lambda directly (lambda:InvokeFunction), authenticated with the shared INTERNAL_SERVICE_SECRET. Examples: User → Auth, Payment → Auth/User/Gym, Gym → Payment, Payment → AI to activate a paid personalized service. The Lambda reads/writes its own logical database on Aurora through the private app subnets, using credentials it resolves from Secrets Manager at runtime. The response returns through API Gateway to the browser. Chat path REST (conversation lists, history): the frontend calls API Gateway ANY /chat/{proxy+}, an HTTP proxy integration that forwards to http://<chat-alb>/chat/{proxy}. Real-time: the frontend opens Socket.IO directly to the Chat ALB (/socket.io/), HTTP on port 80 in DEV. The ALB forwards to the Fargate task on container port 3005; its listener answers /internal/* and /metrics with a fixed 404 so they never reach the container. Target-group stickiness keeps a client on the same task. The task runs in the private app subnets with no public IP; its security group only accepts port 3005 from the ALB’s security group. The Chat Service reads/writes fitness_assistant_chat on Aurora and invokes the Auth/User Lambdas through its ECS task role. DEV runs the ALB on HTTP only, like the S3 website endpoint, so there is no mixed-content problem yet. Moving both to HTTPS needs a domain and an ACM certificate (see 5.2.5).
Background path Scheduled jobs — 13 EventBridge Scheduler schedules (session settlement, auto-confirm, reschedule expiry, workout reminders, membership payouts, referral settlement, payment reconciliation, AI auto-accept and four nightly knowledge refreshes) invoke each service’s jobs Lambda with a {"job": "<name>"} payload. Each service has its own scheduler role that can invoke only its own jobs function. Long AI work — the AI HTTP Lambda queues plan generations on Amazon SQS (fitness-assistant-dev-ai-tasks); the AI Worker Lambda consumes them one at a time (batch size 1, up to 300 s each, 2 attempts before the dead-letter queue) and the frontend polls the job status. Knowledge ingestion — the AI Jobs Lambda fetches PubMed, RSS, web and local evidence nightly, embeds it with Cohere Embed Multilingual v3 (1024 dimensions) and writes it to OpenSearch Serverless. All AI functions call Amazon Bedrock through the NAT Gateway and reach OpenSearch Serverless privately through its VPC endpoint, signing requests with their IAM role (SigV4). Why three separate paths instead of one The Core API path is a textbook fit for Lambda: short-lived, stateless, scales to zero. The Chat path cannot use that model because Socket.IO needs a connection that survives many request/response cycles — hence ECS Fargate and an ALB for that one service. The Background path keeps slow or periodic work out of a user’s HTTP request: API Gateway gives an integration about 30 seconds, while a plan generation can take minutes and a knowledge crawl up to ten.

title: Prerequisite
content:
Before following the Deployment Guide, make sure the following are in place:
5.3.1 AWS account and permissions — the account, the IAM identity used in the console, and the one-time model access steps for Amazon Bedrock. 5.3.2 Deployment region — why everything runs in ap-southeast-1 (Singapore), including Bedrock and OpenSearch Serverless. 5.3.3 Local tools — what is needed on the workstation to build the Lambda artifacts and container images.

title: AWS Services and Selection Rationale
content: AWS Service Used for Why this, not an alternative AWS Lambda Auth, User, Fitness, Gym, Payment and AI — 12 long-lived functions (HTTP, jobs, AI Worker) plus migration functions Six of seven services are short request/response or scheduled work with no need to hold a connection open. Lambda scales to zero between requests — important for a DEV environment that is idle most of the time — and removes the instance-sizing problem this project had already hit with a self-hosted model on EC2 (see Week 8). Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate Chat Service (REST + Socket.IO), and the one-shot database migrator task The one service that cannot be Lambda: Socket.IO holds a persistent connection per session. Fargate runs the container without any server to patch; dev sizing is 0.5 vCPU / 1 GB. The same cluster runs the data-migration task on demand. Amazon ECR Images for the Chat Service and the database migrator Private registry in the same region, pulled by ECS through the task execution role — no Docker Hub credentials or rate limits. Amazon API Gateway (HTTP API) Single entry point for the six Lambda services and the Chat REST routes One routing layer with explicit route prefixes instead of one public endpoint per service; HTTP API is cheaper than REST API and supports per-route throttling, used to protect Bedrock cost. Elastic Load Balancing (ALB) Front door for the Chat Fargate task Handles Socket.IO/WebSocket upgrades, health checks on /health, stickiness and path rules that hide /internal/* and /metrics. Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL Serverless v2 One cluster, seven logical databases Managed PostgreSQL that matches the application’s Prisma schemas, scales capacity (ACU) automatically and can drop to a low floor (0.5 ACU during deployment, 0 when idle). One cluster instead of seven keeps cost and operations down while each service keeps its own database and secret. Amazon Bedrock Chat and vision (Nova Pro via the APAC inference profile) and embeddings (Cohere Embed Multilingual v3) Replaces the self-hosted Ollama model: no instance to size, no API key to manage (IAM only), billed per token, reached from the VPC like any AWS API. Amazon OpenSearch Serverless Vector search for RAG and knowledge retrieval (fitness-assistant-dev-ai-vectors) Replaces the self-hosted Qdrant container: k-NN (FAISS/HNSW, 1024 dimensions) without servers, private through a VPC endpoint, IAM + data-access-policy authorization, and the NextGen collection group scales between 0 and 2 OCU. Amazon SQS AI task queue and its dead-letter queue Decouples long AI generations from the 30-second HTTP path; the Worker processes one message at a time and failed messages land in the DLQ after two attempts. Replaces Redis/BullMQ, which would have needed a running cache cluster. Amazon EventBridge Scheduler 13 schedules for settlements, reminders, payouts, reconciliation and AI jobs Managed cron per job with retries, without a long-running process or setInterval inside an HTTP function. Amazon S3 Static frontend; private uploads (profile photos, PT documents, contracts); deployment artifacts; migration dumps Four buckets with four different access models — public-read website, private with presigned URLs, private artifacts for Lambda, private versioned dumps — so data never shares a bucket with public assets. AWS Secrets Manager Every database credential, the database URL for Chat, the shared internal secret No password in code, images or plain environment variables; each function holds only a secret ID and resolves it at runtime. AWS IAM One role per function or task, scoped to its own secret, queue, model and invoke targets Least privilege per service instead of a broad shared role — see 5.2.5. Amazon VPC, NAT Gateway, Internet Gateway, VPC endpoints Network isolation and controlled egress Lambda, Fargate and Aurora sit in private subnets; one NAT Gateway gives outbound access (Bedrock); interface endpoints keep Secrets Manager and OpenSearch traffic inside the VPC; DB subnets have no internet route at all. Amazon CloudWatch Logs Logs for every Lambda, the Chat task and the migrator Default destination for both compute types; used for troubleshooting during deployment. Alarms are covered in 5.2.6. Amazon CloudFront HTTPS front door for the web app and Chat One distribution serves the frontend over HTTPS and routes /socket.io/* to the Chat ALB, so the browser never makes a mixed-content request. It reaches the frontend bucket through Origin Access Control. Amazon CloudWatch Alarms, Amazon SNS, AWS Budgets, AWS X-Ray Alerting, notification, cost control and tracing 12 alarms (Lambda errors for the six API services, API Gateway 5xx, Aurora CPU and capacity, NAT Gateway health) notify an SNS topic with a confirmed e-mail subscription; a monthly budget alerts on cost; active tracing is on the six API Lambdas. GitHub Actions with AWS CloudFormation CI and gated CD PR validation plus five gated workflows deploy Lambda code, the Chat image and the API Gateway stack (5.4.12, 5.4.13). Optional components (not deployed in DEV) Amazon Route 53 — the site is reached on its CloudFront domain name; a custom domain would add Route 53 and an ACM certificate. AWS WAF — optional; CloudFront is in place, so a web ACL can be attached when needed. Amazon RDS Proxy — optional; the Lambda functions connect to Aurora directly. Amazon ElastiCache — not needed: queues moved to SQS and the Chat Service runs a single task. It becomes necessary only to share Socket.IO state across several Chat tasks.

A schedule that never invokes usually means its role lacks lambda:InvokeFunction on that exact function ARN.
SQS worker Check Expected Queue fitness-assistant-dev-ai-tasks Visibility timeout 600 s (longer than the Worker’s 300 s timeout), DLQ fitness-assistant-dev-ai-tasks-dlq, maximum receives 2 Trigger on fitness-assistant-dev-ai-worker SQS trigger Enabled, batch size 1, Report batch item failures on After a plan generation (POST /plans/workout/generate then GET /plans/job/{id}) The job finishes, the queue drains, the DLQ stays at 0 messages A message in the DLQ means a job failed twice: read the Worker log for that message before re-driving it.

Log message Meaning PrismaClientInitializationError, P1001, Can't reach database Network path to Aurora (subnets, security groups) or a stale credential AccessDeniedException The role is missing a specific permission (secret, invoke, Bedrock, aoss:APIAccessAll, SQS) 403 from OpenSearch IAM permission or data access policy missing — both layers are required Task timed out after … Work that should be queued (AI) or a function timeout set too low CloudWatch alarms already watch the API Lambdas, API Gateway 5xx, Aurora and the NAT Gateway (see 5.5.5). title: Deployment Guide
content:
The services were deployed one at a time, in dependency order: each service only goes live after every service it calls is already running. The pages below follow that order and keep the screenshots captured during the real deployment.
5.4.1 Shared network infrastructure — Internet Gateway, public subnets, NAT Gateway and route tables. 5.4.2 Auth Service and API Gateway — the first Lambda, the HTTP API and its explicit public routes. 5.4.3 Frontend on Amazon S3 — static website hosting and the redeploy procedure. 5.4.4 User Service — Lambda-to-Lambda calls, private S3 uploads and the first scheduled jobs. 5.4.5 Fitness Service — migration from an S3 artifact and two reminder schedules. 5.4.6 Gym Service — QR check-in secret and payout/referral jobs. 5.4.7 Payment Service — VNPAY configuration, reconciliation and the Gym ↔ Payment wiring. 5.4.8 AI Service — database, queue and Bedrock — HTTP Lambda, SQS worker and jobs Lambda on Nova Pro / Cohere. 5.4.9 AI Service — vector search, scheduling and API — OpenSearch Serverless, knowledge ingestion, routes and rate limits. 5.4.10 Chat Service on ECS Fargate — container image, task definition, ALB and Socket.IO. 5.4.11 Data migration to Aurora — restoring 7 local databases with a one-shot Fargate task. 5.4.12 CI/CD pipeline activation — GitHub Actions PR validation via OIDC, and real OIDC → STS federation evidence. 5.4.13 CD pipeline activation — gate-by-gate activation of the actual deploy-to-AWS workflows, starting with the GitHub Environment human-approval gates. 5.4.14 CloudFront, Aurora reader and CloudWatch alarm — the HTTPS front door, the database reader and an alarm with an e-mail notification, each with the creation form. 5.4.15 Infrastructure as code with CloudFormation — the stacks, the template files to download and how to deploy one. 5.4.16 GitHub Actions workflows — the six workflows with the files to download, the approval gates and how to run them. The pattern every Lambda-based service follows Once the shared network exists, each service (Auth, User, Fitness, Gym, Payment, AI) is deployed with the same sequence. The service pages only call out what differs.
# Step Detail 1 Database secret Secrets Manager → Other type of secret with username, password, host, port, database = fitness_assistant_<service>, named fitness-assistant/dev/<service>-database. Rotation off for DEV. 2 Migration role IAM role trusted by Lambda with AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole + AWSLambdaVPCAccessExecutionRole, plus an inline policy allowing secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on only that service’s secret ARN. 3 Migration Lambda fitness-assistant-dev-<service>-migrate, Node.js 22.x, x86_64, 1024 MB, handler dist/migrate-lambda.handler, env DATABASE_SECRET_ID, attached to both private app subnets and fitness-assistant-dev-lambda-sg. Invoked once with {}: it creates the logical database if missing and runs prisma migrate deploy, refusing to run against any other database name. 4 Runtime role Same two managed policies, plus inline policies for the service’s own secret and lambda:InvokeFunction on the exact functions it calls. 5 HTTP Lambda fitness-assistant-dev-<service>, 1024 MB, 30 s timeout, handler dist/lambda.handler, same VPC settings. 6 API Gateway Lambda integration (payload format 2.0) and explicit route prefixes. /internal/* and ANY /{proxy+} are never created. 7 Jobs Lambda fitness-assistant-dev-<service>-jobs, same ZIP, handler dist/jobs-lambda.handler, 1 minute timeout. 8 Scheduler A dedicated role trusted by scheduler.amazonaws.com that can only invoke that jobs Lambda, and one EventBridge schedule per job with a {"job": "<name>"} payload. All screenshots on these pages come from the deployment runbook. Screens that originally showed a secret value (database master password, INTERNAL_SERVICE_SECRET, CHECKIN_TOKEN_SECRET) were redacted at pixel level before being included — the black boxes are intentional.
