title: User Service
content:
After login, the frontend immediately needs the user profile, onboarding and body profile, so the User Service came next. It introduced three patterns reused by later services: calling another Lambda directly instead of through the public API, private S3 uploads with presigned URLs, and scheduled jobs on EventBridge Scheduler.
Item Value Logical database fitness_assistant_user Secret fitness-assistant/dev/user-database Functions fitness-assistant-dev-user (HTTP), fitness-assistant-dev-user-jobs (jobs) Uploads bucket fitness-assistant-uploads-dev-<account-id> (private) In every screenshot below, the red rectangles mark what to fill in or click for the sub-step written just above it. Where the runbook has no screenshot for an action, the text says so.
Step 1 — Create the database secret 1.1 — Enter the connection details. Open Secrets Manager → Store a new secret, choose Other type of secret, and add the key/value rows: username, password (the Aurora master password, taken directly from Secrets Manager — redacted in the screenshot), host (the Aurora cluster endpoint), port = 5432 and database = fitness_assistant_user. Keep the default encryption key and click Next.
1.2 — Name the secret. On the next page enter the name fitness-assistant/dev/user-database, leave rotation off and store the secret. The runbook has no screenshot of these last pages.
Step 2 — Create the execution role 2.1 — Create the role. Open IAM → Roles → Create role, choose the trusted entity AWS service → Lambda, and attach only the managed policies AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole and AWSLambdaVPCAccessExecutionRole — not AdministratorAccess, AmazonRDSFullAccess, SecretsManagerReadWrite or AmazonS3FullAccess. On the last page enter the role name fitness-assistant-dev-user-lambda-role, check the two policies and click Create role.
Step 3 — Allow the role to read only its own secret 3.1 — Open the JSON editor. In the role, open Permissions → Add permissions → Create inline policy, switch to the JSON tab and paste the policy below. Replace SECRET_ARN with the full ARN copied from the secret’s page (the placeholder is boxed). "Resource": "*" is not acceptable. Then click Next.
{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["secretsmanager:GetSecretValue", "secretsmanager:DescribeSecret"], "Resource": "SECRET_ARN" } ] } 3.2 — Name the policy. Enter the policy name fitness-assistant-dev-user-read-database-secret and click Create policy.
3.3 — Check the role. The role now shows two managed policies and one inline policy.
The schema was then migrated with a temporary fitness-assistant-dev-user-migrate Lambda using the common pattern. The outbound network needed by the User Lambda was added at this point too — see 5.4.1.
Step 4 — Create the User Lambda 4.1 — Create the function. Open Lambda → Create function, choose Author from scratch, enter the name fitness-assistant-dev-user, runtime Node.js 22.x, architecture x86_64, and under Additional settings → Custom execution role pick the existing role fitness-assistant-dev-user-lambda-role. Then click Create function.
4.2 — Configure the function. Set the values below. The runbook has no screenshot for the VPC and memory settings; they follow the same screens as in 5.4.2, steps 1.1 and 1.3.
Setting Value VPC fitness-assistant-dev-vpc, subnets private-app-a + private-app-b, SG fitness-assistant-dev-lambda-sg Memory / timeout 1024 MB / 30 s DATABASE_SECRET_ID fitness-assistant/dev/user-database NODE_ENV production AUTH_SERVICE_URL the API Gateway invoke URL USER_UPLOAD_BUCKET fitness-assistant-uploads-dev-<account-id> INTERNAL_SERVICE_SECRET the same value as the Auth Lambda (one shared secret, never a new one) 4.3 — Add the environment variables. In Configuration → Environment variables → Edit, add the five variables from the table and click Save. The list then looks like the screenshot (the secret value is redacted).
Variables for services not deployed yet (GYM_SERVICE_URL, PAYMENT_SERVICE_URL, AI_SERVICE_URL, CHAT_SERVICE_URL) are left out until those services exist.
Step 5 — Allow profile-photo uploads to one S3 prefix Add an inline policy that grants s3:PutObject on arn:aws:s3:::fitness-assistant-uploads-dev-<account-id>/profile-photos/* only — not AmazonS3FullAccess.
5.1 — Write the policy. In the role, open Add permissions → Create inline policy → JSON and enter a statement with Action: s3:PutObject and the profile-photos/* resource, then click Next.
5.2 — Name the policy. Enter the policy name fitness-assistant-dev-user-profile-upload and click Create policy. The summary shows the single S3 write permission limited to profile-photos/*.
Step 6 — Upload the code 6.1 — Upload the ZIP. In the function, open Code → Upload from → .zip file, click Choose file, select backend/services/user-service/artifacts/user-lambda.zip and click Update.
6.2 — Set the handler. Open Runtime settings → Edit and set Handler to dist/lambda.handler. The runbook has no screenshot for the HTTP function; the same screen for the jobs function is shown in step 11.5.
Step 7 — Add the API Gateway integration 7.1 — Create the integration. Open API Gateway → fitness-assistant-dev-api → Integrations → Manage integrations → Create. Choose Integration type: Lambda function, region ap-southeast-1, function fitness-assistant-dev-user, timeout 30000, payload format version 2.0, keep Grant API Gateway permission to invoke your Lambda function switched on (API Gateway adds the invoke permission on the function), and click Create.
7.2 — Check the list. The API now has the Auth integrations and the new User integration fitness-assistant-dev-user.
Step 8 — Create greedy routes per prefix The User Service exposes more than 100 endpoints, so instead of creating each route by hand, one greedy route is created per public prefix and attached to the User integration:
GET /health ANY /profile/{proxy+} ANY /inbody/{proxy+} ANY /pt-applications/{proxy+} ANY /contracts/{proxy+} ANY /notifications/{proxy+} ANY /sessions/{proxy+} ANY /availability/{proxy+} ANY /admin/{proxy+} ANY /locations/{proxy+} ANY /pt/{proxy+} ANY /me/{proxy+} 8.1 — Create one route per line. Open Routes → Create, choose the method (ANY, or GET for /health), enter the path, e.g. /me/{proxy+}, and click Create. Repeat for each line. The green banner at the top of the screenshot confirms the previous route was created.
8.2 — Attach the integration. Open Integrations → Attach integrations to routes and attach fitness-assistant-dev-user to every new route. The runbook has no screenshot of this screen.
ANY /{proxy+} and ANY /internal/{proxy+} are never created — /internal/* is service-to-service only. /webhooks/dropbox-sign is also skipped because it is disabled while REQUIRE_CONTRACT_ESIGN=false.
A route that exists but has no integration attached returns {"message":"Not Found"}. After creating routes, always open Integrations → Attach integrations to routes and check that every route has a target.
Step 9 — Call Auth directly with Lambda Invoke Some User flows call /auth/internal/*, which is intentionally not public. Instead of exposing it, the User Lambda invokes the Auth Lambda directly.
9.1 — Write the policy. In the role, open Add permissions → Create inline policy → JSON, enter the policy below and click Next:
{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "InvokeAuthLambda", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "lambda:InvokeFunction", "Resource": "arn:aws:lambda:ap-southeast-1:<account-id>:function:fitness-assistant-dev-auth" } ] } 9.2 — Name the policy. Enter the policy name fitness-assistant-dev-user-invoke-auth and click Create policy.
9.3 — Add AUTH_LAMBDA_NAME. In the User Lambda, open Configuration → Environment variables → Edit, click Add environment variable, enter the key AUTH_LAMBDA_NAME and the value fitness-assistant-dev-auth (keeping AUTH_SERVICE_URL for now) and click Save.
9.4 — Check the result. The function now has six variables, including AUTH_LAMBDA_NAME (the secret value is redacted).
Step 10 — Final S3 permissions and CORS for presigned uploads Profile photos, PT application documents and contract PDFs all live in the private uploads bucket.
10.1 — Replace the upload policy. Edit the inline policy fitness-assistant-dev-user-profile-upload so it has three statements, each limited to one prefix. The runbook has no screenshot of this edit.
{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "UserProfilePhotos", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["s3:PutObject", "s3:GetObject", "s3:DeleteObject"], "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::fitness-assistant-uploads-dev-<account-id>/profile-photos/*" }, { "Sid": "PTApplicationDocuments", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["s3:PutObject", "s3:GetObject", "s3:DeleteObject"], "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::fitness-assistant-uploads-dev-<account-id>/pt-applications/*" }, { "Sid": "ContractDocuments", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["s3:PutObject", "s3:GetObject", "s3:DeleteObject"], "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::fitness-assistant-uploads-dev-<account-id>/contracts/*" } ] } No s3:*, no s3:ListBucket.
10.2 — Add the CORS rule. The browser uploads directly to S3 with a presigned URL, so the uploads bucket needs a CORS rule while staying private. Open the bucket’s Permissions → Cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) → Edit, paste the JSON below and click Save changes.
[ { "AllowedOrigins": ["http://fitness-assistant-frontend-dev-<account-id>.s3-website-ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com"], "AllowedMethods": ["PUT", "GET", "HEAD"], "AllowedHeaders": ["content-type", "x-amz-*"], "ExposeHeaders": ["ETag"], "MaxAgeSeconds": 300 } ] Step 11 — Create the jobs Lambda Background jobs run in a separate function so the HTTP Lambda never runs timers.
11.1 — Create the function. Open Lambda → Create function → Author from scratch, enter the name fitness-assistant-dev-user-jobs, runtime Node.js 22.x, the existing role fitness-assistant-dev-user-lambda-role, and click Create function.
11.2 — Attach the VPC. In Configuration → VPC → Edit, select the VPC, both private app subnets and fitness-assistant-dev-lambda-sg, then click Save.
11.3 — Set memory and timeout. In Configuration → General configuration → Edit, set Memory to 1024 MB and Timeout to 1 min 0 sec, then click Save.
11.4 — Upload the code. Open Code → Upload from → .zip file, choose the same user-lambda.zip and click Update.
11.5 — Set the handler. Open Runtime settings → Edit, set Handler to dist/jobs-lambda.handler (architecture stays x86_64) and click Save.
11.6 — Add the environment variables: DATABASE_SECRET_ID, NODE_ENV, AUTH_LAMBDA_NAME, USER_UPLOAD_BUCKET, REQUIRE_CONTRACT_ESIGN=false and the shared INTERNAL_SERVICE_SECRET, in Configuration → Environment variables → Edit → Save.
Step 12 — Create the scheduler role 12.1 — Create the role with a custom trust policy. Open IAM → Roles → Create role, choose the trusted entity type Custom trust policy and paste the policy below for EventBridge Scheduler:
{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "Service": "scheduler.amazonaws.com" }, "Action": "sts:AssumeRole" } ] } Continue without attaching a managed policy (the permission is added as an inline policy in the next sub-step), name the role fitness-assistant-dev-user-jobs-scheduler-role and create it. The runbook has no screenshot of these last pages.
12.2 — Write the inline policy. In the new role, open Add permissions → Create inline policy → JSON and allow lambda:InvokeFunction on fitness-assistant-dev-user-jobs only, then click Next. The scheduler never reuses a Lambda execution role and never gets lambda:*.
12.3 — Name the policy. Enter the policy name fitness-assistant-dev-invoke-user-jobs and click Create policy.
Step 13 — Create the three schedules One schedule per job, each sending {"job": "<name>"} to fitness-assistant-dev-user-jobs:
Schedule Rate Payload fitness-assistant-dev-user-session-settlement rate(5 minutes) {"job": "session-settlement"} fitness-assistant-dev-user-session-auto-confirm rate(10 minutes) {"job": "session-auto-confirm"} fitness-assistant-dev-user-reschedule-expiry rate(10 minutes) {"job": "reschedule-expiry"} The screenshots follow the first schedule, session-settlement.
13.1 — Start the wizard. Open Amazon EventBridge → Scheduler → Schedules and click Create schedule.
13.2 — Name the schedule. Enter the schedule name fitness-assistant-dev-user-session-settlement and keep the default schedule group.
13.3 — Set the pattern. Choose Recurring schedule, time zone (UTC+07:00) Asia/Saigon, Rate-based schedule, rate 5 minutes, and Flexible time window Off.
13.4 — Leave the timeframe empty (the schedule runs indefinitely) and click Next.
13.5 — Choose the target. With Templated targets selected, pick AWS Lambda → Invoke.
13.6 — Set the function and payload. Choose the Lambda function fitness-assistant-dev-user-jobs, enter the payload {"job": "session-settlement"} and click Next.
13.7 — Settings. Keep: schedule state Enable, action after completion NONE, Retry on with maximum age of event 5 minutes and 2 retry attempts, dead-letter queue None (DEV), AWS-owned encryption key, and execution role Use existing role → fitness-assistant-dev-user-jobs-scheduler-role (not Create new role). Click Next, then Create schedule on the review page.
13.8 — Check the schedule. The new schedule is Enabled with rate (5 minutes) in the Asia/Saigon time zone.
13.9 — Repeat for the other two. Create the second schedule the same way with the name fitness-assistant-dev-user-session-auto-confirm and rate(10 minutes), then the third, fitness-assistant-dev-user-reschedule-expiry, with rate(10 minutes), each with its own payload from the table. The runbook shows only the second schedule’s first page; the third has no screenshot.

content:
Week 4 Objectives: Complete self-study of Module 3: Optimizing the system Deepen understanding across the Operate, Security, and Reliability pillars of the AWS Well-Architected Framework Turn the module’s lessons into concrete requirements for the Fitness Assistant’s AWS design Start the AWS deployment: shared network, Aurora, the Auth service behind API Gateway, the frontend on S3 and the User service Tasks to be carried out this week: Task Start Date Completion Date Reference Materials Study and complete Module 3: Optimizing the system 24-8-2026 29-8-2026 Operate: 22: https://000022.awsstudygroup.com/ 27: https://000027.awsstudygroup.com/ 29: https://000029.awsstudygroup.com/ 31: https://000031.awsstudygroup.com/ 58: https://000058.awsstudygroup.com/ Security: 18: https://000018.awsstudygroup.com/ 26: https://000026.awsstudygroup.com/ 30: https://000030.awsstudygroup.com/ 33: https://000033.awsstudygroup.com/ 44: https://000044.awsstudygroup.com/ Reliability: 13: https://000013.awsstudygroup.com/ 19: https://000019.awsstudygroup.com/ 20: https://000020.awsstudygroup.com/ Deploy the shared network (VPC, subnets, NAT Gateway, security groups), Aurora PostgreSQL Serverless v2, the Auth service on Lambda behind API Gateway, and the frontend on S3 26-8-2026 27-8-2026 5.4.1 Shared network 5.4.2 Auth Service and API Gateway 5.4.3 Frontend on S3 Deploy the User service (database, Lambda functions and schedules) 27-8-2026 27-8-2026 5.4.4 User Service Week 4 Achievements: Overview:
During this week, I focused on system optimization (Module 3) by exploring three crucial pillars: Operations, Security, and Reliability. Besides the labs, I used each pillar as a checklist for the Fitness Assistant: what its AWS design must guarantee for access control, private networking, secrets, backups and monitoring, and what it would still cost while nobody is using it. The deployment itself also started this week: the shared network, Aurora, the Auth service behind API Gateway and the frontend on S3 on 26–27 August, then the User service on 27 August.
Learned theory:
Operations (Operate): Mastered programmatic cost optimization for EC2 instances using AWS Lambda, resource management through Tagging and Resource Groups, system monitoring with Amazon CloudWatch and visualization with Grafana, and centralized server management utilizing AWS Systems Manager.
Security: Deepened my understanding of access restrictions using IAM Permission Boundaries and condition keys. Explored threat detection with AWS Security Hub, web traffic filtering with AWS WAF, and data encryption strategies at rest (AWS KMS).
Reliability: Studied enterprise-grade network interconnectivity using VPC Peering and AWS Transit Gateway, alongside automated data retention utilizing AWS Backup.
Hands-on labs:
Operate:
Configured Lambda function to automatically start/stop EC2 instances on schedule (reduce costs when dev environment not in use) Set up CloudWatch dashboards for the lab resources Practised resource tagging and Resource Groups to find resources by environment and service Tested Systems Manager Session Manager for EC2 access without SSH keys Security:
Implemented IAM Permission Boundaries to limit developer user permissions Configured Security Groups with least privilege principle (only open necessary ports) Researched AWS WAF rules to protect API endpoints from common attacks (SQL injection, XSS) Studied KMS encryption at rest for databases and S3 buckets Reliability:
Designed a backup plan with AWS Backup (daily snapshots, 7-day retention) Researched multi-AZ deployment for production environment (ensuring high availability) Evaluated VPC Peering vs Transit Gateway for future microservices expansion Applied to Fitness Assistant:
Cost: The lab saves money by stopping idle EC2 instances on a schedule. For this project I took the idea one step further: use compute that costs nothing while idle (Lambda for the HTTP services and jobs, Aurora Serverless v2 with a low capacity floor), so there is nothing to stop. What still costs money when idle (NAT Gateway, load balancer, VPC endpoints) became the “sleep mode” in the budget. Security requirements (applied from the Auth service onward): one IAM role per function, scoped to its own secret, queue and model; database credentials in Secrets Manager, one secret per service database; compute and database only in private subnets; security groups that reference each other instead of IP ranges. Reliability requirements: private subnets in two Availability Zones, Aurora automated backups, load-balancer health checks that replace an unhealthy container, and a dead-letter queue so a failing background job is not retried forever. Monitoring plan: CloudWatch Logs for every function and task from day one, then alarms on the few signals that matter: function errors and throttles, dead-letter queue depth, database capacity and the chat target’s health. Difficulties Encountered: IAM Permission Boundaries complexity: The concept of Permission Boundaries (maximum permission limits) vs inline policies was quite confusing initially. Took considerable time to understand real-world use cases.
Cost optimization trade-offs: When researching Lambda-based EC2 scheduling, realized there are trade-offs between cost savings and developer convenience. Stopping dev instances might cause inconvenience if developers need to work outside regular hours.
Monitoring overhead: Setting up comprehensive monitoring requires upfront effort (define metrics, create dashboards, configure alarms). Need to balance between “monitor everything” vs “monitor what matters”.
How It Was Resolved: Permission Boundaries: Drew diagrams to visualize relationships between identity-based policies, permission boundaries, and resource-based policies. Practiced with concrete examples in labs.
Cost optimization: Avoided the trade-off instead of tuning a schedule: services that scale to zero need no stop/start at all, and the few fixed-cost resources are paused on purpose between test sessions (see 5.7 Clean-up).
Monitoring strategy: Adopted “start simple, iterate” approach: logs first (Lambda functions and ECS tasks send them to CloudWatch with almost no setup), then a short list of alarms on the signals above. The EC2 host metrics used in the lab (CPU, memory, disk) do not apply, because a serverless design has no host to watch.
AWS Skills / Services Learned: Services:
AWS Lambda (event-driven automation) Amazon CloudWatch (logs, metrics, alarms) AWS Systems Manager (Session Manager, Patch Manager) AWS IAM (Permission Boundaries, condition keys) AWS Security Hub (security posture management) AWS WAF (web application firewall) AWS KMS (encryption key management) AWS Backup (automated backup orchestration) VPC Peering and AWS Transit Gateway (network connectivity) Skills:
Cost optimization strategies for cloud infrastructure Security best practices (least privilege, defense in depth) Centralized monitoring and observability Infrastructure automation with Lambda Backup and disaster recovery planning Connection to Fitness Assistant Architecture: Module 3 insights directly applicable:
Operate: CloudWatch Logs for every Lambda function and the chat task; alarms on errors, throttles, dead-letter queue depth and database capacity (planned) Security: least-privilege role per function, credentials in Secrets Manager, KMS encryption for user data; AWS WAF cannot be attached to an API Gateway HTTP API directly, so it is planned together with CloudFront Reliability: private subnets in two AZs, Aurora automated backups, health checks with automatic task replacement, dead-letter queue for failed jobs Related Workshop Sections: 5.2.5 Security and IAM - Network isolation, least-privilege roles and secrets 5.2.6 Scalability and Operations - Operations, logging and monitoring

title: Fitness Service
content:
The Fitness Service (exercises, workouts, nutrition, training cycles, coaching data) was the first service whose artifacts were too large for a direct console upload, so its code is attached from the deployments bucket.
Item Value Logical database fitness_assistant_fitness (48 Prisma migrations) Secret fitness-assistant/dev/fitness-database Functions fitness-assistant-dev-fitness, fitness-assistant-dev-fitness-jobs, temporary fitness-assistant-dev-fitness-migrate Calls Auth and User Lambdas (direct invoke) In every screenshot below, the red rectangles mark what to fill in or click for the sub-step written just above it. Where the runbook has no screenshot for an action, the text says so.
Step 1 — Upload the migration artifact to the deployments bucket 1.1 — Open the upload page. Open S3 → fitness-assistant-deployments-dev-<account-id> → Upload and click Add files. The destination shown is the deployments bucket.
1.2 — Select and upload the file. Choose backend/services/fitness-service/artifacts/fitness-migrate-lambda.zip (70.8 MB) and click Upload. The object stays private. The status page shows the progress.
1.3 — Wait for success. When the banner Upload succeeded appears and the file shows Succeeded, click Close.
Step 2 — Create the migration role 2.1 — Create the role. Open IAM → Roles → Create role, choose AWS service → Lambda (the screen is the same as in step 5.1) and click Next. The runbook has no screenshot of this screen for the migration role.
2.2 — Attach the managed policies. Select AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole and AWSLambdaVPCAccessExecutionRole. The review page lists both.
2.3 — Name the role. Enter the role name fitness-assistant-dev-fitness-migrate-role and click Create role.
2.4 — Add an inline policy. In the new role, open Permissions → Add permissions → Create inline policy.
2.5 — Paste the JSON. Switch to the JSON tab and paste the policy below — read access to this service’s secret only. Then click Next.
{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["secretsmanager:GetSecretValue", "secretsmanager:DescribeSecret"], "Resource": "arn:aws:secretsmanager:ap-southeast-1:<account-id>:secret:fitness-assistant/dev/fitness-database*" } ] } 2.6 — Name the policy. Enter the policy name fitness-assistant-dev-fitness-migration-secret and click Create policy.
Step 3 — Create the migration Lambda and run the migrations 3.1 — Create the function. Open Lambda → Create function, choose Author from scratch, enter the name fitness-assistant-dev-fitness-migrate, runtime Node.js 22.x, and under Additional settings → Custom execution role pick the existing role fitness-assistant-dev-fitness-migrate-role. Then click Create function.
The remaining settings for this function:
Setting Value Memory / timeout 1024 MB / 15 minutes (48 migrations) Handler dist/migrate-lambda.handler DATABASE_SECRET_ID fitness-assistant/dev/fitness-database (no need to set AWS_REGION — Lambda provides it) VPC private-app-a + private-app-b, fitness-assistant-dev-lambda-sg 3.2 — Set memory and timeout. In Configuration → General configuration → Edit, set Memory 1024 MB and Timeout 15 min 0 sec, then click Save.
3.3 — Set the handler. In Runtime settings → Edit, set Handler to dist/migrate-lambda.handler, keep architecture x86_64 and click Save.
3.4 — Add the secret name. In Configuration → Environment variables → Edit, add DATABASE_SECRET_ID = fitness-assistant/dev/fitness-database and click Save.
3.5 — Attach the VPC. In Configuration → VPC → Edit, select the VPC, both private app subnets and fitness-assistant-dev-lambda-sg, then click Save.
3.6 — Open the code update menu. On the Code tab, click Update and choose Update from a file in Amazon S3. (The ZIP is too large for a direct upload.)
3.7 — Point at the S3 object. Keep Copy mode (default), paste the object’s S3 URI s3://fitness-assistant-deployments-dev-<account-id>/fitness-migrate-lambda.zip into Amazon S3 link, and click Update.
3.8 — Check the code properties. The function now shows a 70.8 MB package with code storage mode Copy (default).
Before invoking, re-check VPC, handler, environment and role once more, then invoke the function with {}. After all 48 migrations were applied, the temporary migration Lambda was deleted — the green “Successfully deleted function: fitness-assistant-dev-fitness-migrate” banner is visible in the next screenshots.
Step 4 — Upload the main artifact 4.1 — Upload fitness-lambda.zip. Repeat step 1 for fitness-lambda.zip (53.3 MB) in the same deployments bucket. When the upload finishes, check the Succeeded status and click Close.
Step 5 — Create the runtime role 5.1 — Choose the trusted entity. Open IAM → Roles → Create role, choose AWS service, use case Lambda, and click Next.
5.2 — Attach the managed policies. Select the same two managed policies, AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole and AWSLambdaVPCAccessExecutionRole.
5.3 — Name the role. Enter the role name fitness-assistant-dev-fitness-lambda-role and click Create role. The page also shows the trust policy for lambda.amazonaws.com.
5.4 — Add the first inline policy. In the role, open Permissions → Add permissions → Create inline policy.
5.5 — Secret policy. On the JSON tab paste the same secret statement as in step 2.5, click Next, name it fitness-assistant-dev-fitness-database-secret and click Create policy.
5.6 — Invoke policy. Create a second inline policy named fitness-assistant-dev-fitness-service-invoke with this JSON. The runbook has no screenshot of it.
{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "lambda:InvokeFunction", "Resource": [ "arn:aws:lambda:ap-southeast-1:<account-id>:function:fitness-assistant-dev-auth", "arn:aws:lambda:ap-southeast-1:<account-id>:function:fitness-assistant-dev-user" ] } ] } No S3, SQS, Bedrock or Redis permissions are added — the Fitness Service does not use them in AWS.
Step 6 — Create the Fitness Lambda 6.1 — Create the function. Open Lambda → Create function → Author from scratch, enter the name fitness-assistant-dev-fitness, runtime Node.js 22.x, x86_64, the custom execution role fitness-assistant-dev-fitness-lambda-role, and click Create function.
6.2 — Attach the code. Set memory to 1024 MB and timeout to 30 s, then on Code → Update → Update from a file in Amazon S3 use s3://fitness-assistant-deployments-dev-<account-id>/fitness-lambda.zip in Copy mode, exactly as in steps 3.6–3.7. The runbook has no screenshot of these screens for this function.
6.3 — Set the handler. In Runtime settings → Edit, set Handler to dist/lambda.handler and click Save.
6.4 — Add the environment variables listed below in Configuration → Environment variables → Edit, click Add environment variable for each one, then Save.
Variable Value NODE_ENV production DATABASE_SECRET_ID fitness-assistant/dev/fitness-database AUTH_LAMBDA_NAME fitness-assistant-dev-auth USER_LAMBDA_NAME fitness-assistant-dev-user FITNESS_DISABLE_REDIS true INTERNAL_SERVICE_SECRET the shared value used by Auth/User AI_SERVICE_URL, CHAT_SERVICE_URL, REDIS_HOST, REDIS_PORT and PEXELS_API_KEY are left unset because those dependencies are not deployed or not enabled.
6.5 — Attach the VPC. In Configuration → VPC → Edit, select the VPC, both private app subnets and fitness-assistant-dev-lambda-sg, then click Save.
Step 7 — Connect the Fitness Lambda to API Gateway 7.1 — Create the integration. Open API Gateway → fitness-assistant-dev-api → Integrations → Manage integrations → Create. Choose Lambda function, region ap-southeast-1, function fitness-assistant-dev-fitness, payload format version 2.0, keep Grant API Gateway permission to invoke your Lambda function on, and click Create.
7.2 — Create the routes. For each public prefix, create both the root route and the greedy route so that /workouts and /workouts/... both resolve (Routes → Create, method ANY). The runbook has no screenshot of route creation for this service; the procedure is the one shown in 5.4.4, step 8.
ANY /exercises ANY /exercises/{proxy+} ANY /workouts ANY /workouts/{proxy+} ANY /nutrition ANY /nutrition/{proxy+} ANY /stats ANY /stats/{proxy+} ANY /food ANY /food/{proxy+} ANY /training-cycles ANY /training-cycles/{proxy+} ANY /coach ANY /coach/{proxy+} ANY /equipment ANY /equipment/{proxy+} ANY /imports ANY /imports/{proxy+} ANY /exports ANY /exports/{proxy+} ANY /templates ANY /templates/{proxy+} /internal, /internal/{proxy+} and /{proxy+} are not created, and the existing global GET /health (owned by Auth) is not duplicated.
7.3 — Check the attachment. Open Integrations → Attach integrations to routes. Select a new route such as ANY /exercises/{proxy+}: its details show the Lambda function fitness-assistant-dev-fitness.
Step 8 — Create the jobs Lambda fitness-assistant-dev-fitness-jobs: same role, same fitness-lambda.zip from S3, handler dist/jobs-lambda.handler, 1024 MB, 1 minute, same VPC and the same environment variables as the HTTP Lambda. It runs two jobs: workout-upcoming-reminder and workout-unfinished-reminder.
8.1 — Create the function. Open Lambda → Create function → Author from scratch, enter the name fitness-assistant-dev-fitness-jobs, runtime Node.js 22.x, the custom execution role fitness-assistant-dev-fitness-lambda-role, and click Create function.
8.2 — Attach the VPC. In Configuration → VPC → Edit, select the VPC, both private app subnets and the Lambda security group, then click Save.
8.3 — Add the environment variables (the same six as the HTTP Lambda) in Configuration → Environment variables → Edit → Save. The list afterwards looks like this (secret redacted). The runbook has no screenshot for the memory, timeout, handler and code settings of this function; they follow steps 3.2, 3.3, 3.6 and 3.7 with the values above.
Step 9 — Create the scheduler role 9.1 — Choose the custom trust policy. Open IAM → Roles → Create role, choose Custom trust policy and paste the trust policy for scheduler.amazonaws.com, then continue without a managed policy.
9.2 — Name the role. Enter the role name fitness-assistant-dev-fitness-jobs-scheduler-role and click Create role.
9.3 — Add the inline policy. In the role, open Add permissions → Create inline policy → JSON and allow lambda:InvokeFunction on the jobs Lambda only, then click Next.
9.4 — Name the policy. Enter the policy name fitness-assistant-dev-invoke-fitness-jobs and click Create policy.
Step 10 — Create the two reminder schedules Schedule Rate Payload What it does fitness-assistant-dev-workout-upcoming-reminder rate(30 minutes) {"job": "workout-upcoming-reminder"} Sweeps today’s NOT_STARTED workouts that have not been reminded yet fitness-assistant-dev-workout-unfinished-reminder rate(30 minutes) {"job": "workout-unfinished-reminder"} Reminds about IN_PROGRESS workouts started at least 3 hours ago Both use the Asia/Saigon time zone, flexible window off, state enabled, action NONE, retry (5 minutes / 2 attempts), no DLQ, AWS-owned key and the existing scheduler role. The screenshots first follow the upcoming-reminder schedule.
10.1 — Name it and set the pattern. In EventBridge → Scheduler → Schedules → Create schedule, enter the schedule name fitness-assistant-dev-workout-upcoming-reminder, keep the default group, choose Recurring schedule, time zone (UTC+07:00) Asia/Saigon and Rate-based schedule.
10.2 — Set the rate. Enter rate 30 minutes and keep Flexible time window Off. Leave the timeframe empty and click Next.
10.3 — Choose the target. With Templated targets selected, pick AWS Lambda → Invoke.
10.4 — Function and payload. Choose the Lambda function fitness-assistant-dev-fitness-jobs, enter the payload {"job": "workout-upcoming-reminder"} and click Next.
10.5 — Retry settings. Keep Retry on with maximum age of event 5 minutes (0 hours) and 2 retry attempts, and dead-letter queue None.
10.6 — Permissions. Under Execution role, choose Use existing role and select fitness-assistant-dev-fitness-jobs-scheduler-role, then click Next and Create schedule on the review page. In this particular full-page screenshot the Retry switch is shown off; the retry values come from the previous screenshot, so check this switch when you repeat the step.
10.7 — Second schedule: name and rate. Create the second schedule the same way: name fitness-assistant-dev-workout-unfinished-reminder, recurring, rate-based, rate 30 minutes.
10.8 — Second schedule: payload. Target AWS Lambda → Invoke, function fitness-assistant-dev-fitness-jobs, payload {"job": "workout-unfinished-reminder"}, then Next.
10.9 — Second schedule: settings. Keep: Enable, action NONE, Retry on with maximum age 5 minutes and 2 attempts, DLQ None, and Use existing role with the same scheduler role. Then create the schedule.
The upcoming-workout reminder only has day granularity: the current schema stores no planned start time, so the job cannot send “your workout starts in 30 minutes”. It reminds about workouts scheduled for today that have not been reminded yet.

title: Security and IAM
content:
Network isolation Lambda functions and the Chat Fargate task run only in the two private application subnets; the only resources in public subnets are the NAT Gateway and the internet-facing Chat ALB. Aurora sits in private DB subnets whose route table has no NAT or internet route, so the database tier can neither reach nor be reached from the internet. Security groups reference each other instead of IP ranges: Security group Inbound fitness-assistant-dev-aurora-sg 5432 from lambda-sg and from chat-sg only fitness-assistant-dev-chat-sg 3005 from chat-alb-sg only fitness-assistant-dev-chat-alb-sg 80 from the internet (DEV, HTTP) fitness-assistant-dev-vpce-sg 443 from lambda-sg (Secrets Manager and OpenSearch endpoints) fitness-assistant-dev-lambda-sg none OpenSearch Serverless is reachable only through its VPC endpoint (public access disabled). The Chat ALB answers /internal/* and /metrics with a fixed 404, and API Gateway has no /internal/*, /metrics or catch-all route, so service-to-service endpoints are not reachable from the internet at all. IAM — least privilege per function Every function and task has its own role. Lambda roles start from AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole (logs) and AWSLambdaVPCAccessExecutionRole (VPC networking) and add inline policies that name exact resources:
Need How it is scoped Database credentials secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on that service’s own secret ARN only Calling another service lambda:InvokeFunction on the exact target function ARNs (e.g. Payment → Auth, User, Gym, AI), never lambda:* Private uploads s3:PutObject/GetObject/DeleteObject on three prefixes of the uploads bucket only (profile-photos/, pt-applications/, contracts/), no s3:ListBucket AI queue HTTP Lambda: sqs:SendMessage; Worker: ReceiveMessage, DeleteMessage, GetQueueAttributes — on the one queue Bedrock bedrock:InvokeModel on the APAC Nova Pro inference profile, on the Nova Pro foundation model only when called through that profile (IAM condition), and on Cohere Embed Multilingual v3 — no AmazonBedrockFullAccess, no streaming permission OpenSearch aoss:APIAccessAll on the one collection ARN, plus a data access policy that grants index read/write/create to the three AI roles but not DeleteIndex Schedules One scheduler role per service, trusted by scheduler.amazonaws.com, allowed to invoke only that service’s jobs function ECS Execution role (pull image, write logs, inject the two Chat secrets) separated from the task role (invoke Auth/User only) Migration task Read only the dumps prefix of the migration bucket and the database credential The Cohere Marketplace subscription was accepted once by an administrator; runtime roles have no aws-marketplace:* permission.
Secrets All database credentials are in AWS Secrets Manager, one secret per service database (fitness-assistant/dev/<service>-database); functions hold only DATABASE_SECRET_ID. The Chat task receives its database URL and the internal secret as ECS secrets (valueFrom), never as plain values. Service-to-service calls carry the shared INTERNAL_SERVICE_SECRET, separate from any user JWT. The Gym Service signs QR check-in codes with its own CHECKIN_TOKEN_SECRET, deliberately different from the internal secret. Payment provider keys are entered only once real sandbox credentials exist and are never copied into chat, documentation or source control. Bedrock needs no API key — every model call is authorized by the function’s IAM role. Abuse and cost protection API Gateway route throttling on the AI routes (1 request/s with a burst of 3; 3/6 for the marketplace) caps how fast any client can trigger billable Bedrock calls; the frontend shows a “too many requests” message on HTTP 429. SQS dead-letter queue (2 attempts) prevents a failing AI job from being retried forever.

content:

During this intensive week, I accomplished two major tracks: system performance/cost optimization (Module 3) and application modernization (Module 4). The extensive lab workload spanned containerization, robust serverless computing, data lakes, and complex cost analytics. Module 4 also explained the pattern the deployment had followed since Week 4 (most of the Fitness Assistant does not need servers at all), and I applied it to the Fitness service on 2 September.
Note: Certain sections within the modernization labs (specifically 47, 54, and 55) mandated the use of AWS Cloud9. As AWS Cloud9 is currently inaccessible in my environment, these specific sections were strategically skipped, while the underlying architectural concepts were still thoroughly studied.
Learned theory:
Performance & Cost Optimization: Learned deployment paradigms using Docker and Amazon ECS. Mastered CI/CD automation with AWS CodePipeline. Studied Data Lake foundations and explored financial governance via Savings Plans, EC2 right-sizing, and AWS Glue/Athena querying.
Modernization & Microservices: Grasped architectural patterns for migrating monolithic applications to microservices. Explored decoupled messaging/eventing systems and integrating orchestration tools like AWS Step Functions.
Serverless Architecture: Deepened my expertise in the serverless ecosystem utilizing AWS Lambda, Amazon API Gateway, the Serverless Application Model (SAM), Amazon Cognito for identity, SQS/SNS for asynchronous processing, and AppSync.
Hands-on labs:
Successfully deployed containerized applications on ECS, integrating them with automated CI/CD pipelines Configured enterprise storage solutions including File Storage Gateways and FSx for Windows, alongside Data Lake optimizations Executed advanced cost tracking and query analysis utilizing AWS Glue and Amazon Athena Engineered and deployed fully serverless applications (e.g., Serverless Bookstore), encompassing frontend API integration, SSL setup, CI/CD workflows, and CloudWatch/X-Ray distributed tracing Skipped specific execution steps in Labs 47, 54, and 55 due to an inability to provision AWS Cloud9 environments, though the theoretical framework for Step Functions, Messaging/Eventing, and SPA configurations was thoroughly reviewed Applied to Fitness Assistant:
Modernization Path (the pattern every service follows):
The application is already split into services (auth, user, fitness, gym, payment, ai, chat) that run together with Docker Compose locally. Six of them only answer short HTTP requests or run scheduled jobs, which is exactly the Lambda model; only chat has to keep a Socket.IO connection open. Each of the six HTTP services runs as Lambda functions behind one API Gateway HTTP API, which replaces the application gateway container as the single entry point (Auth and User since Week 4, Fitness this week). Scheduled work (session settlement, workout reminders, payouts, payment reconciliation, AI knowledge refresh) moves from timers inside the process to EventBridge Scheduler, which invokes one jobs function per service. Long AI work (workout and nutrition plan generation) moves to an SQS queue and a worker function, so no HTTP call has to wait past API Gateway’s ~30-second limit. This also replaces the Redis/BullMQ queue, which would have needed a cache cluster running all the time. Chat stays a container; where to run it is evaluated in Week 6. Performance Optimization:
Memory is the only sizing setting on Lambda (CPU grows with it), so there are no instance types to right-size Considered CloudFront CDN for frontend assets to reduce latency, postponed until the site has a domain and HTTPS Cost Optimization:
Pay-per-use services for the application tier (Lambda, HTTP API, which is cheaper than a REST API, SQS, EventBridge Scheduler) and Aurora Serverless v2 instead of a fixed-size database instance Listed the costs that remain while the app is idle (NAT Gateway, load balancer, VPC endpoints, the database’s capacity floor); they became the main lines of the budget One naming scheme for every resource (fitness-assistant-dev-<service>-…), so cost and clean-up can be filtered per service Researched Savings Plans for predictable workloads (Compute Savings Plans also cover Lambda and Fargate) Set up AWS Budgets and Cost Anomaly Detection alerts CI/CD:
Sketched a pipeline: build each service’s Lambda package into the deployments bucket and the chat image into ECR, then update the functions and the ECS service. Not built yet: deployments are manual and documented step by step in 5.4, and CI/CD is the largest open item. Difficulties Encountered: Cloud9 Limitation: Unable to access AWS Cloud9 (possibly due to region restrictions or account limitations), resulting in skipped hands-on steps in labs 47, 54, 55. However, conceptual learning was maintained through documentation and video tutorials.
Mapping Docker Compose to serverless: In Docker Compose every service is a long-running container that calls the others by hostname. On Lambda there is no long-running process and no hostname, so in-process timers, the Redis queue and service-to-service calls all had to change.
Serverless Cold Start Trade-offs: When researching Lambda migration, realized cold start latency could impact user experience for synchronous APIs. Needed to carefully evaluate which workloads are suitable for serverless.
Cost Calculation Complexity: AWS cost model is very granular (per request, per GB-second, data transfer costs). Difficult to forecast costs accurately when planning serverless migration.
How It Was Resolved: Cloud9 Workaround: Used local development environment with AWS CLI and SAM CLI to simulate Cloud9 workflows. Read lab documentation thoroughly to understand intended outcomes.
Mapping: Listed every long-running part of each service and chose a managed replacement for each: timers → EventBridge Scheduler and a jobs function, Redis/BullMQ → SQS and a worker, sockets → the chat container on ECS, service-to-service HTTP calls → direct Lambda invocations on exact function ARNs.
Cold Start Mitigation: Accepted cold starts for the DEV environment, where they only affect the first request after an idle period. Provisioned concurrency remains the option for production, so the synchronous APIs did not need to stay on containers.
Cost Forecasting: Used AWS Pricing Calculator to estimate costs. Set up granular billing alerts. Deployed one service at a time (Auth and User in Week 4, Fitness this week), so the cost of each step could be checked.

AWS Lambda Amazon API Gateway AWS SAM (Serverless Application Model) Amazon Cognito Amazon SQS/SNS AWS AppSync AWS Step Functions Services - Storage & Data:
AWS Storage Gateway Amazon FSx AWS Glue Amazon Athena Data Lake architecture Services - Cost & Monitoring:

title: Monitoring and alerting with Amazon CloudWatch
content:
This page shows how the DEV environment is observed through logs, metrics and alarms, how an alert reaches a person, and how to test each layer. All values below were read from the live account.
1. Monitoring layers Layer AWS service What it covers Logs Amazon CloudWatch Logs One log group per Lambda, plus the Chat task and the database migrator Metrics Amazon CloudWatch Metrics Lambda, API Gateway, Aurora, SQS, NAT Gateway and ECS built-in metrics Alarms Amazon CloudWatch Alarms 12 alarms on errors, 5xx responses, database load and NAT health Notification Amazon SNS Topic fitness-assistant-dev-app-alerts with a confirmed e-mail subscription Tracing AWS X-Ray Active tracing on the six API Lambdas (auth, user, fitness, gym, payment, AI) Cost AWS Budgets Monthly budget with three notifications The alarms and the topic are created by the CloudFormation stack fitness-assistant-dev-app-monitoring, so they are reproducible and not clicked together by hand.
2. Logs Log group Retention Note /aws/lambda/fitness-assistant-dev-<service> and -jobs, -worker, -migrate Never expire (default) Structured JSON written by pino: level 30 is info, 40 warning, 50 error /ecs/fitness-assistant-dev-chat 30 days Chat service /ecs/fitness-assistant-dev-db-migrator 14 days One-off database migrator Two CloudWatch Logs Insights queries cover most of the troubleshooting:
fields @timestamp, @message | filter @message like /"level":50/ | sort @timestamp desc | limit 20 fields @timestamp, @message | filter @message like /Task timed out|AccessDenied|ECONNREFUSED|P1001/ | sort @timestamp desc | limit 20 The first lists the latest errors of a function; the second finds the four most common infrastructure failures (timeout, missing permission, refused connection, database unreachable). The meaning of each message is listed in 5.5.4.
3. Metrics worth watching Namespace Metric Why AWS/Lambda Errors, Throttles, Duration, ConcurrentExecutions Function health and the 30-second timeout AWS/ApiGateway Count, 4xx, 5xx, Latency Client mistakes versus server failures at the entry point AWS/RDS ServerlessDatabaseCapacity, CPUUtilization Aurora Serverless v2 scaling and load AWS/SQS ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible on the queue and its dead-letter queue Backlog of AI jobs, failed jobs AWS/NATGateway ActiveConnectionCount, PacketsDropCount, ErrorPortAllocation Outbound path used by Bedrock and e-mail 4. Alarms All 12 alarms use TreatMissingData: notBreaching, so a stopped environment does not raise false alerts. Each alarm sends both its ALARM and its OK transition to the SNS topic.
Alarm Metric Condition fitness-assistant-dev-auth-lambda-errors AWS/Lambda Errors, Sum ≥ 5 in 5 minutes fitness-assistant-dev-user-lambda-errors same ≥ 5 in 5 minutes fitness-assistant-dev-fitness-lambda-errors same ≥ 5 in 5 minutes fitness-assistant-dev-gym-lambda-errors same ≥ 5 in 5 minutes fitness-assistant-dev-payment-lambda-errors same ≥ 5 in 5 minutes fitness-assistant-dev-ai-lambda-errors same ≥ 5 in 5 minutes fitness-assistant-dev-apigw-5xx-high AWS/ApiGateway 5xx, Sum ≥ 10 in 5 minutes fitness-assistant-dev-aurora-cpu-high AWS/RDS CPUUtilization, Average > 80 for 2 periods of 5 minutes fitness-assistant-dev-aurora-capacity-pinned AWS/RDS ServerlessDatabaseCapacity, Average ≥ 1.8 ACU for 3 periods of 5 minutes (the cluster scales between 0.5 and 2.0 ACU, so this means it is pinned near the maximum) NAT-Gateway-High-Active-Connections ActiveConnectionCount, Average > 1000 NAT-Gateway-Packet-Drops PacketsDropCount, Sum > 100 NAT-Gateway-Port-Allocation-Errors ErrorPortAllocation, Sum > 0 Notification path: alarm → SNS topic fitness-assistant-dev-app-alerts → e-mail (1 confirmed subscription, 0 pending). Alarms change state on their own: for example, the API 5xx alarm history shows OK → ALARM and ALARM → OK transitions on 23 October 2026, and the alarm returned to OK by itself each time.
The 12 alarms in CloudWatch → Alarms.
The SNS topic with one confirmed e-mail subscription.
Lambda → Configuration → Monitoring and operations tools: logs and metrics enabled, Lambda service traces (X-Ray) enabled.
The step-by-step creation of an alarm, with its form, is in 5.4.14.
5. Cost monitoring The budget fitness-assistant-monthly has a limit of 15 USD per month with three notifications: actual spend above 50 percent and above 100 percent of the limit, and forecasted spend above 100 percent. This matters because several resources bill by the hour (NAT Gateway, load balancer, Aurora, endpoints), which is why the environment has an on-demand start and stop procedure (5.7).
6. Tests and validation 6.1 Sample requests. These were run against the deployed API and CloudFront; the actual results are listed.
# Request Expected Result 1 GET /health 200 and the service name 200 {"status":"ok","service":"auth-service"} 2 POST /auth/login with a wrong password 401, no detail about which field is wrong 401 {"error":"Invalid credentials"} 3 POST /auth/login with malformed JSON ({"email":) 400 and no stack trace 400 Bad Request 4 POST /auth/login with an empty body {} 400 with the missing fields 400 Validation failed, listing email and password as required 5 GET /plans/workout without a token 401 401 UNAUTHORIZED (“Request must carry a valid Bearer token…”) 6 GET /plans/workout with a fake token 401 401 UNAUTHORIZED (“Invalid or expired token”) 7 GET /me/gym-memberships without a token 401 401 UNAUTHORIZED (“Authentication required”) 8 GET /does-not-exist 404 from the API Gateway 404 {"message":"Not Found"} 9 GET / on the CloudFront domain 200, served from S3 200, Server: AmazonS3, response header shows CloudFront Example for test 2:
curl -s -X POST https://<api-id>.execute-api.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com/auth/login \ -H "content-type: application/json" \ -d '{"email":"nobody@example.com","password":"wrong"}' 6.2 Log verification. After tests 2 to 4, the /aws/lambda/fitness-assistant-dev-auth log group contains one structured entry per request with the method POST and the URL /auth/login, and the Lambda Errors metric stays at 0: a rejected login is a handled 4xx, not a function failure.
6.3 Metric verification. A few minutes later, AWS/ApiGateway Count and 4xx increase by the number of requests sent, while 5xx stays at 0. Metrics are delayed by one to a few minutes.
6.4 Alarm test. To prove the whole alert path without breaking anything, force one alarm into the ALARM state and check that an e-mail arrives, then let it return to OK:
aws cloudwatch set-alarm-state \ --alarm-name fitness-assistant-dev-apigw-5xx-high \ --state-value ALARM --state-reason "Alert path test" The alarm evaluates its real metric again at the next period and goes back to OK by itself.
6.5 Error-case checks. The negative tests above (wrong password, malformed body, missing token, fake token, unknown route) confirm that failures are rejected at the right layer with the right status code, and that none of them raises the function-error alarms.

title: Gym Service
content:
The Gym Service handles gyms, PT listings, owner and admin tools, collaborations and QR check-in. It is the first service with a second secret of its own: the key that signs check-in QR codes.
In every screenshot below, the red rectangles mark what to fill in or click for the sub-step written just above it.
Item Value Logical database fitness_assistant_gym (9 Prisma migrations) Secret fitness-assistant/dev/gym-database Functions fitness-assistant-dev-gym, fitness-assistant-dev-gym-jobs Calls Auth, User and (after 5.4.7) Payment Lambdas Step 1 — Create the database secret 1.1 — Choose the secret type and fill in the pairs. Open Secrets Manager → Store a new secret, choose Other type of secret, then add the same five key/value rows as the other services: username, password, host, port and database = fitness_assistant_gym. Then click Next and save the secret as fitness-assistant/dev/gym-database.
The runbook has no screenshot of the final name and Store click.
Step 2 — Upload the artifacts 2.1 — Upload gym-lambda.zip. Open the S3 bucket fitness-assistant-deployments-dev-<account-id>, click Upload, add gym-lambda.zip (~36 MiB — small enough for a direct upload, but S3 is used for consistency) and click Upload. gym-migrate-lambda.zip (~69 MiB) must go through S3 the same way.
2.2 — Check the result. The status page must show Succeeded next to the file. Click Close.
At this point in the runbook the Gym migration was skipped, even though the service has 9 migrations: the Lambda and its routes can be deployed, but every route that touches the database fails until fitness_assistant_gym has its schema. The migration was run with a fitness-assistant-dev-gym-migrate function following the common pattern — it appears in the function list in 5.4.10 — and the deployment status table records the Gym migration as complete.
Step 3 — Create the runtime role 3.1 — Create the role. In IAM → Roles → Create role, choose AWS service → Lambda, attach the two managed policies and name it fitness-assistant-dev-gym-lambda-role.
The runbook has no screenshot of this action.
3.2 — Add the secret policy. On the role, open Add permissions → Create inline policy, switch to JSON, and paste the policy below. Name it fitness-assistant-dev-gym-database-secret.
{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [{ "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["secretsmanager:GetSecretValue", "secretsmanager:DescribeSecret"], "Resource": "arn:aws:secretsmanager:ap-southeast-1:<account-id>:secret:fitness-assistant/dev/gym-database*" }] } 3.3 — Add the invoke policy. Create a second inline policy in the same way, named fitness-assistant-dev-gym-service-invoke, allowing lambda:InvokeFunction on fitness-assistant-dev-auth and fitness-assistant-dev-user only.
3.4 — Check the role. Both inline policies must now be listed on the role.
Payment is deliberately not in the invoke list yet — it is added in 5.4.7 once the Payment Lambda exists.
Step 4 — Create the Gym Lambda 4.1 — Fill in the function. Open Lambda → Create function, keep Author from scratch, set the name to fitness-assistant-dev-gym and the runtime to Node.js 22.x (x86_64). Under Additional settings → Custom execution role choose fitness-assistant-dev-gym-lambda-role, then click Create function.
4.2 — Set memory and timeout. Open Configuration → General configuration → Edit, set Memory to 1024 MB and Timeout to 0 min 30 sec, then click Save.
4.3 — Set the handler. Open Code → Runtime settings → Edit, enter dist/lambda.handler and click Save.
4.4 — Load the code. Open Upload from → Amazon S3 location, keep Copy mode, paste s3://fitness-assistant-deployments-dev-<account-id>/gym-lambda.zip and click Update.
Step 5 — Environment variables and VPC 5.1 — Add the variables. Open Configuration → Environment variables → Edit and add:
Variable Value NODE_ENV production DATABASE_SECRET_ID fitness-assistant/dev/gym-database AUTH_LAMBDA_NAME fitness-assistant-dev-auth USER_LAMBDA_NAME fitness-assistant-dev-user INTERNAL_SERVICE_SECRET the shared service-to-service value CHECKIN_TOKEN_SECRET a new, strong random value CHECKIN_TOKEN_SECRET must be different from INTERNAL_SERVICE_SECRET: it signs the QR codes shown to gym members, so leaking one must not compromise the other. PAYMENT_LAMBDA_NAME and FITNESS_LAMBDA_NAME are not set yet.
5.2 — Attach the VPC. Open Configuration → VPC → Edit, choose the project VPC (10.0.0.0/16), select both private app subnets (private-app-a and private-app-b) and the fitness-assistant-dev-lambda-sg security group, then click Save.
Step 6 — Connect the Gym Lambda to API Gateway 6.1 — Create the integration. In API Gateway → fitness-assistant-dev-api → Integrations → Create, choose Lambda function, region ap-southeast-1, pick fitness-assistant-dev-gym and keep payload format 2.0.
6.2 — Attach the routes. Create the root + greedy route pair for each prefix and attach each to this integration:
ANY /gyms ANY /gyms/{proxy+} ANY /pt ANY /pt/{proxy+} ANY /me ANY /me/{proxy+} ANY /owner ANY /owner/{proxy+} ANY /admin ANY /admin/{proxy+} ANY /collaborations ANY /collaborations/{proxy+} 6.3 — Check one route. Under Attach integrations to routes, select a route such as ANY /collaborations; the details on the right must show fitness-assistant-dev-gym.
/me, /admin and /pt can already exist from the User Service. An HTTP API cannot route the same method and path to two integrations, so when the console reports an existing route it is not overwritten — the conflict is resolved by checking which service’s code actually owns that path. The Payment Service later avoids the problem entirely by using more specific prefixes such as /me/wallet.
The API now routes:
fitness-assistant-dev-api ├── /auth/* → Auth Lambda ├── User routes → User Lambda ├── Fitness routes → Fitness Lambda └── Gym routes → Gym Lambda ──► Auth / User Lambda, Aurora (fitness_assistant_gym) Step 7 — Create the jobs Lambda fitness-assistant-dev-gym-jobs uses the same role and artifact as the Gym Lambda.
7.1 — Fill in the function. Open Lambda → Create function, keep Author from scratch, set the name to fitness-assistant-dev-gym-jobs, runtime Node.js 22.x, and under Additional settings → Custom execution role choose fitness-assistant-dev-gym-lambda-role. Then click Create function.
7.2 — Set memory and timeout. Configuration → General configuration → Edit: Memory 1024 MB, Timeout 1 min 0 sec, then Save.
7.3 — Set the handler. Code → Runtime settings → Edit: dist/jobs-lambda.handler, then Save.
7.4 — Load the code. Upload from → Amazon S3 location: paste the same gym-lambda.zip link, keep Copy mode, click Update.
7.5 — Attach the VPC. Configuration → VPC → Edit: same VPC, subnets and security group as the Gym Lambda, then Save. Copy the environment variables as well, including CHECKIN_TOKEN_SECRET.
Step 8 — Scheduler role and schedules 8.1 — Create the scheduler role. Create fitness-assistant-dev-gym-jobs-scheduler-role (trust scheduler.amazonaws.com) with an inline policy fitness-assistant-dev-invoke-gym-jobs allowing lambda:InvokeFunction on the Gym jobs Lambda only.
The runbook has no screenshot of this action.
8.2 — Create the two schedules in EventBridge → Schedules:
Schedule Rate Payload fitness-assistant-dev-gym-membership-payout rate(10 minutes) {"job":"membership-payout-sweep"} fitness-assistant-dev-gym-referral-settlement rate(10 minutes) {"job":"referral-settlement-sweep"} Both: flexible window off, enabled, maximum event age 5 minutes, 2 retry attempts, no DLQ, AWS-owned key, the existing scheduler role. Both jobs need the Payment Service, which is why the Gym jobs Lambda also receives PAYMENT_LAMBDA_NAME in the next page.
The runbook has no screenshot of the schedule creation.

title: Scalability and Operations
content:
How each component scales Component Scaling model Notes Service Lambdas (HTTP and jobs) Per invocation, automatic, scale to zero 1024 MB each; cold starts on idle functions are the trade-off, not yet measured. No reserved concurrency, so one hot route cannot starve the others by configuration. AI Worker One Lambda per SQS message (batch size 1) Throughput grows with queue depth; failed messages go to the DLQ after 2 receives. Chat Service (ECS Fargate) Fixed at 1 task (0.5 vCPU / 1 GB) Deliberate: Socket.IO session state is in memory, so a second task would split sessions until a shared adapter (e.g. Redis) exists. No service auto scaling yet. Aurora PostgreSQL Serverless v2 Capacity in ACUs between a floor and a ceiling Floor kept at 0.5 ACU during deployment so auto-pause/resume does not disturb smoke tests; can go to 0 when idle. OpenSearch Serverless (NextGen) 0–2 OCU for indexing and for search Scales to zero after ~10 idle minutes; the first request afterwards can take 10–30 s. API Gateway, SQS, EventBridge, S3 Fully managed No capacity planning needed at DEV traffic. AI routes are intentionally throttled. Keeping slow work out of the request path Scheduled work runs from EventBridge Scheduler into dedicated jobs functions, so no user request ever triggers a settlement or reconciliation run. Long AI work goes through SQS to the AI Worker (300 s timeout) and knowledge ingestion runs in the AI Jobs function (600 s timeout), while the HTTP function stays under API Gateway’s ~30 s integration limit. That is why the AI Service has three functions instead of one.
Operating the system today Deployments are manual and documented step by step in 5.4: ZIPs uploaded from the deployments bucket, task definition revisions rolled out with Force new deployment, and schema changes applied with each service’s migration function. Logs for every function and task are in CloudWatch Logs (/aws/lambda/…, /ecs/…); 5.5.4 lists what to look for. Changing a secret (for example a rotated Aurora password) requires recycling the Lambda execution environments, because functions cache the secret while warm — the Auth deployment did this by editing a harmless DEPLOY_REVISION variable. CI/CD and monitoring CI/CD is in place — GitHub Actions validates every PR and deploys Lambda code, the Chat image and the API Gateway stack through reviewer-gated workflows. Monitoring is in place — 12 CloudWatch alarms (Lambda errors for the six API services, API Gateway 5xx, Aurora CPU and capacity, NAT Gateway health) notify an SNS topic with a confirmed e-mail subscription; a monthly AWS Budget alerts on cost; active X-Ray tracing is on the six API Lambdas.

title: Week 6 Worklog
content:
Week 6 Objectives: Complete Module 5: Container services Master the orchestration and deployment of containerized applications across Lightsail, ECS, and EKS Engage with the professional community and integrate further into the office environment Deploy the Gym and Payment services, and plan where the Chat service will run Tasks to be carried out this week: Task Start Date Completion Date Reference Materials Study and complete Module 5: Container services 07-9-2026 12-9-2026 46: https://000046.awsstudygroup.com/ 67: https://000067.awsstudygroup.com/ 152: https://000152.awsstudygroup.com/ Deploy the Gym and Payment services (databases, functions and schedules) 08-9-2026 08-9-2026 5.4.6 Gym Service 5.4.7 Payment Service Week 6 Achievements: Overview:
During this week, I focused on AWS Container services (Module 5), exploring how to run and orchestrate containers at varying scales of complexity using Amazon Lightsail, ECS, and EKS. On 8 September I also deployed the Gym and Payment services. Beyond technical skill acquisition, I deepened my professional involvement by working from the office for the second time and actively participating in a weekend technology meetup.
Learned theory:
Amazon Lightsail Containers: Learned how to rapidly deploy and run containerized applications within a simplified, predictable pricing environment.
Amazon ECS & Fargate: Understood the architectural strategies for modernizing legacy Monolithic applications into Microservices utilizing Docker, Amazon ECS, and the serverless AWS Fargate compute engine.
Amazon EKS & CI/CD: Grasped the fundamentals of Kubernetes cluster management on AWS (EKS) and learned how to establish a continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipeline using AWS CodePipeline for automated container deployments.
Gained valuable networking and professional experience by attending community events and integrating into the workplace.
Hands-on labs:
Successfully deployed a containerized application utilizing Amazon Lightsail Containers Migrated a monolithic application to a microservices architecture using Docker, orchestrating the deployment via ECS and Fargate Configured a robust CI/CD pipeline for Amazon EKS using AWS CodePipeline to automate Kubernetes deployments Applied to Fitness Assistant:
Container Strategy Evaluation:
By this week Auth, User and Fitness were running on Lambda (see Week 5), and Gym and Payment followed on 8 September. The question for this week was narrower: where should the one service that needs a long-running process run? That service is Chat, which keeps a Socket.IO connection open for every user. I compared the three platforms from the module:
Amazon Lightsail Containers:
Pros: Simple setup, predictable pricing ($10-40/month), good for MVP Cons: Limited scaling, and harder to integrate with the private VPC, per-service IAM roles and Secrets Manager used by the rest of the design Decision: Not used Amazon ECS with Fargate:
Pros: Serverless (no server management), good AWS integration, cost-effective for small-medium scale Cons: Vendor lock-in (AWS-specific), learning curve Decision: Chosen for the Chat service, deployed in Week 8. The same cluster can also run one-off tasks, later used for the database migration job Amazon EKS (Kubernetes):
Pros: Industry standard, portable, powerful orchestration Cons: Complex setup, a control-plane fee for every cluster, overkill for a single container service Decision: Not needed at this scale Implementation Plan for the Chat Service:
Phase 1 - Image and registry:
Build the production image of chat-service for linux/amd64 Push it to a private Amazon ECR repository in the same region Phase 2 - Task and service:
One task definition: 0.5 vCPU / 1 GB, container port 3005, database URL and internal secret injected from Secrets Manager One ECS service with the Fargate launch type in the private application subnets Phase 3 - Load balancer and routing:
Internet-facing Application Load Balancer in the public subnets, with an IP target group checked on /health Target-group stickiness and a longer idle timeout, so Socket.IO connections are not cut Listener rules that answer /internal/* and /metrics with 404; REST calls under /chat/* reach the ALB through API Gateway Later:
Run more than one Chat task only after adding a shared Socket.IO adapter (session state is kept in memory today) CI/CD for the image; CloudWatch Container Insights and an alarm on target health Architecture Comparison:
First plan (lift-and-shift onto one host):
User → EC2 (Docker Compose with all services, Ollama, Qdrant, Redis) → RDS Chosen design:
Browser → S3 static website (frontend) Browser → API Gateway (HTTP API) → Lambda (auth, user, fitness, gym, payment, ai) → Aurora PostgreSQL Browser → Chat ALB (Socket.IO; REST through API Gateway /chat/*) → ECS Fargate (chat) → Aurora PostgreSQL Difficulties Encountered: ECS vs EKS Decision: Initially confused about when to use ECS vs EKS. ECS simpler but AWS-specific, EKS industry standard but much more complex.
Task Definition Complexity: ECS Task Definitions have many configuration options (CPU, memory, networking mode, volume mounts, environment variables, secrets). Hard to optimize correctly.
Fargate Pricing Model: Fargate pricing based on vCPU and memory allocated per second, and the load balancer in front of it is a fixed monthly cost. At DEV traffic, the always-on chat path costs more than all six Lambda services together.
Service-to-service calls: In Docker Compose the services call each other by hostname on a shared network. Neither Lambda functions nor a Fargate task behind a load balancer have that, and AWS Cloud Map for service discovery has its own learning curve.
How It Was Resolved: Platform Decision: ECS on Fargate for Chat only: production-ready, AWS-integrated, manageable complexity, lower cost than EKS. EKS stays an option if the project ever needs Kubernetes or multi-cloud portability.
Task Definitions: Started from the smallest task definition that works (one container, one port, secrets from Secrets Manager) and kept every change as a new revision.
Cost Management: Used AWS Pricing Calculator to estimate Fargate and ALB costs. Kept Chat at one small task that can be scaled to zero between test sessions; Savings Plans only if a steady baseline appears.
Service-to-service calls: No Cloud Map: internal calls are direct Lambda invocations on exact function ARNs that carry a shared internal secret, and the chat task calls Auth and User the same way. API Gateway has no /internal/* route, so these endpoints are never public.
AWS Skills / Services Learned: Services:
Amazon Lightsail Containers Amazon ECS (Elastic Container Service) AWS Fargate (serverless compute for containers) Amazon EKS (Elastic Kubernetes Service) AWS CodePipeline (for container CI/CD) Amazon ECR (Elastic Container Registry) AWS Cloud Map (service discovery) Application Load Balancer (ALB) AWS Copilot CLI Skills:
Container orchestration strategies ECS vs EKS evaluation and selection Fargate serverless container management Kubernetes fundamentals (EKS) CI/CD pipeline design for containers Microservices deployment patterns Service discovery and inter-service communication Container cost optimization Connection to Fitness Assistant Architecture: Immediate Actions:
Production Dockerfile for chat-service (the other services are packaged as Lambda ZIP files instead of images) One task definition and one ECS service for Chat ALB rules for Socket.IO and for hiding internal paths Medium-term Goals:
Implement full CI/CD pipeline Shared Socket.IO adapter before scaling Chat beyond one task Alarm on the chat target’s health Related Workshop Sections: 5.4.1 Shared network infrastructure - VPC, subnets and NAT setup 5.4.10 Chat Service on ECS Fargate - Container deployment on ECS Fargate behind an ALB

title: Sharing and Feedback
content:
Here I share my personal opinions about my experience in the First Cloud AI Journey program, to help the FCAJ team improve based on the following aspects:
Overall Evaluation 1. Working Environment The program gave me a clear way of working: a set of requirements for the report, a workshop website template, and rules for blogs, events and worklogs. The in-person events I attended (FCAJ Community Day at Bitexco Financial Tower, and AWS for Software & Financial Services Companies Day at the Sheraton Saigon Grand Opera) were well organised, and the community around the AWS Study Group made it easy to share what I was learning. After the first two months of team activities, I carried out the 12-week project on my own, so the daily work was mostly independent. It would be nice to have a few more regular gatherings in that phase to keep the team spirit alive.
2. Support from Mentor / Team Admin I received guidance mostly through the program’s framework: the report structure, the workshop requirements and the examples to compare against. This pushed me to look for answers in the AWS documentation and in real logs and metrics before asking, and I valued having room to try things and solve problems myself. Because I was working alone in the second phase, short regular check-ins on the major design decisions would have been very helpful.
3. Relevance of Work to Academic Major The project fits my Information Systems major well. I applied what I learned about databases, system design and software engineering to a real application, and learned a lot that is new: serverless architecture, networking and security on AWS, CI/CD, monitoring, and cost control.
4. Learning & Skill Development Opportunities I learned many new skills: designing and deploying a multi-service system on AWS, using least-privilege IAM and cross-account access, monitoring with CloudWatch, building CI/CD with GitHub Actions and CloudFormation, controlling cost, and writing bilingual technical documentation. The events also showed me how AWS approaches AI and agents, including a hands-on workshop where I built a game with Kiro by writing requirements and design first.
5. Company Culture & Team Spirit During the first two months, working with my teammates taught me how to split work, explain a design and give each other feedback. When the program moved to daily worklogs and my teammates had finished, I became the only one left on the project. Even so, the community and events kept me connected, and the experience taught me to take full responsibility for a product from design to operation.
6. Internship Policies / Benefits The AWS credits for the DEV environment let me build and test a real system without worrying about the budget, and the credits provided at the Kiro workshop let everyone build freely for a day. At the same time, I learned that many resources bill by the hour even without users, which made cost control a real part of the work.
Additional Questions What did you find most satisfying during your internship? Seeing a complete system running on AWS that I built end to end: users can register, log in, create a training plan with an AI coach, chat with a trainer and pay through a sandbox gateway, all behind CloudFront over HTTPS. Setting up the CI/CD pipeline and watching a deployment go through reviewer gates was also very satisfying.
What do you think the program should improve for future interns? Give early guidance on service quotas for new accounts (the Bedrock model quota on my main account was 0, which cost me time), on cost control for hourly-billed resources, and keep some form of check-in for people who end up working alone.
If recommending to a friend, would you suggest they join this program? Why or why not? Yes. It is a place to learn by doing real work on AWS, with a community and events that widen your view. It suits people who like to explore and take ownership of what they build.
Suggestions & Expectations Do you have any suggestions to improve the internship experience? Provide one complete sample project covering architecture, cost and testing so learners know the expected level of completeness, and keep peer review for the long solo phase.
Would you like to continue this program in the future? Yes. I would like to keep taking part in the community and events, and to continue improving Fitness Assistant.
Any other comments: I plan to keep improving the project after the program: putting chat behind HTTPS on a custom domain, adding automated tests, and going deeper into AI on AWS with Amazon Bedrock and AgentCore. Thank you to the FCAJ team and the community for the opportunity to learn.

Every resource name starts with fitness-assistant-dev- (or fitness-assistant/dev/ for secrets), and everything lives in ap-southeast-1. Use Resource Groups & Tag Editor with that prefix to double-check nothing is left.
