title: Cost Optimization and Clean-up
content:
Cost estimate with the AWS Pricing Calculator The monthly cost of the DEV environment was estimated with the AWS Pricing Calculator for the Singapore Region (ap-southeast-1), assuming everything runs 24×7. The shared estimate is here: Gymini DEV ap-southeast-1 estimate (the calculator keeps a shared link for one year).
The estimate lists five services with their monthly cost.
Service Configuration used Monthly cost (USD) Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL Serverless v2 Writer and Reader at the 0.5 ACU floor (1 ACU in total), 730 hours, 10 GB storage 75.28 AWS PrivateLink (interface VPC endpoints) 2 endpoints (Secrets Manager, OpenSearch) in 2 Availability Zones, 10 GB per month 38.06 AWS Fargate (Chat service) 1 task running 24 hours a day, 0.5 vCPU, 1 GB memory, 20 GB ephemeral storage 22.50 Elastic Load Balancing 1 Application Load Balancer, light traffic 18.98 AWS Secrets Manager 9 secrets, 100,000 API calls per month 4.10 Total of the estimate 158.92 per month (1,907.04 per 12 months) Not in the shared estimate, priced separately:
NAT Gateway: the calculator makes a “Regional NAT Gateway” entry mandatory next to the standard one, which would overstate the cost, so it was left out. One gateway for 730 hours plus 20 GB of data is about 44 USD per month (the calculator showed 44.25 USD for that configuration while the form was open, before it was discarded). With it the running total is about 203 USD per month, inside the 190–230 USD range of the proposal. Usage-based items with very small DEV volume: Lambda, API Gateway, S3, CloudWatch, SQS, EventBridge, OpenSearch Serverless (scales to zero when idle) and Amazon Bedrock (per token). Reading the number. These are the costs of leaving everything on for a full month. The sleep procedure (5.7) removes the NAT Gateway, stops Aurora and scales the Chat service to zero outside test sessions, which is why the real spend is a fraction of this figure.
How the estimate was built Open the calculator, click Add service, keep Search by location type, choose the Region Asia Pacific (Singapore) and type the service name in Find Service. Step 1: choose the Region (1) and search for the service (2).
Click Configure on the service card and fill in its form. For the Chat service on Fargate: Number of tasks 1 per day (1), Average duration 1 day (2), Amount of vCPU 0.5 (3), Amount of memory 1 GB. Then click Save and add service. Step 2: the Fargate form (shown with its default values before they were changed).
Repeat for Aurora PostgreSQL (choose the Serverless edition, 1 ACU, 10 GB), the VPC form with AWS PrivateLink (2 endpoints, 2 Availability Zones), Elastic Load Balancing (1 Application Load Balancer, a small amount of processed data) and Secrets Manager (9 secrets). Open the summary. Click Edit next to the name to rename the estimate, then click Share (2) and Agree and continue. Use Add service (1) to add more services at any time. Step 4: the summary shows 158.92 USD per month.
The calculator stores the estimate on AWS public servers and shows a public link. Click Copy public link (1) to copy it. Anyone with the link can open the estimate. Step 5: the shared link of the estimate.
Cost levers already in use Lambda for six of seven services — pay per invocation instead of an instance running all day; DEV traffic and the scheduled jobs largely fit in the Lambda free tier. Aurora Serverless v2 with a low floor — 0.5 ACU while services were being deployed (to avoid auto-pause noise in smoke tests), designed to go to 0 ACU when the environment is idle. One Aurora cluster with seven logical databases instead of seven clusters. OpenSearch Serverless NextGen at 0–2 OCU — scales to zero when idle instead of the default maximum of 96 OCU. Bedrock on demand — no model hosting cost; per-route throttling on the AI routes stops a client or frontend bug from generating runaway token usage. CloudFront and S3 for the frontend — near-zero cost for a build that never changes at request time, with caching and HTTPS. One NAT Gateway for the whole DEV VPC rather than one per Availability Zone. Right-sized Fargate task — 0.5 vCPU / 1 GB for the Chat Service; the migrator task (1 vCPU / 2 GB) only exists while it runs. Interface VPC endpoints for Secrets Manager and OpenSearch keep that traffic off the NAT Gateway’s per-GB processing charge. Where the fixed cost is With almost everything usage-based, the hourly costs that run even when nobody uses the system are the NAT Gateway, the Chat ALB, the Fargate task, Aurora’s minimum capacity, the interface VPC endpoints and the public IPv4 addresses (NAT Elastic IP and the ALB’s addresses). The Proposal’s budget estimates them; they are the targets of the “sleep” strategy below.
Pausing between sessions DEV sleep strategy — Aurora to 0 ACU, the Chat service to 0 tasks out of hours, and the NAT Gateway deleted between test sessions (see 5.7). Clean-up The full, dependency-ordered teardown of every resource in this architecture is in 5.7 Clean-up.

title: Payment Service
content:
The Payment Service handles wallet top-ups, PT-contract payments, withdrawals and the provider webhooks. Its sensitive internal endpoints (checkout, wallet transfer, contract release, no-show, termination, gym withdrawals) are only reachable through direct Lambda invoke from Gym, User and AI — never through the public API.
In every screenshot below, the red rectangles mark what to fill in or click for the sub-step written just above it.
Item Value Logical database fitness_assistant_payment (11 Prisma migrations) Secret fitness-assistant/dev/payment-database Functions fitness-assistant-dev-payment, fitness-assistant-dev-payment-jobs, temporary fitness-assistant-dev-payment-migrate Provider PAYMENT_PROVIDER=VNPAY (MoMo, PayOS, ZaloPay supported by the code) With Payment’s database the Aurora cluster reaches this layout:
fitness-assistant-dev-aurora ├── fitness_assistant → Auth ├── fitness_assistant_user → User ├── fitness_assistant_fitness → Fitness ├── fitness_assistant_gym → Gym └── fitness_assistant_payment → Payment Step 1 — Secret and artifacts 1.1 — Create the secret. In Secrets Manager → Store a new secret choose Other type of secret, enter the same five pairs as the other services with database = fitness_assistant_payment, and name it fitness-assistant/dev/payment-database.
The runbook has no screenshot of this action; the form is the same as in 5.4.6 Step 1.
1.2 — Upload both zips. In the deployments bucket click Upload, add payment-lambda.zip (36 MB) and payment-migrate-lambda.zip (~69 MiB, so S3 is mandatory), and start the upload. The screenshot shows both files in the list (105.1 MB in total).
Step 2 — Migration role 2.1 — Create the role. In IAM → Roles → Create role choose AWS service → Lambda, attach AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole and AWSLambdaVPCAccessExecutionRole, and name it fitness-assistant-dev-payment-migrate-role.
2.2 — Write the secret policy. On the role open Add permissions → Create inline policy, switch to JSON and allow secretsmanager:GetSecretValue / DescribeSecret on fitness-assistant/dev/payment-database* only.
2.3 — Name and create the policy. Enter the name fitness-assistant-dev-payment-migration-secret and click Create policy.
Step 3 — Migration Lambda 3.1 — Fill in the function. Lambda → Create function, keep Author from scratch, name fitness-assistant-dev-payment-migrate, runtime Node.js 22.x, custom execution role fitness-assistant-dev-payment-migrate-role, then Create function.
3.2 — Set memory and timeout. Configuration → General configuration → Edit: Memory 1024 MB, Timeout 15 min 0 sec, Save.
3.3 — Set the handler. Code → Runtime settings → Edit: dist/migrate-lambda.handler, Save.
3.4 — Add the environment variable. Configuration → Environment variables → Edit: key DATABASE_SECRET_ID, value fitness-assistant/dev/payment-database, Save.
3.5 — Attach the VPC. Configuration → VPC → Edit: the project VPC, both private app subnets and fitness-assistant-dev-lambda-sg, Save.
3.6 — Load the code. Upload from → Amazon S3 location: s3://fitness-assistant-deployments-dev-<account-id>/payment-migrate-lambda.zip, copy mode, Update.
The runbook has no screenshot of this action; it is the same dialog as in 5.4.6 Step 4.4.
Step 4 — Run the 11 migrations 4.1 — Invoke once. Check that the secret really says database = fitness_assistant_payment, then open the Test tab and invoke the function once with {}. The handler has a safety guard that only accepts this database name, creates the logical database if it is missing, and only runs prisma migrate deploy.
Expected result: database = fitness_assistant_payment, migrateExitCode = 0, 11 migrations found, All migrations have been successfully applied.
Step 5 — Runtime role 5.1 — Create the role. IAM → Roles → Create role, AWS service → Lambda, the same two managed policies, name fitness-assistant-dev-payment-lambda-role.
5.2 — Add two inline policies. fitness-assistant-dev-payment-database-secret for the Payment secret, and fitness-assistant-dev-payment-service-invoke:
{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "lambda:InvokeFunction", "Resource": [ "arn:aws:lambda:ap-southeast-1:<account-id>:function:fitness-assistant-dev-auth", "arn:aws:lambda:ap-southeast-1:<account-id>:function:fitness-assistant-dev-user", "arn:aws:lambda:ap-southeast-1:<account-id>:function:fitness-assistant-dev-gym" ] } ] } Step 6 — Payment Lambda 6.1 — Fill in the function. Lambda → Create function, name fitness-assistant-dev-payment, runtime Node.js 22.x, custom execution role fitness-assistant-dev-payment-lambda-role, Create function.
6.2 — Set memory and timeout. Memory 1024 MB, Timeout 0 min 30 sec, Save.
6.3 — Set the handler. dist/lambda.handler, Save.
6.4 — Load the code. Upload from → Amazon S3 location: s3://fitness-assistant-deployments-dev-<account-id>/payment-lambda.zip, copy mode, Update.
6.5 — Attach the VPC. The same VPC, subnets and security group as the other database Lambdas, Save.
6.6 — Add the environment variables.
Variable Value NODE_ENV production DATABASE_SECRET_ID fitness-assistant/dev/payment-database INTERNAL_SERVICE_SECRET the shared value AUTH_LAMBDA_NAME / USER_LAMBDA_NAME / GYM_LAMBDA_NAME the three function names PAYMENT_PROVIDER VNPAY VNPAY_SIMULATE false FRONTEND_URL the S3 website endpoint PAYMENT_PUBLIC_URL the API Gateway invoke URL (used to build provider callback URLs) Provider credentials (VNPAY_TMN_CODE, VNPAY_HASH_SECRET, MoMo / PayOS / ZaloPay keys) are only added once a real sandbox credential exists.
The runbook has no screenshot of the environment-variable form for this function.
Step 7 — API Gateway routes 7.1 — Create the integration. API Gateway → fitness-assistant-dev-api → Integrations → Create: Lambda function fitness-assistant-dev-payment, payload 2.0.
The runbook has no screenshot of this action; the form is the same as in 5.4.6 Step 6.1.
7.2 — Create the routes. ANY /me and ANY /admin are already owned by other services, so Payment uses specific prefixes:
Group Routes Public payments and provider webhooks ANY /payments, ANY /payments/{proxy+} — covers GET /payments/webhook/vnpay, POST /payments/webhook/{provider}, GET /payments/vnpay/return User ANY /me/payments, /me/wallet, /me/pt-wallet, /me/withdrawals — each with its /{proxy+} route Admin ANY /admin/payments, ANY /admin/payments/{proxy+} /internal and /internal/{proxy+} are never created.
7.3 — Check the attachment. Open Integrations → Attach integrations to routes, select each Payment route and confirm it points at fitness-assistant-dev-payment — a route without an integration returns Not Found.
Step 8 — Jobs Lambda and the reconciliation schedule fitness-assistant-dev-payment-jobs uses the same role, artifact, VPC and environment as the HTTP Lambda.
8.1 — Fill in the function. Lambda → Create function, name fitness-assistant-dev-payment-jobs, runtime Node.js 22.x, role fitness-assistant-dev-payment-lambda-role, Create function.
8.2 — Set the handler. dist/jobs-lambda.handler, Save.
8.3 — Set memory and timeout. Memory 1024 MB, Timeout 1 min 0 sec, Save.
8.4 — Attach the VPC. Same VPC, subnets and security group, Save. Load the same payment-lambda.zip code and copy the environment variables.
8.5 — Create the scheduler role. fitness-assistant-dev-payment-jobs-scheduler-role (trust scheduler.amazonaws.com, inline policy fitness-assistant-dev-invoke-payment-jobs for the Payment jobs Lambda only).
The runbook has no screenshot of this action.
8.6 — Name the schedule. EventBridge → Schedules → Create schedule: name fitness-assistant-dev-payment-reconciliation, Recurring schedule, Rate-based schedule, rate 5 minutes.
8.7 — Choose the target. Select the AWS Lambda — Invoke tile, pick fitness-assistant-dev-payment-jobs and enter the payload {"job": "reconciliation"}.
8.8 — Choose the settings. Keep retry on with maximum age 0 hours 5 minutes and 2 retry attempts, DLQ None, the AWS-owned key, and Use existing role with fitness-assistant-dev-payment-jobs-scheduler-role. Then click Next and create the schedule.
The banner at the top of the last three screenshots still names the previously created Gym schedule (fitness-assistant-dev-gym-referral-settlement); the form itself is for the Payment reconciliation schedule.
Every 5 minutes the reconciliation job polls the gateway for pending confirmations, retries activations and refund cancellations, and cleans up stale transactions.
Step 9 — Wire Gym to Payment Gym was deployed before Payment existed, so it has to be told about it:
9.1 — Add the variable to both Gym functions. Add PAYMENT_LAMBDA_NAME=fitness-assistant-dev-payment to both fitness-assistant-dev-gym and fitness-assistant-dev-gym-jobs (payout and referral settlement also call Payment). No PAYMENT_SERVICE_URL is needed with direct invoke.
9.2 — Extend the Gym role’s invoke policy (or add fitness-assistant-dev-gym-invoke-payment):
{ "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "lambda:InvokeFunction", "Resource": [ "arn:aws:lambda:ap-southeast-1:<account-id>:function:fitness-assistant-dev-auth", "arn:aws:lambda:ap-southeast-1:<account-id>:function:fitness-assistant-dev-user", "arn:aws:lambda:ap-southeast-1:<account-id>:function:fitness-assistant-dev-payment" ] } The runbook has no screenshots of Step 9.
The Gym scheduler role does not need this permission — the scheduler only invokes gym-jobs, and it is gym-jobs that calls Payment.
The payment loop is now closed:
Gym Lambda ──direct invoke──► Payment Lambda ──► Payment DB ──► Provider (VNPAY) │ webhook Gym Lambda ◄──callback── Payment Lambda ◄── API Gateway /payments ◄┘ The remaining work for this service is configuring at least one real sandbox provider (VNPAY first, since it is the code default) with its callback/webhook URLs, so checkout can be tested end to end.

title: Troubleshooting
content:
This page lists the real problems met while deploying and operating Gymini on AWS, how each one was found, how it was fixed, and what to check first next time. Every entry was confirmed against logs, API responses or the AWS console, not guessed.
# Problem Layer Status 1 Login blocked by CORS API Gateway Fixed 2 Chat blocked as mixed content CloudFront, ALB Fixed 3 Chat returns 503 after the environment is switched on ECS, ALB, CloudFront Fixed, one manual step remains 4 Lambda times out or returns 500 in a “cold” environment VPC, Aurora Fixed by start order 5 Chat task crashes with URL must start with postgresql:// ECS, Secrets Manager Fixed 6 Bedrock model quota is 0 on the main account Bedrock Fixed with a cross-account role 7 Bedrock calls still denied (Converse, marketplace model) IAM Fixed 8 Password-reset link never appears Auth Lambda, SMTP Worked around, controlled 9 CI/CD gates failing or refusing to start GitHub Actions, CloudFormation Fixed 10 A stale CloudFormation change set CloudFormation Avoided 1. Login blocked by CORS Symptom: the login page shows a generic error. The browser console reports that /auth/login was blocked by CORS policy because no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header is present. How it was found: a direct curl to /auth/login returned the correct 401 for a wrong password, so the service was healthy. Reading the API’s own CORS configuration showed that AllowOrigins still listed only the old S3 website URL. Fix: add the CloudFront URL to AllowOrigins with a single additive update-api --cors-configuration call, keeping the old origin. Re-test both the preflight and the real POST: both now carry access-control-allow-origin with the CloudFront domain. Next time: when the frontend moves to a new domain, update the API’s allowed origins in the same change. 2. Chat blocked as mixed content Symptom: the chat panel shows “Network Error”. Cause: the page is served over HTTPS by CloudFront, but the frontend pointed the Socket.IO client straight at the chat load balancer over plain HTTP. Browsers block that combination. The load balancer only has an HTTP listener on port 80; a custom domain and a certificate would be needed to add HTTPS. Fix: add a CloudFront origin for the load balancer (http-only towards the origin) and a behavior /socket.io/* with caching disabled and all viewer headers forwarded, then set chatWsUrl in runtime-config.json to the CloudFront domain. The browser now talks to one HTTPS origin. Verify: GET /socket.io/?EIO=4&transport=polling through CloudFront returns 200 with an Engine.IO handshake (sid, upgrades: ["websocket"]). 3. Chat returns 503 after the environment is switched on Symptom: CloudFront reaches the load balancer but the answer is 503. Causes found: (a) the ECS service had desiredCount: 0, so the target group had no healthy target; (b) the load balancer is on demand and gets a new DNS name every time it is recreated, so the CloudFront origin and the runtime configuration still pointed at the previous one. Fix: scale the ECS service to 1, point the CloudFront origin to the current load balancer DNS name, and write the HTTPS chat URL back into runtime-config.json. Wait for the distribution to finish deploying, then repeat the Engine.IO check. Next time: after dev-start, check three things in order: ECS running count, CloudFront origin domain, chatWsUrl. 4. Lambda times out or returns 500 in a “cold” environment Symptom: a call to a Lambda attached to the VPC hangs for the full 30 seconds, or later returns 500. Causes found: the NAT Gateway was switched off, so a function that needs the internet (for example to send e-mail) had no outbound path and timed out. After the NAT was back, a database-backed call returned 500 because the Aurora cluster was still stopped. Fix: bring the layers up in order: network (NAT), then the database, then the schedules. The start script does exactly this and only re-enables the EventBridge schedules after Aurora is available. Next time: a timeout points at the network path; a 500 on a database call points at the database being stopped. 5. Chat task crashes with URL must start with postgresql:// Symptom: the first Chat task fails at start and Prisma reports the invalid URL. Cause: in the task definition the two secret entries had value type Value with a secret name, so the container received the name instead of the connection string. Fix: register a new task definition revision where the secrets use ValueFrom with the full secret ARN plus the JSON key suffix, then update the service with a forced new deployment. Secrets never go into plain environment variables. 6. Bedrock model quota is 0 on the main account Symptom: every on-demand model call fails with a quota error. How it was confirmed: Service Quotas showed the account-level on-demand quota for the chosen models as 0 and not adjustable. Fix: keep the AI service on Bedrock but call it through a second AWS account that has real quota. A role in that account trusts only the AI Lambda execution roles and requires an ExternalId; the AI service assumes it with STS for each call. No static keys are stored anywhere. Result: logs show successful llm_call entries with provider: bedrock. 7. Bedrock calls still denied after the role existed Symptom: AccessDeniedException in the AI Lambda logs. Causes found: (a) bedrock:InvokeModel does not cover the Converse API, which needs its own action on the same resources; (b) a marketplace model such as the Cohere embedding model needs the calling principal to have aws-marketplace:ViewSubscriptions and aws-marketplace:Subscribe. Fix: add bedrock:Converse next to InvokeModel on the inference profile and its destination model, and add the marketplace actions as a separate small policy. Each change was checked with iam:SimulatePrincipalPolicy and then with a real call. 8. Password-reset link never appears Symptom: the reset request returns the generic message and no link, and there is no real mailbox for the seeded admin address. Cause: in non-production mode the service returns a development reset link only when e-mail is not configured. The deployed Lambda has all four SMTP settings, so it really sends and reports success even for an address that does not exist. Controlled workaround: for a few minutes, switch NODE_ENV to development and blank only SMTP_HOST on the auth Lambda, request the reset, complete it by invoking the Lambda directly, then restore the original environment from a saved copy and read it back (NODE_ENV=production, SMTP_HOST restored, all variables present). Next time: the real fix is a reachable reset flow for real users (see problem 9). 9. CI/CD gates failing or refusing to start Symptom Cause Fix A new workflow was rejected: 'name' is already defined A duplicated name: line after combining a header and a body Remove the duplicate line, diff against the original A manual workflow does not appear in the list workflow_dispatch only works for workflows on the default branch (master) Copy the two manual workflows to master byte for byte The apply job failed on an AccessDenied for cloudformation:GetTemplate The apply role could not read the change set’s template Add that one action, scoped to the single stack, and verify with a policy simulation The post-apply check failed on every correct apply It treated the 10 known source-only routes as a failure Add an opt-in -AllowKnownSourceOnly switch, used only by that step; mismatched routes still fail A pull request showed 104 commits and 1,215 files The branch was cut from a local tip with many unpushed commits Cut a new branch from the real remote tip and cherry-pick the single commit 10. A stale CloudFormation change set Symptom: an old change set with no changes looked safe to apply. Cause: it carried the load balancer DNS name from the day it was created, and that load balancer no longer existed. The digest check only proves the template is unchanged, not that baked-in parameter values are still current. Fix: do not apply it. Create a fresh plan, which has the current parameter value, and apply that one.

title: AI Service — database, queue and Bedrock
content:
The AI Service is split into three Lambdas, each with a different timing requirement:
Function Handler Timeout Job fitness-assistant-dev-ai dist/lambda.handler 29–30 s HTTP API: chat, plans, marketplace, admin AI. Long generations are queued instead of run inline. fitness-assistant-dev-ai-worker dist/worker-lambda.handler 300 s Consumes the SQS queue and runs long workout/nutrition generations on Nova Pro. fitness-assistant-dev-ai-jobs dist/jobs-lambda.handler 600 s Scheduled jobs: personalized-service auto-accept and knowledge ingestion (PubMed, RSS, web, local evidence). Before deploying, the code was updated so that the AI Lambda verifies Bearer JWTs by invoking the Auth Lambda, calls Auth/User/Fitness/Payment by direct invoke, and its migration Lambda reads DATABASE_SECRET_ID and creates fitness_assistant_ai on its own.
In every screenshot below, the red rectangles mark what to fill in or click for the sub-step written just above it.
Step 1 — Database secret No CREATE DATABASE by hand: the migration Lambda connects to the postgres maintenance database, checks pg_database, creates fitness_assistant_ai if missing, then runs prisma migrate deploy, and refuses to run against any other database.
1.1 — Choose the type and fill in the pairs. Secrets Manager → Store a new secret, choose Other type of secret, enter the same five pairs as the other services with database = fitness_assistant_ai, then click Next.
1.2 — Name the secret. Enter fitness-assistant/dev/ai-database and click Next (then store it).
Step 2 — Migration role and Lambda 2.1 — Create the role. fitness-assistant-dev-ai-migrate-role: AWS service → Lambda with the two managed policies (AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole, AWSLambdaVPCAccessExecutionRole).
The runbook has no screenshot of the role creation; the form is the same as in Step 5.
2.2 — Add the secret policy. On the role, Add permissions → Create inline policy → JSON: allow secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on fitness-assistant/dev/ai-database*, then click Next and name it fitness-assistant-dev-ai-migrate-secret.
2.3 — Fill in the function. Lambda → Create function, Author from scratch, name fitness-assistant-dev-ai-migrate, runtime Node.js 22.x (x86_64), custom execution role fitness-assistant-dev-ai-migrate-role, then Create function.
2.4 — Set memory and timeout. Configuration → General configuration → Edit: Memory 1024 MB, Timeout 5 min 0 sec, Save.
2.5 — Set the handler. Code → Runtime settings → Edit: dist/migrate-lambda.handler, Save.
2.6 — Upload the code. Upload from → .zip file, choose ai-migrate-lambda.zip (~21 MiB, so a direct upload is enough) and click Update.
2.7 — Attach the VPC. Configuration → VPC → Edit: the project VPC, both private app subnets and fitness-assistant-dev-lambda-sg, Save.
2.8 — Add the environment variables. NODE_ENV=production, DATABASE_SECRET_ID=fitness-assistant/dev/ai-database, AI_DATABASE_NAME=fitness_assistant_ai. The screenshot shows the saved result; the Edit button is where you add them.
Step 3 — Run the 22 migrations 3.1 — Create the test event. On the Test tab choose Create new event, name it test-db-ai, keep {} (or {"database": "fitness_assistant_ai"}) and click Test.
3.2 — Read the result. The execution must succeed with the response below.
Expected result: status = ok, database = fitness_assistant_ai, databaseCreated = true, migrateExitCode = 0, 22 migrations found, All migrations have been successfully applied. The 22 migrations contain no DROP or TRUNCATE — only one de-duplication DELETE that does not affect a new database.
Step 4 — SQS queues SQS replaces Redis/BullMQ for AI plan generation in AWS.
4.1 — Create the dead-letter queue. SQS → Create queue, type Standard, name fitness-assistant-dev-ai-tasks-dlq, keep the defaults and click Create queue.
4.2 — Check the DLQ. The banner must say the queue was created.
4.3 — Name the main queue and set the visibility timeout. Create queue, Standard, name fitness-assistant-dev-ai-tasks, Visibility timeout 10 Minutes — longer than the Worker’s 300 s timeout, so a message is not redelivered while still being processed.
4.4 — Enable the dead-letter queue. Scroll to Dead-letter queue, choose Enabled, pick the ARN of fitness-assistant-dev-ai-tasks-dlq and set Maximum receives to 2.
4.5 — Create the queue. Review the redrive section and click Create queue.
Copy the queue URL (https://sqs.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com/<account-id>/fitness-assistant-dev-ai-tasks) — it becomes AI_TASKS_QUEUE_URL.
Step 5 — Role for the AI HTTP Lambda 5.1 — Choose the trusted entity. IAM → Roles → Create role: AWS service, use case Lambda, Next.
5.2 — Name the role. fitness-assistant-dev-ai-lambda-role.
5.3 — Check the managed policies. AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole and AWSLambdaVPCAccessExecutionRole, then create the role.
5.4 — Write the runtime policy. On the role open Add permissions → Create inline policy → JSON and paste:
{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "secretsmanager:GetSecretValue", "Resource": "arn:aws:secretsmanager:ap-southeast-1:<account-id>:secret:fitness-assistant/dev/ai-database*" }, { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "sqs:SendMessage", "Resource": "arn:aws:sqs:ap-southeast-1:<account-id>:fitness-assistant-dev-ai-tasks" }, { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "lambda:InvokeFunction", "Resource": [ "arn:aws:lambda:ap-southeast-1:<account-id>:function:fitness-assistant-dev-auth", "arn:aws:lambda:ap-southeast-1:<account-id>:function:fitness-assistant-dev-user", "arn:aws:lambda:ap-southeast-1:<account-id>:function:fitness-assistant-dev-fitness", "arn:aws:lambda:ap-southeast-1:<account-id>:function:fitness-assistant-dev-payment" ] } ] } 5.5 — Name and create the policy. fitness-assistant-dev-ai-runtime-policy, then Create policy.
5.6 — Check the role. The runtime policy must appear next to the two managed policies.
Gym is not in the list because the AI code never calls it. The HTTP Lambda can only send to the queue; consuming is the Worker’s job.
Step 6 — Create the AI HTTP Lambda 6.1 — Fill in the function. Lambda → Create function, name fitness-assistant-dev-ai, runtime Node.js 22.x (x86_64); under Additional settings → Custom execution role choose fitness-assistant-dev-ai-lambda-role and click Save, then Create function.
6.2 — Upload the code. Upload from → .zip file, ai-lambda.zip (34.68 MB), Update.
6.3 — Set the handler. dist/lambda.handler, Save.
6.4 — Set memory and timeout. Memory 1024 MB, Timeout 0 min 30 sec (later 29 s, just under API Gateway’s integration limit), Save.
6.5 — Attach the VPC. Private app subnets and the Lambda security group, Save.
6.6 — Add the first environment. It still targeted the Anthropic API (LLM_PROVIDER=anthropic, called through the NAT Gateway because the endpoint is outside AWS). AI_TASKS_QUEUE_URL is the queue URL from Step 4.
6.7 — Save. The same list scrolled down to the Save button.
Step 7 — Switch to Amazon Bedrock 7.1 — Look at the model catalog. In Amazon Bedrock → Model catalog (region ap-southeast-1) filter on the providers Anthropic and Cohere.
7.2 — Check Nova and Cohere. Filter on Amazon and Cohere: Amazon Nova Pro and Cohere Embed Multilingual are both available. Decision: no Anthropic API key needed — the AI Service moved to Bedrock, which removes the external API key, keeps traffic on AWS and is billed through the same account. Cohere is a Marketplace model: accept its subscription/EULA once as an administrator (5.3.1).
7.3 — Add the Bedrock statements. Add these statements to fitness-assistant-dev-ai-runtime-policy (without removing the existing ones):
{ "Sid": "InvokeNovaProApacInferenceProfile", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "bedrock:InvokeModel", "Resource": ["arn:aws:bedrock:ap-southeast-1:<account-id>:inference-profile/apac.amazon.nova-pro-v1:0"] }, { "Sid": "InvokeNovaProOnlyThroughApacProfile", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "bedrock:InvokeModel", "Resource": ["arn:aws:bedrock:*::foundation-model/amazon.nova-pro-v1:0"], "Condition": { "StringLike": { "bedrock:InferenceProfileArn": "arn:aws:bedrock:ap-southeast-1:<account-id>:inference-profile/apac.amazon.nova-pro-v1:0" } } }, { "Sid": "InvokeCohereEmbedMultilingualV3", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "bedrock:InvokeModel", "Resource": ["arn:aws:bedrock:ap-southeast-1::foundation-model/cohere.embed-multilingual-v3"] } A cross-region inference profile can route to the foundation model in several APAC regions, so IAM must allow both the profile and the underlying foundation model — the condition limits the second statement to calls made through this profile. AmazonBedrockFullAccess and bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream are not added; the code only uses InvokeModel.
The runbook has no screenshot of editing this policy; the same three statements are visible in the Worker role editor in Step 8.3.
7.4 — Upload the Bedrock build. Upload the new ai-lambda.zip (35,076,525 bytes compressed, 105,103,760 bytes uncompressed — it bundles the Bedrock Runtime SDK and the Prisma rhel-openssl-3.0.x engine) and keep the handler and VPC.
7.5 — Replace the environment.
Variable Value NODE_ENV production DATABASE_SECRET_ID fitness-assistant/dev/ai-database INTERNAL_SERVICE_SECRET the shared value AUTH_LAMBDA_NAME, USER_LAMBDA_NAME, FITNESS_LAMBDA_NAME, PAYMENT_LAMBDA_NAME the four function names QUEUE_PROVIDER / AI_TASKS_QUEUE_URL sqs / the queue URL LLM_PROVIDER / BEDROCK_REGION bedrock / ap-southeast-1 BEDROCK_CHAT_MODEL / BEDROCK_VISION_MODEL apac.amazon.nova-pro-v1:0 EMBEDDING_PROVIDER / BEDROCK_EMBEDDING_MODEL bedrock / cohere.embed-multilingual-v3 KNOWLEDGE_VECTOR_SIZE 1024 LLM_TIMEOUT_MS 25000 PLATFORM_COMMISSION_RATE / PERSONALIZED_SERVICE_AUTO_ACCEPT_DAYS 0.10 / 3 ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, LLM_BASE_URL and OLLAMA_BASE_URL are removed. No migration is needed for the switch — the schema did not change.
The embedding dimension changed from 768 (Ollama, local development) to 1024 (Cohere). The code fails loudly if it is asked to write 1024-dimension vectors into an old 768-dimension index instead of corrupting it, so knowledge ingestion stays disabled until a 1024-dimension vector store exists — see 5.4.9.
Step 8 — AI Worker role Role fitness-assistant-dev-ai-worker-role with the two managed policies and the inline fitness-assistant-dev-ai-worker-runtime-policy. Not added: AmazonBedrockFullAccess, AmazonSQSFullAccess, AWSLambdaFullAccess.
8.1 — Name the role. fitness-assistant-dev-ai-worker-role, description “Execution role for Gymini AI Worker Lambda”.
8.2 — Check the managed policies and create the role. Click Create role.
8.3 — Write the runtime policy. The JSON contains: the AI secret; sqs:ReceiveMessage, sqs:DeleteMessage, sqs:GetQueueAttributes on fitness-assistant-dev-ai-tasks; invoke on Auth/User/Fitness/Payment; and the same three Bedrock statements as in Step 7.3.
8.4 — Name and create the policy. fitness-assistant-dev-ai-worker-runtime-policy, Create policy. The summary lists Bedrock, Lambda, Secrets Manager and SQS.
The resulting flow:
AI HTTP Lambda ──sqs:SendMessage──► fitness-assistant-dev-ai-tasks ──ReceiveMessage──► AI Worker Lambda ├── Nova Pro ├── Cohere Embed ├── Aurora └── internal Lambdas Step 9 — AI Worker Lambda 9.1 — Fill in the function. Lambda → Create function, name fitness-assistant-dev-ai-worker, runtime Node.js 22.x (x86_64), and in the custom execution role panel choose fitness-assistant-dev-ai-worker-role, Save.
9.2 — Create the function. Check Additional settings (the custom execution role is the Worker role) and click Create function.
9.3 — Upload the code. Upload from → .zip file → Choose file: ai-worker-lambda.zip (the new Bedrock build), then Update.
9.4 — Set the handler. dist/worker-lambda.handler (not dist/lambda.handler), Save.
9.5 — Set memory and timeout. Memory 1024 MB, Timeout 5 min 0 sec (300 s), ephemeral storage stays 512 MB, Save.
9.6 — Attach the VPC. Private app subnets only (never the DB subnets) and the Lambda security group, Save.
9.7 — Add the environment. Copy the HTTP Lambda’s environment with one important change: LLM_TIMEOUT_MS=180000 instead of 25000, because generations can run for minutes. AWS_REGION is not set manually (Lambda provides it), and no Anthropic/Ollama/Redis variables are needed.
Step 10 — SQS trigger for the Worker 10.1 — Check the queue. Open fitness-assistant-dev-ai-tasks: default visibility timeout 10 minutes, Dead-letter queue: Enabled, DLQ fitness-assistant-dev-ai-tasks-dlq, maximum receives 2.
10.2 — Open Add trigger. Lambda → fitness-assistant-dev-ai-worker → Configuration → Triggers — it says No triggers. Click Add trigger.
10.3 — Configure the SQS trigger. Source SQS, queue fitness-assistant-dev-ai-tasks, Activate trigger ticked, Batch size 1, batch window 0, no maximum concurrency, Report batch item failures ticked (the Worker returns batchItemFailures, so one failed message does not force the whole batch to retry), then Add.
10.4 — Check the trigger. The banner says it was added and the Triggers list shows the SQS queue.
Step 11 — AI Jobs role and Lambda Role fitness-assistant-dev-ai-jobs-role (two managed policies + inline fitness-assistant-dev-ai-jobs-runtime-policy: the AI secret and the three Bedrock statements — Cohere for embeddings, Nova for LLM/safety judging).
11.1 — Choose the trusted entity. AWS service, use case Lambda, Next.
11.2 — Name the role. fitness-assistant-dev-ai-jobs-role.
11.3 — Check the managed policies and create the role.
11.4 — Write the runtime policy. The JSON holds the secret statement and the three Bedrock statements.
11.5 — Name and create the policy. fitness-assistant-dev-ai-jobs-runtime-policy, Create policy. The summary lists Bedrock and Secrets Manager.
11.6 — Check the role. The role now has three policies.
11.7 — Fill in the function. fitness-assistant-dev-ai-jobs, Node.js 22.x, custom execution role fitness-assistant-dev-ai-jobs-role, Create function.
11.8 — Upload the code. ai-lambda.zip (35.08 MB), Update.
11.9 — Set the handler. dist/jobs-lambda.handler, Save.
11.10 — Set memory and timeout. Memory 1024 MB, Timeout 10 min 0 sec (600 s — crawling plus embedding is long-running I/O and is not bound by API Gateway’s ~30 s limit), Save.
11.11 — Attach the VPC. Private app subnets and the Lambda security group, Save.
11.12 — Add the environment. NODE_ENV, DATABASE_SECRET_ID, the shared INTERNAL_SERVICE_SECRET, LLM_PROVIDER=bedrock, BEDROCK_REGION, BEDROCK_CHAT_MODEL, BEDROCK_VISION_MODEL, EMBEDDING_PROVIDER=bedrock, BEDROCK_EMBEDDING_MODEL, KNOWLEDGE_VECTOR_SIZE=1024, then Save.
No schedule is attached yet: the knowledge jobs must not run until the 1024-dimension vector store exists. That is the next page.

title: AI Service — vector search, scheduling and API
content:
The local development stack used Qdrant as the vector store. For AWS, the code was given a vector-store abstraction with an OpenSearch implementation (58/58 tests passing), so production no longer needs QDRANT_HOST / QDRANT_PORT. Requests to OpenSearch are signed with SigV4 (service aoss) using each Lambda’s IAM role — there is no OpenSearch username, password or API key.
In every screenshot below, the red rectangles mark what to fill in or click for the sub-step written just above it.
Step 1 — Re-upload the three AI Lambdas The new build includes the OpenSearch client and SigV4 support (HTTP/Worker ZIP ≈ 36,325,814 bytes), so it is uploaded first, keeping each handler. For each function use Code → Upload from → .zip file (or S3) and click Update:
Function Artifact Handler fitness-assistant-dev-ai ai-lambda.zip dist/lambda.handler fitness-assistant-dev-ai-worker ai-worker-lambda.zip dist/worker-lambda.handler fitness-assistant-dev-ai-jobs ai-lambda.zip dist/jobs-lambda.handler No database migration is required for this change.
The runbook has no screenshot of this re-upload; the dialog is the same as in 5.4.8 Step 6.2.
Step 2 — Collection group with scale-to-zero 2.1 — Name the group. Amazon OpenSearch Service → Serverless → Collection groups → Create collection group: name fitness-assistant-dev-ai, generation NextGen, description “Gymini AI vector search collection group”.
2.2 — Set the capacity. Scroll to Capacity management and set:
Capacity Min Max Indexing 0 OCU 2 OCU Search 0 OCU 2 OCU Then click Create. A minimum of 0 enables scale-to-zero: after about 10 idle minutes indexing and search drop to 0 OCU, and the first request after that can take an extra 10–30 seconds to wake up. A 0–2 OCU range is far more sensible for DEV than the default maximum of 96.
2.3 — Check the group. The list must show fitness-assistant-dev-ai, NextGen, indexing 0 / 2 OCUs and search 0 / 2 OCUs.
Step 3 — Private VPC endpoint 3.1 — Open the VPC endpoints page. OpenSearch Service → Serverless → VPC endpoints and click Create VPC endpoint. The page itself warns that it manages endpoints for Classic collections and that NextGen collections use the Amazon EC2 VPC endpoints console — keep that in mind if the endpoint does not show up in the NextGen collection later.
3.2 — Fill in the endpoint. Name fitness-dev-opensearch-vpce, VPC fitness-assistant-dev-vpc, subnets private-app-a and private-app-b. The runbook specifies the existing fitness-assistant-dev-vpce-sg (TCP 443 from the Lambda SG); the endpoint captured below shows the Lambda SG attached — whichever group is attached must allow inbound TCP 443 from the Lambda security group. Wait for Available (the screenshot was taken while it was still Pending) and note the endpoint ID (vpce-…, not the endpoint URL).
Step 4 — Vector search collection 4.1 — Start the collection. Serverless → Collections → Create collection.
4.2 — Name it and choose the type. NextGen, name fitness-assistant-dev-ai-vectors, description “Gymini AI vector store for RAG and knowledge retrieval”, collection type Vector search.
4.3 — Choose Standard create and the group. Choose Standard create (not Express — private networking and access policies must be controlled), Select existing collection group and pick fitness-assistant-dev-ai.
4.4 — Network access. Keep the AWS-owned encryption key, choose access type Private (recommended), tick VPC endpoints for access and select the endpoint from Step 3 — no public access.
4.5 — Data access policy, part 1. Create as a new data access policy, name fitness-dev-ai-vector-access, definition method JSON rather than ticking permissions in the visual editor.
4.6 — Data access policy, part 2. Paste the JSON:
[ { "Description": "Fitness Assistant AI vector data access", "Rules": [ { "ResourceType": "collection", "Resource": ["collection/fitness-assistant-dev-ai-vectors"], "Permission": ["aoss:DescribeCollectionItems"] }, { "ResourceType": "index", "Resource": ["index/fitness-assistant-dev-ai-vectors/*"], "Permission": [ "aoss:CreateIndex", "aoss:DescribeIndex", "aoss:UpdateIndex", "aoss:ReadDocument", "aoss:WriteDocument" ] } ], "Principal": [ "arn:aws:iam::<account-id>:role/fitness-assistant-dev-ai-lambda-role", "arn:aws:iam::<account-id>:role/fitness-assistant-dev-ai-worker-role", "arn:aws:iam::<account-id>:role/fitness-assistant-dev-ai-jobs-role" ] } ] aoss:DeleteIndex is deliberately not granted.
4.7 — OpenSearch UI. The wizard also creates an OpenSearch application and workspace for browsing the data: Create new OpenSearch application aoss-fitness-dev-ai and Create new workspace fitness-dev-ai-vectors.
4.8 — Administrators and creation. Leave IAM Identity Center unticked, grant administrator permission to the account’s IAM principal only, then click Create collection.
4.9 — Wait for creation. The page shows “Creating collection”; do not navigate away until the collection details page appears.
When the collection is Active, copy its ARN (for IAM) and OpenSearch endpoint (https://<collection-id>.aoss.ap-southeast-1.on.aws, for the Lambdas) with the console’s copy buttons. Indexes are not created by hand.
Step 5 — IAM permission on all three AI roles The data access policy and IAM are two separate layers; missing either one returns 403. Do the two sub-steps below for each of fitness-assistant-dev-ai-lambda-role, -ai-worker-role and -ai-jobs-role (the screenshots show the first one).
5.1 — Paste the policy. IAM → Roles → the role → Add permissions → Create inline policy → JSON:
{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "AccessAiVectorCollection", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "aoss:APIAccessAll", "Resource": "arn:aws:aoss:ap-southeast-1:<account-id>:collection/<collection-id>" } ] } Not used: AmazonOpenSearchServerlessFullAccess, aoss:DashboardsAccessAll, aoss:* — the Lambdas only need the data-plane API.
5.2 — Name and create it. fitness-assistant-dev-opensearch-access, Create policy.
Step 6 — Environment variables 6.1 — Add the variables on all three AI Lambdas (Configuration → Environment variables → Edit), and remove QDRANT_HOST / QDRANT_PORT if present:
VECTOR_STORE_PROVIDER=opensearch OPENSEARCH_REGION=ap-southeast-1 OPENSEARCH_SERVERLESS_ENDPOINT=https://<collection-id>.aoss.ap-southeast-1.on.aws KNOWLEDGE_VECTOR_SIZE=1024 The Worker keeps LLM_TIMEOUT_MS=180000. The screenshot shows the three OpenSearch rows on the AI Lambda and the Save button (KNOWLEDGE_VECTOR_SIZE was already set in 5.4.8).
Amazon Bedrock / \ Nova Pro Cohere Embed (1024) │ ▼ OpenSearch Serverless (NextGen) ▲ ┌───────────────┼───────────────┐ AI HTTP AI Worker AI Jobs Step 7 — Let the code create the indexes No action in the console. The collection shows Indexes: - and stays that way: the indexes exercises, fitness_knowledge, fitness_faq and fitness_evidence are bootstrapped by the code on first use with the exact mapping it expects — vector field vector, type knn_vector, dimension 1024, engine faiss, method hnsw, space cosinesimil. If an index exists with the wrong dimension the code fails instead of deleting data.
Step 8 — Scheduler role for the AI jobs 8.1 — Choose the custom trust policy. IAM → Roles → Create role, choose Custom trust policy and paste a statement with principal scheduler.amazonaws.com and action sts:AssumeRole.
8.2 — Name the role. fitness-assistant-dev-ai-jobs-scheduler-role, then Create role.
8.3 — Write the inline policy. On the role, Add permissions → Create inline policy → JSON: lambda:InvokeFunction on fitness-assistant-dev-ai-jobs only.
8.4 — Name and create it. fitness-assistant-dev-invoke-ai-jobs, Create policy.
Step 9 — Five schedules 9.1 — Name the auto-accept schedule. EventBridge → Schedules → Create schedule: name fitness-assistant-dev-ai-autoaccept, Recurring schedule, Rate-based schedule.
9.2 — Set the rate. 15 minutes, flexible time window Off, then Next.
9.3 — Choose the target. Click the AWS Lambda — Invoke tile, pick fitness-assistant-dev-ai-jobs and enter the payload {"job": "personalized-service-autoaccept-sweep"}.
9.4 — Choose the settings. Keep the schedule enabled, retry on with maximum age 0 hours 5 minutes, 2 retry attempts and DLQ None.
9.5 — Choose the role. Use existing role: fitness-assistant-dev-ai-jobs-scheduler-role, then Next and create the schedule.
9.6 — Create the four nightly schedules the same way, but cron-based, time zone Asia/Ho_Chi_Minh so they run at night Vietnam time:
Schedule Expression Payload fitness-assistant-dev-ai-local-evidence cron(0 2 * * ? *) {"job":"local-evidence-refresh"} fitness-assistant-dev-ai-pubmed cron(30 2 * * ? *) {"job":"pubmed-refresh"} fitness-assistant-dev-ai-rss cron(0 3 * * ? *) {"job":"rss-refresh"} fitness-assistant-dev-ai-web cron(30 3 * * ? *) {"job":"web-refresh"} The runbook has no screenshots of the four cron schedules.
EventBridge Scheduler → AI Jobs Lambda → PubMed / RSS / Web / Local → Cohere Embed Multilingual v3 (1024) → OpenSearch Serverless → fitness_knowledge / fitness_evidence … Step 10 — Connect the AI Lambda to API Gateway 10.1 — Create the integration. API Gateway → fitness-assistant-dev-api → Integrations → Create: Lambda function, region ap-southeast-1, pick fitness-assistant-dev-ai, payload format 2.0, keep Grant API Gateway permission to invoke your Lambda function, then Create.
10.2 — Create and attach eight routes.
ANY /ai ANY /ai/{proxy+} ANY /plans ANY /plans/{proxy+} ANY /marketplace ANY /marketplace/{proxy+} ANY /admin/ai ANY /admin/ai/{proxy+} The greedy routes cover POST /ai/ask, GET /ai/conversations, POST /ai/agent/goal-image, POST /plans/workout/generate, GET /plans/job/{id}, GET /admin/ai/overview and so on. Route authorization stays NONE: the AI Lambda verifies the Bearer JWT itself through the Auth Lambda and rejects spoofed x-user-id / x-user-role headers, so adding an API Gateway JWT authorizer would create a second, inconsistent auth layer. /internal/*, /metrics and /{proxy+} are not created.
10.3 — Check one route. Under Attach integrations to routes, select ANY /admin/ai; the details must show fitness-assistant-dev-ai.
Step 11 — Payment → AI After a successful payment, Payment activates the personalized service by invoking the AI Lambda’s internal endpoint POST /internal/personalized-service/orders/:id/activate-after-payment (idempotent, so retries are safe).
11.1 — Add the variable. Add AI_LAMBDA_NAME=fitness-assistant-dev-ai to both fitness-assistant-dev-payment and fitness-assistant-dev-payment-jobs.
11.2 — Allow the invoke. Add to the Payment role:
{ "Sid": "InvokeAiService", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "lambda:InvokeFunction", "Resource": "arn:aws:lambda:ap-southeast-1:<account-id>:function:fitness-assistant-dev-ai" } The runbook has no screenshot of the policy edit.
No public URL, /internal route or Lambda Function URL is created for this. The chain is now: user → AI marketplace → Payment → provider → webhook/reconciliation → Payment Lambda → (direct invoke) AI Lambda → activate service.
Step 12 — Rate-limit the AI routes to protect Bedrock cost The old application gateway limited /ai/ask to 20 requests per 60 seconds, and the AI Service has no per-user token budget, so without a limit a frontend bug could send hundreds of billable Bedrock calls. In API Gateway → fitness-assistant-dev-api → Stages → $default → route throttling, limit only the AI routes (not the whole API):
Route Rate (req/s) Burst ANY /ai, ANY /ai/{proxy+} 1 3 ANY /plans, ANY /plans/{proxy+} 1 3 ANY /marketplace, ANY /marketplace/{proxy+} 3 6 ANY /admin/ai, ANY /admin/ai/{proxy+} 1 3 The runbook has no screenshot of the throttling settings.
API Gateway uses a token bucket and returns HTTP 429 when the limit is exceeded; the limits are best-effort targets, not hard ceilings, and they apply per route, not per user. The frontend must show a “too many requests, try again later” message with backoff instead of retrying in a loop. Usage plans / API keys (a REST API feature) and Lambda reserved concurrency (which would throttle all AI routes together) are deliberately not used.
The full AI path now has: JWT → API Gateway route throttling → AI HTTP Lambda (Auth, Aurora, Nova Pro, Cohere, OpenSearch, SQS) → AI Worker; EventBridge → AI Jobs → OpenSearch; Payment → AI internal endpoint.

title: Week 9 Worklog
content:
Week 9 Objectives: Reflect on the Fitness Assistant AWS deployment so far and write it up as a technical case study Look into AWS CloudFormation as a way to close the “no CI/CD yet” gap already tracked in the Workshop Work Completed This Week: Task Start Date Completion Date Reference Materials Wrote Blog 2, “Challenges and Cost Optimization in AWS Deployment: Lessons Learned from Gymini”, as a technical case study, and shared it to the AWS Study Group VN Facebook group 28-9-2026 03-10-2026 AWS CloudFormation User Guide AWS Well-Architected Framework — Cost Optimization Pillar Post on Facebook Week 9 Results: Overview:
This week was dedicated to reviewing the AWS deployment experience so far, writing it up as Blog 2 and sharing it with the AWS Study Group VN: why a multi-service deployment is not a one-day task, the concrete troubleshooting incidents already documented in the Workshop (the Chat service’s secret-value mistake, Lambda’s secret caching), and why AWS CloudFormation is worth adopting given that deployment today is entirely manual.
Theoretical Knowledge Gained:
Free Tier vs. promotional credit vs. pay-as-you-go: three different things, and having credit does not mean the infrastructure is free — it only postpones real billing. Fixed-cost vs. usage-based resources: most of this project’s services bill by usage, but a few (NAT Gateway, Aurora’s capacity floor, the Chat Fargate task, the ALB, VPC endpoints, public IPv4) bill by the hour regardless of traffic, which is exactly the resource profile already estimated in the Proposal’s budget. AWS CloudFormation: stacks, templates, parameters, outputs, Change Sets, drift detection, and — importantly — what it does not guarantee (cost reduction, or that deleting a stack removes every resource). Technical Writing: structuring a case study that separates confirmed facts from reasonable inference, instead of presenting everything as equally certain. Hands-on Labs Completed:
Wrote Blog 2 as a case study, pulling concrete evidence from the Workshop pages already written (5.2.6, 5.2.7, 5.4.10) instead of writing generic advice, and published it to the AWS Study Group VN Facebook group Application to Fitness Assistant:
Writing this case study turned into an honest audit of the project’s own operational gaps:
No CI/CD pipeline yet — every deployment step in 5.4 is done by hand through the console No CloudWatch alarms and no AWS Budgets alert yet (5.2.6, 5.2.7) A documented but not yet executed clean-up order (5.7) CloudFormation (or the Terraform already named in the proposed target architecture) is the natural next step once the project moves past manual deployment Related Workshop Links: 3.2 Blog 2 - Challenges and Cost Optimization in AWS Deployment 5.2.7 Cost Optimization and Clean-up - The real fixed-cost items this case study is grounded in

title: Chat Service on ECS Fargate
content:
Chat is the only service that does not run on Lambda: Socket.IO keeps a connection open for the whole chat session, which does not fit Lambda’s per-invocation model. It runs as one container on ECS Fargate, behind its own Application Load Balancer.
In every screenshot below, the red rectangles mark what to fill in or click for the sub-step written just above it.
Item Value Logical database fitness_assistant_chat (3 Prisma migrations) Secrets fitness-assistant/dev/chat-database (migration), fitness-assistant/dev/chat-database-url (runtime), fitness-assistant/dev/internal-service-secret Image ECR fitness-assistant-dev-chat:dev-20260922-1 Runtime Cluster fitness-assistant-dev-cluster, service fitness-assistant-dev-chat-service, task definition fitness-assistant-dev-chat — 0.5 vCPU / 1 GB, container port 3005 Entry points Socket.IO → ALB fitness-assistant-dev-chat-alb (HTTP 80); REST → API Gateway ANY /chat/{proxy+} → ALB Internet ─:80─► chat-alb-sg ─:3005─► chat-sg (Fargate task, private subnets) ─:5432─► aurora-sg Part A — Database Step 1 — Database secret. Reuse the username/password/host/port of a working database secret and change only the database name. The secret only stores connection details — the database itself is created by the migration Lambda.
1.1 — Open Secrets Manager. The list shows the existing secrets (AI, payment, gym, fitness, user, base). Click Store a new secret.
1.2 — Paste the JSON. Choose Other type of secret, open the Plaintext tab and replace the content with the JSON below (placeholders — use the real Aurora credentials; the screenshot’s own placeholders are in Vietnamese).
{ "username": "<Aurora username>", "password": "<Aurora password>", "host": "fitness-assistant-dev-aurora.cluster-<id>.ap-southeast-1.rds.amazonaws.com", "port": 5432, "database": "fitness_assistant_chat" } 1.3 — Name it. Name fitness-assistant/dev/chat-database, description “Chat Service Aurora PostgreSQL database – dev”, then Next. The default aws/secretsmanager key stays.
1.4 — Leave rotation off. Keep Automatic rotation off and click Next.
1.5 — Store it. Review the summary and click Store.
Step 2 — Migration role. fitness-assistant-dev-chat-migrate-role (“Execution role for Chat Service database migration Lambda”) with AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole + AWSLambdaVPCAccessExecutionRole and the inline policy fitness-assistant-dev-chat-migrate-secret (secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on fitness-assistant/dev/chat-database* only). No Bedrock, SQS, OpenSearch or invoke permissions — the migration needs only logs, VPC access and its secret.
2.1 — Start the role. IAM → Roles → Create role.
2.2 — Trusted entity. AWS service, use case Lambda, Next.
2.3 — Pick the managed policies. Search AWSLambdaVPCAccessExecutionRole and tick it next to AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole (2 selected), then Next.
2.4 — Name the role. fitness-assistant-dev-chat-migrate-role, description “Execution role for Chat Service database migration Lambda”.
2.5 — Create the role. The summary lists the two managed policies; click Create role.
2.6 — Add an inline policy. On the new role click Add permissions → Create inline policy.
2.7 — Write the policy. Switch to JSON and allow secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on arn:aws:secretsmanager:ap-southeast-1:<account-id>:secret:fitness-assistant/dev/chat-database*.
2.8 — Name and create it. fitness-assistant-dev-chat-migrate-secret, Create policy.
2.9 — Check the role. It now has three permission entries.
Step 3 — Migration Lambda. At this point the account already ran 15 functions.
3.1 — Open the function list. Lambda → Functions shows 15 functions; click Create function.
3.2 — Fill in the function. Author from scratch, name fitness-assistant-dev-chat-migrate, runtime Node.js 22.x (x86_64), and in the custom execution role panel choose fitness-assistant-dev-chat-migrate-role, Save.
3.3 — Create it. Check that the custom execution role is the migrate role and click Create function.
3.4 — Upload the code. Upload from → .zip file with backend/services/chat-service/artifacts/chat-migrate-lambda.zip, then Update.
The runbook has no screenshot of this upload; the dialog is the same as in 5.4.8 Step 2.6.
3.5 — Set the handler. Code → Runtime settings → Edit: dist/migrate-lambda.handler, Save.
3.6 — Set memory and timeout. Memory 1024 MB, Timeout 1 min 0 sec, Save.
3.7 — Open the environment variables. There are none yet; click Edit.
3.8 — Add the variable. DATABASE_SECRET_ID = fitness-assistant/dev/chat-database, Save.
3.9 — Open the VPC settings. No VPC is configured yet; click Edit.
3.10 — Attach the VPC. The project VPC, both private app subnets and the Lambda SG, Save.
Step 4 — Run the migration.
4.1 — Create the test event. On the Test tab choose Create new event, name chat-migrate, keep {} and click Test.
4.2 — Read the result. Expected: status: ok, database: fitness_assistant_chat, databaseCreated: true (false if it already existed), migrateExitCode: 0, 3 migrations applied. If it fails, record the error instead of re-running it repeatedly.
Part B — Container image Step 5 — ECR repository.
5.1 — Open ECR. The private repositories (8) come from the earlier container phase. Click Create repository.
5.2 — Fill in the repository. Private, name fitness-assistant-dev-chat, tag mutability Mutable (tags are reused during DEV; production should use commit-based tags such as git-a84f23c), AES-256 encryption, then Create. The scan-on-push option now shows as “deprecated” in this console.
Step 6 — Push the image from PowerShell on the workstation. Build only if the image is missing:
docker images gymini-chat-service # only if missing: docker build --platform linux/amd64 -t gymini-chat-service:aws-local -f backend/services/chat-service/Dockerfile . aws ecr get-login-password --region ap-southeast-1 | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin <account-id>.dkr.ecr.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com docker tag gymini-chat-service:aws-local <account-id>.dkr.ecr.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com/fitness-assistant-dev-chat:dev-20260922-1 docker push <account-id>.dkr.ecr.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com/fitness-assistant-dev-chat:dev-20260922-1 6.1 — Check the local image. Run docker images gymini-chat-service; the image gymini-chat-service:aws-local (146 MB compressed) must be listed.
6.2 — Log in to ECR. Run the aws ecr get-login-password … | docker login … line. Login Succeeded must appear before tagging; 'aws' is not recognized, Unable to locate credentials or AccessDeniedException mean stopping to fix the CLI setup first.
6.3 — Tag the image. Run docker tag … with the ECR URI and the tag dev-20260922-1.
6.4 — Push. Run docker push …; every layer must say Pushed and the last line shows the digest.
6.5 — Check in ECR. Open the repository: the tag dev-20260922-1 is listed (image index plus its two images).
Part C — Logs and IAM Step 7 — Log group.
7.1 — Create it. CloudWatch → Log groups → Create log group: name /ecs/fitness-assistant-dev-chat (ECS convention, not /aws/lambda/...), retention 1 month (30 days), then Create.
7.2 — Check the list. Filter the log group list for /ecs/fitness-assistant-dev-chat.
Step 8 — Task execution role (used by ECS itself to pull the image, write logs and inject secrets — not by the application).
8.1 — Start the role. IAM → Roles → Create role (the banner is the earlier policy confirmation).
8.2 — Trusted entity. AWS service, service Elastic Container Service, use case Elastic Container Service Task.
8.3 — Managed policy. Search AmazonECSTaskExecutionRolePolicy, tick it and click Next.
8.4 — Name the role. fitness-assistant-dev-chat-execution-role, description “ECS task execution role for Chat Service dev”; the trust policy names ecs-tasks.amazonaws.com.
8.5 — Create the role. The summary shows one managed policy; click Create role.
8.6 — Add an inline policy. On the created role open Add permissions → Create inline policy.
8.7 — Write the policy. secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on the Chat secrets (at first only chat-database*; it is extended in Step 13). Name it fitness-assistant-dev-chat-execution-secrets.
8.8 — Check the role. It now has the managed policy plus the inline policy.
Step 9 — Task role (what the Chat code uses at runtime). Same trusted entity (ECS Task), no managed policy, name fitness-assistant-dev-chat-task-role. No Secrets Manager permissions here — secrets are injected by the execution role.
9.1 — Create the role and open Add permissions. The role exists with 0 policies; click Add permissions → Create inline policy.
9.2 — Write the policy. JSON: lambda:InvokeFunction on fitness-assistant-dev-auth and fitness-assistant-dev-user only, then Next.
9.3 — Name and create it. fitness-assistant-dev-chat-service-invoke, Create policy.
Part D — Network Step 10 — Security group for the task.
10.1 — Open Security groups. EC2 → Security Groups lists the five existing groups; click Create security group.
10.2 — Fill in the group. Name fitness-assistant-dev-chat-sg, description “Security group for Chat Service Fargate tasks”, the project VPC, no inbound rule yet, default outbound (the task calls the Auth/User Lambdas, Aurora and DNS). Click Create security group.
Step 11 — Let the task reach Aurora. Never open 5432 to 0.0.0.0/0.
11.1 — Open the Aurora security group. RDS → fitness-assistant-dev-aurora → Connectivity & security, then click the Aurora security group link under Security group rules.
11.2 — Edit the inbound rules. On the Inbound rules tab click Edit inbound rules.
11.3 — Add the rule. Add rule: PostgreSQL, TCP 5432, source = the security group fitness-assistant-dev-chat-sg, description “Allow Chat Fargate tasks to Aurora”, then Save rules.
Step 12 — ECS cluster.
12.1 — Start the cluster. ECS → Clusters shows none; click Create cluster.
12.2 — Fill in the cluster. Name fitness-assistant-dev-cluster, infrastructure Fargate only, no EC2 capacity, no Service Connect, then Create.
12.3 — Check the cluster. It appears in the list.
Part E — Runtime secrets and task definition Step 13 — Runtime secrets. The Chat code reads CHAT_DATABASE_URL, not DATABASE_URL.
13.1 — Open Secrets Manager. The new chat-database secret is at the top of the list. Click Store a new secret again.
13.2 — Create the URL secret. Other type of secret, a key/value row with key CHAT_DATABASE_URL and value postgresql://USERNAME:PASSWORD@<aurora-endpoint>:5432/fitness_assistant_chat?schema=public (URL-encode special characters in the password, e.g. @ → %40). Name fitness-assistant/dev/chat-database-url, description “Chat Service PostgreSQL connection URL - dev”, then Next and store it.
13.3 — Internal secret. Reuse the shared internal secret as fitness-assistant/dev/internal-service-secret (same value the Lambdas use, never a new one).
The runbook has no screenshot of this action.
13.4 — Extend the execution role policy. In fitness-assistant-dev-chat-execution-secrets list both ARNs (chat-database* and chat-database-url*; also the internal secret) and click Next.
Step 14 — Task definition. ECS → Task definitions → Create new task definition:
Setting Value Family fitness-assistant-dev-chat Launch type / OS AWS Fargate, Linux/X86_64, network mode awsvpc Task size 0.5 vCPU, 1 GB Task role / execution role fitness-assistant-dev-chat-task-role / fitness-assistant-dev-chat-execution-role Container chat-service, essential, image …/fitness-assistant-dev-chat:dev-20260922-1 Port mapping 3005/TCP, app protocol HTTP, name chat-http Environment NODE_ENV=production, CHAT_SERVICE_PORT=3005, CORS_ORIGIN=<S3 website URL>, ENABLE_REST_CORS=true, AUTH_LAMBDA_NAME, USER_LAMBDA_NAME Secrets (ValueFrom) CHAT_DATABASE_URL ← <chat-database-url secret ARN>:CHAT_DATABASE_URL::; INTERNAL_API_SECRET (alias INTERNAL_SERVICE_SECRET) ← internal-service-secret Logging awslogs, group /ecs/fitness-assistant-dev-chat, region ap-southeast-1, stream prefix chat Health check none in the task; the ALB checks /health (the image may not contain curl/wget) 14.1 — Open the page. There are no task definitions yet; click Create new task definition.
14.2 — Family, size and roles. Family fitness-assistant-dev-chat, AWS Fargate, Linux/X86_64, .5 vCPU, 1 GB, task role fitness-assistant-dev-chat-task-role, execution role fitness-assistant-dev-chat-execution-role.
14.3 — Container. Name chat-service, essential Yes, image URI <account-id>.dkr.ecr.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com/fitness-assistant-dev-chat:dev-20260922-1, container port 3005, TCP, port name chat-http, app protocol HTTP.
14.4 — Environment. Add the eight variables. For the two secret entries, CHAT_DATABASE_URL and INTERNAL_SERVICE_SECRET, choose value type ValueFrom and paste the full secret ARN plus the JSON key suffix (for example …:CHAT_DATABASE_URL::). Plain values go in the other six rows.
14.5 — Logging. Tick Use log collection, destination Amazon CloudWatch, awslogs-group = /ecs/fitness-assistant-dev-chat, awslogs-region = ap-southeast-1, awslogs-stream-prefix = chat.
14.6 — Storage and tags. Leave ephemeral storage at 20 GiB; add tags Project=fitness-assistant, Environment=dev, Service=chat; click Create.
Secrets must use ValueFrom with the full secret ARN so the container receives the real connection string at start. Never paste real secret values into plain environment variables.
Part F — Load balancer Step 15 — ALB security group. HTTP 80 from 0.0.0.0/0 (the frontend itself is still HTTP; HTTPS 443 comes with a domain and ACM certificate).
15.1 — Check the list. The banner confirms chat-sg was created (6 groups). Click Create security group.
15.2 — Fill in the group. Name fitness-assistant-dev-chat-alb-sg, description “ALB security group for Fitness Assistant Chat dev”, the project VPC; inbound rule HTTP, source Anywhere-IPv4 0.0.0.0/0; Create security group.
15.3 — Check it. The banner confirms the creation; the group has one inbound entry (HTTP 80, 0.0.0.0/0).
Step 16 — Only the ALB may reach the task. Port 3005 is never opened to 0.0.0.0/0.
16.1 — Edit the task group’s inbound rules. In fitness-assistant-dev-chat-sg add Custom TCP, port 3005, source = security group fitness-assistant-dev-chat-alb-sg, description “Allow Chat ALB to reach ECS task”, then Save rules.
16.2 — Check. chat-sg now has one inbound rule: Custom TCP 3005 from the ALB SG.
Step 17 — Second public subnet. An internet-facing ALB needs two Availability Zones, so fitness-assistant-dev-public-b (10.0.2.0/24, ap-southeast-1b) was added — see 5.4.1, step 6.
Step 18 — Target group.
18.1 — Open Target groups. EC2 → Target groups shows none; click Create target group.
18.2 — Settings. Target type IP addresses (Fargate uses awsvpc, so not Instances), name fitness-assistant-dev-chat-tg, protocol HTTP, port 3005, IPv4, the project VPC, protocol version HTTP1.
18.3 — Health check. Path /health; healthy threshold 2, unhealthy 3, timeout 5 s, interval 20 s, success code 200.
18.4 — Register no targets. The ECS service registers task IPs itself; just click Next.
18.5 — Review and create. Check the summary (HTTP 3005, /health, 0 targets) and click Create target group.
18.6 — Stickiness. Afterwards set deregistration delay to 30 s and Turn on stickiness: load-balancer generated cookie, 1 day — this suits Socket.IO’s polling fallback.
Step 19 — Application Load Balancer. fitness-assistant-dev-chat-alb, internet-facing, IPv4, subnets public-a and public-b, security group fitness-assistant-dev-chat-alb-sg only, listener HTTP:80 → forward to fitness-assistant-dev-chat-tg.
19.1 — Open Load balancers. None yet; click Create load balancer.
19.2 — Choose the type. Click Create under Application Load Balancer.
19.3 — Basic configuration and network mapping. Name fitness-assistant-dev-chat-alb, Internet-facing, IPv4, the project VPC, and tick both zones with their public subnets: ap-southeast-1a → public-a, ap-southeast-1b → public-b. Choose the security group fitness-assistant-dev-chat-alb-sg only (further down the page).
19.4 — Listener. Protocol HTTP, port 80, default action Forward to target groups, target group fitness-assistant-dev-chat-tg. Then click Create load balancer.
19.5 — Read the DNS name. Open the new load balancer; state Provisioning while it starts. Record the DNS name fitness-assistant-dev-chat-alb-<id>.ap-southeast-1.elb.amazonaws.com, and open the HTTP:80 listener.
Step 20 — Idle timeout 120 s.
20.1 — Edit the attribute. ALB → Attributes → Edit: Connection idle timeout 0 hours 2 minutes 0 seconds (120 s), better suited to long-lived WebSocket connections; Save changes.
Step 21 — Hide internal paths. The default listener action forwards every path, including /internal/* and /metrics. Add two rules to HTTP:80; /health, /chat/* and /socket.io/* still reach the container.
21.1 — Rule 1: /internal/*. In the listener click Add rule. Condition Path with the value /internal/* (value matching); action Return fixed response: response code 404, content type text/plain, body Not found; click Next.
21.2 — Priority. Set priority 1 (above the default rule) and click Next, then create the rule.
21.3 — Rule 2: /metrics. Repeat 21.1–21.2 with path /metrics and priority 2 (the same fixed 404 response).
The runbook has no screenshot of the second rule; the ECS service screen in Step 22 lists both rules.
Part G — Service Step 22 — ECS service. Cluster → Services → Create:
Setting Value Compute Launch type FARGATE, platform LATEST Task definition fitness-assistant-dev-chat (latest revision) Service name fitness-assistant-dev-chat-service, replica, 1 desired task Networking private-app-a + private-app-b only, security group fitness-assistant-dev-chat-sg, public IP off Load balancing existing ALB fitness-assistant-dev-chat-alb, container chat-service 3005:3005, existing listener HTTP:80, existing target group fitness-assistant-dev-chat-tg Health check grace period 60 s Service Connect / discovery / auto scaling off 22.1 — Open the cluster. The banner says task definition fitness-assistant-dev-chat:1 was created; the cluster has no services. Click Create in the Services tab.
22.2 — Compute. Compute options Launch type, launch type Fargate, platform version LATEST.
22.3 — Service details. Task definition family fitness-assistant-dev-chat, revision (latest — the screenshot shows 1), service name fitness-assistant-dev-chat-service.
22.4 — Deployment configuration. Scheduling strategy Replica, Desired tasks 1, health check grace period 60 seconds (the screenshot still shows the empty default 0).
22.5 — Networking. The project VPC, the two private app subnets (private-app-a, private-app-b), Use an existing security group with fitness-assistant-dev-chat-sg, and Public IP turned off.
22.6 — Load balancer. Tick Use load balancing, type Application Load Balancer, container chat-service 3005:3005, Use an existing load balancer fitness-assistant-dev-chat-alb.
22.7 — Listener and target group. Use an existing listener HTTP:80 (the rules list shows /internal/* priority 1, /metrics priority 2 and the default rule) and Use an existing target group fitness-assistant-dev-chat-tg.
22.8 — Create. Leave VPC Lattice, auto scaling, volume and tags off, and click Create.
Desired count stays 1: Socket.IO session state is kept in memory, so a second task would split sessions until a shared adapter (e.g. Redis) is added. Right after creation the service shows Running 0 / Pending 1 while it pulls the image, injects secrets and creates the ENI. If a task stops, read Stopped reason and the service Events instead of recreating the service.
Step 23 — Verify.
23.1 — Service state. The service is Active, deployment Completed and the tasks column reads 1/1 Tasks running.
23.2 — Target health. In the target group, Healthy is 1 and the registered target 10.0.11.164:3005 is Healthy.
23.3 — Call it. Open http://<alb-dns>/health, and the Socket.IO handshake http://<alb-dns>/socket.io/?EIO=4&transport=polling, which must answer 0{"sid":"…","upgrades":["websocket"],…} — not 404, 502 or 503. See 5.5.3.
Part H — Wire it into the API and the frontend Step 24 — REST through API Gateway.
24.1 — Create the integration. In fitness-assistant-dev-api create an integration attached to route ANY /chat/{proxy+}: type HTTP URI, method ANY, URL http://<alb-dns>/chat/{proxy}, then Create. The {proxy} part matters — /chat/conversations must reach the backend as /chat/conversations.
24.2 — Test. GET https://<api-id>.execute-api.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com/chat/conversations (a Bearer token is needed for real data).
Step 25 — Frontend. Set the Socket.IO URL (VITE_CHAT_WS_URL) to the ALB, rebuild and republish with the redeploy procedure:
REST: Frontend → API Gateway → /chat/{proxy+} → Chat ALB → ECS Socket.IO: Frontend → Chat ALB → /socket.io/ → ECS Step 26 — Roll out the fixed task definition. ECS → fitness-assistant-dev-cluster → fitness-assistant-dev-chat-service → Update → task definition fitness-assistant-dev-chat:3, everything else unchanged, Force new deployment. Target state: 1 running, 0 pending, deployment Completed, and no more URL must start with postgresql:// in /ecs/fitness-assistant-dev-chat.
