title: Data migration to Aurora
content:
The schemas on Aurora were created by each service’s migration Lambda. This last step moved the data of the 7 local PostgreSQL databases into them — keeping the original IDs, without reseeding — using a one-shot ECS Fargate task that runs pg_restore inside the VPC.
In every screenshot below, the red rectangles mark what to fill in or click for the sub-step written just above it.
The order was fixed in advance so nothing could be corrupted halfway:
Upload the 7 dumps and their manifest to a private S3 bucket. Make sure all 7 logical databases exist on Aurora (including fitness_assistant_chat). Apply the latest schema migrations to all 7. Build and push a migrator image to ECR. Run a read-only preflight task. Restore every database. Compare row counts / primary keys. Only then handle uploaded files and vector data. Step 1 — Private migration bucket 1.1 — Create the bucket. S3 → Create bucket fitness-assistant-data-migration-dev-<account-id> in ap-southeast-1: Block all public access on, versioning enabled, SSE-S3 encryption, no static website. A dedicated bucket keeps dumps away from the public frontend bucket and the user-uploads bucket. The banner confirms the creation.
1.2 — Create the first folder. Click Create folder, enter the name full-local-migration and click Create folder again. Then repeat for 2026-09 inside it, and for dumps, manifests and user-files inside 2026-09. The screenshot shows the form (folder name box and the Create folder button).
1.3 — Open full-local-migration/. The folder is empty; click Create folder again to add 2026-09.
1.4 — Check the result. 2026-09/ contains the three folders dumps/, manifests/ and user-files/.
Step 2 — Upload the dumps and the manifest 2.1 — Add the 7 dumps. Open dumps/, click Upload → Add files and choose the 7 audited dumps unchanged (not unzipped, not converted to SQL): gymcoach_auth, _user, _fitness, _gym, _payment, _chat and _ai .data.dump — 72.9 MB in total. The destination must read …/full-local-migration/2026-09/dumps/.
2.2 — Start the upload and check it. Click Upload at the bottom of the page. The status page must say Upload succeeded with 7 files and 0 failed. Click Close.
2.3 — Upload the manifest. Open manifests/, click Upload → Add files, choose the SHA-256 manifest.json and click Upload.
Never upload .env, .env.production, database passwords, JWT_SECRET, INTERNAL_SERVICE_SECRET, AWS credentials or provider API keys to this bucket.
Step 3 — Migrator image A minimal image with only pg_restore and the AWS CLI, reusable for all 7 databases (and later for CI/CD).
3.1 — Create the ECR repository. ECR → Create repository: private, name fitness-assistant-dev-db-migrator, tag mutability Mutable, AES-256, then Create. (The deprecated scan-on-push toggle is shown on by default in this console.)
3.2 — Write the Dockerfile. tools/db-migrator/Dockerfile:
FROM postgres:16-bookworm RUN apt-get update \ && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends awscli ca-certificates \ && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* WORKDIR /work ENTRYPOINT ["/bin/bash", "-lc"] CMD ["echo 'db-migrator ready'"] 3.3 — Build, test, log in, tag and push. From PowerShell in tools/db-migrator:
docker build -t fitness-assistant-db-migrator:dev . docker run --rm fitness-assistant-db-migrator:dev "pg_restore --version && aws --version" # pg_restore 16.15, aws-cli 2.9.19 aws ecr get-login-password --region ap-southeast-1 | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin <account-id>.dkr.ecr.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com docker tag fitness-assistant-db-migrator:dev <account-id>.dkr.ecr.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com/fitness-assistant-dev-db-migrator:dev-20260923-1 docker push <account-id>.dkr.ecr.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com/fitness-assistant-dev-db-migrator:dev-20260923-1 The screenshot shows only the final push: every layer Pushed and the digest line.
Step 4 — Roles 4.1 — Execution role, policy. IAM → Roles → Create role → AWS service → Elastic Container Service Task, then search AmazonECSTaskExecutionRolePolicy, tick it and click Next — it pulls the image and writes logs.
4.2 — Execution role, name. fitness-assistant-dev-db-migrator-execution-role (trusted by ecs-tasks.amazonaws.com), then Create role.
4.3 — Task role. Create fitness-assistant-dev-db-migrator-task-role the same way (same trusted entity, no managed policy — the banner at the top of its form is the earlier execution-role confirmation), then add the inline policy fitness-assistant-dev-db-migrator-runtime — read the dumps prefix only, and read the Aurora credential:
{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "ReadMigrationDumps", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["s3:GetObject"], "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::fitness-assistant-data-migration-dev-<account-id>/full-local-migration/2026-09/dumps/*"] }, { "Sid": "ListMigrationDumpPrefix", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["s3:ListBucket", "s3:GetBucketLocation"], "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::fitness-assistant-data-migration-dev-<account-id>"], "Condition": { "StringLike": { "s3:prefix": ["full-local-migration/2026-09/dumps/*"] } } }, { "Sid": "ReadAuroraCredential", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["secretsmanager:GetSecretValue"], "Resource": ["arn:aws:secretsmanager:ap-southeast-1:<account-id>:secret:fitness-assistant/dev/chat-database-*"] } ] } 4.4 — Paste the policy. In the policy editor (JSON) paste the policy above and click Next.
4.5 — Name and create it. fitness-assistant-dev-db-migrator-runtime, Create policy; the summary lists S3 and Secrets Manager.
Step 5 — Task definition ECS → Create new task definition fitness-assistant-dev-db-migrator: Fargate, Linux/X86_64, awsvpc, 1 vCPU / 2 GB, the two roles, container db-migrator with image …/fitness-assistant-dev-db-migrator:dev-20260923-1, no port mapping needed, environment AWS_REGION=ap-southeast-1, DB_SECRET_ID=fitness-assistant/dev/chat-database, DUMP_S3_PREFIX=s3://fitness-assistant-data-migration-dev-<account-id>/full-local-migration/2026-09/dumps, logs to /ecs/fitness-assistant-dev-db-migrator, default ephemeral storage (far more than the 73 MB of dumps). No command is set — it is overridden at run time.
5.1 — Family, launch type and size. Family fitness-assistant-dev-db-migrator, AWS Fargate, Linux/X86_64, CPU 1 vCPU, memory 2 GB.
5.2 — Roles and container. Task role fitness-assistant-dev-db-migrator-task-role, task execution role fitness-assistant-dev-db-migrator-execution-role, container name db-migrator, image URI <account-id>.dkr.ecr.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com/fitness-assistant-dev-db-migrator:dev-20260923-1.
5.3 — Port mapping. The console pre-fills container port 80; the runbook needs no port, so remove that mapping (Remove) — the screenshot shows the untouched default.
5.4 — Environment variables and logging. Add AWS_REGION, DB_SECRET_ID and DUMP_S3_PREFIX with the values above and keep Use log collection ticked.
5.5 — Storage and create. Leave ephemeral storage at the default (the console shows 21) and click Create.
Step 6 — Inject the database URL as a secret (revision 2) 6.1 — Extend the execution role. Give the execution role secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on the chat-database-url secret: Add permissions → Create inline policy → JSON with the statement ReadDatabaseUrl, named fitness-assistant-dev-db-migrator-secret.
6.2 — Create revision 2. From the task definition choose Create new revision and add a secret environment variable DATABASE_URL, value type ValueFrom, value <chat-database-url secret ARN>:CHAT_DATABASE_URL::; remove DB_SECRET_ID, which is no longer needed. The confirmation shows fitness-assistant-dev-db-migrator:2 as ACTIVE with its two roles.
The script derives the server URL from DATABASE_URL and switches the database name per restore, so one credential serves all 7 logical databases on the same cluster.
Step 7 — Preflight (read-only) 7.1 — Run a new task. ECS → fitness-assistant-dev-cluster → Tasks → Run new task: FARGATE, fitness-assistant-dev-db-migrator:2, 1 task, private app subnets, security group fitness-assistant-dev-chat-sg (already allowed into Aurora on 5432 and into the Secrets Manager endpoint), public IP disabled, no load balancer.
The runbook has no screenshot of the networking part of this form.
7.2 — Override the command. Under Container overrides → db-migrator paste into Command override:
set -euo pipefail; echo "=== DB MIGRATOR PREFLIGHT START ==="; echo "Region=$AWS_REGION"; echo "Prefix=$DUMP_S3_PREFIX"; test -n "${DATABASE_URL:-}"; PSQL_URL="${DATABASE_URL%%\?*}"; mkdir -p /work/dumps; aws s3 ls "$DUMP_S3_PREFIX/"; aws s3 cp "$DUMP_S3_PREFIX/" /work/dumps/ --recursive --only-show-errors; ls -lh /work/dumps; for f in gymcoach_auth.data.dump gymcoach_user.data.dump gymcoach_fitness.data.dump gymcoach_gym.data.dump gymcoach_payment.data.dump gymcoach_chat.data.dump gymcoach_ai.data.dump; do test -s "/work/dumps/$f"; pg_restore -l "/work/dumps/$f" >/dev/null; echo "OK dump: $f"; done; echo "Checking Aurora databases..."; psql "$PSQL_URL" -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -Atc "select datname from pg_database where datname in ('fitness_assistant','fitness_assistant_user','fitness_assistant_fitness','fitness_assistant_gym','fitness_assistant_payment','fitness_assistant_chat','fitness_assistant_ai') order by datname;"; echo "=== DB MIGRATOR PREFLIGHT OK ===" The environment overrides below it keep the three variables (the screenshot’s AWS_REGION, DB_SECRET_ID and DUMP_S3_PREFIX rows). Click Create to start the task.
7.3 — Read the log. Expected result at the end of /ecs/fitness-assistant-dev-db-migrator: === DB MIGRATOR PREFLIGHT OK === — every dump downloads and is readable by pg_restore -l, and all 7 databases exist. If the task stops with an error, record the stopped reason and last log lines before going further.
The runbook has no screenshot of the log output.
Step 8 — Restore Destructive DEV operation. This step empties every table (except _prisma_migrations) in the 7 Aurora DEV databases and replaces the data with the local dumps. The schema and migration history are not touched. Run it only after the preflight succeeded.
8.1 — Run the task again. Same run-task settings, with this command override:
set -euo pipefail; echo "=== FULL RESTORE START ==="; mkdir -p /work/dumps; aws s3 cp "$DUMP_S3_PREFIX/" /work/dumps/ --recursive --only-show-errors; PSQL_URL="${DATABASE_URL%%\?*}"; BASE="${PSQL_URL%/*}"; restore_db(){ DB="$1"; DUMP="$2"; URL="$BASE/$DB"; echo "=== CLEAN $DB ==="; T=$(psql "$URL" -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -Atc "select string_agg(format('%I.%I', schemaname, tablename), ',') from pg_tables where schemaname='public' and tablename <> '_prisma_migrations';"); if [ -n "$T" ]; then psql "$URL" -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -c "TRUNCATE TABLE $T RESTART IDENTITY CASCADE;"; fi; echo "=== RESTORE $DB FROM $DUMP ==="; pg_restore --exit-on-error --no-owner --no-privileges --data-only --exclude-table-data=public._prisma_migrations --dbname="$URL" "/work/dumps/$DUMP"; echo "=== DONE $DB ==="; }; restore_db fitness_assistant gymcoach_auth.data.dump; restore_db fitness_assistant_user gymcoach_user.data.dump; restore_db fitness_assistant_fitness gymcoach_fitness.data.dump; restore_db fitness_assistant_gym gymcoach_gym.data.dump; restore_db fitness_assistant_payment gymcoach_payment.data.dump; restore_db fitness_assistant_chat gymcoach_chat.data.dump; restore_db fitness_assistant_ai gymcoach_ai.data.dump; echo "=== FULL RESTORE OK ===" Expected result: === DONE fitness_assistant_ai === followed by === FULL RESTORE OK ===.
The runbook has no screenshot of Step 8.
Step 9 — Handle schema drift with a scripted migrator The local dumps and the Aurora schemas were not guaranteed to be identical — for example the Gym data could use brand_id where the Aurora schema still had gym_id, which would make the restore fail or require a deliberate patch. The one-line command was therefore replaced by a script inside the image, selected with a MODE variable, and the task definition went through further revisions (up to fitness-assistant-dev-db-migrator:11). From PowerShell:
$CLUSTER = "fitness-assistant-dev-cluster" $TASKDEF = "fitness-assistant-dev-db-migrator:11" $REGION = "ap-southeast-1" $NET = "awsvpcConfiguration={subnets=[<private-app-a-id>,<private-app-b-id>],securityGroups=[<chat-sg-id>],assignPublicIp=DISABLED}" aws ecs run-task ` --cluster $CLUSTER ` --task-definition $TASKDEF ` --launch-type FARGATE ` --network-configuration $NET ` --region $REGION ` --overrides '{\"containerOverrides\":[{\"name\":\"db-migrator\",\"environment\":[{\"name\":\"MODE\",\"value\":\"apply-prepatch\"}]}]}' MODE=apply-prepatch applies the schema pre-patches; the log must show schema-prepatch applied and the task must stop with exit code 0. Review the generated db-migrator-output/generated/needs-review.fitness_assistant_gym.sql in the migration bucket and decide the gym_id → brand_id case deliberately. Run MODE=restore. The runbook has no screenshots of Step 9.
Result According to the deployment status table, all 7 of 7 service databases were restored and 23 of 23 audited foreign keys were applied and validated. Uploaded user files (user-files/) and re-embedding the local Qdrant data into OpenSearch are separate follow-ups, done only after the relational data was verified.

title: CI/CD pipeline activation
content:
The DEV account already had five least-privilege GitHub OIDC roles (GyminiDevCiReadRole, GyminiDevAppDeployRole, GyminiDevInfraPlanRole, GyminiDevInfraApplyRole, GyminiDevCfnExecutionRole) provisioned by CloudFormation ahead of time — no static AWS keys anywhere. This step activates the first real GitHub Actions workflow: PR validation only (install/lint/typecheck/unit tests/IaC lint/Docker build + the repo’s own PowerShell CI-helper test suites), plus a temporary, tightly-scoped job that proves the OIDC → STS → GyminiDevCiReadRole federation works before it is removed. No application deployment, no infrastructure deployment, and no AWS mutation beyond one read-only call happen in this step.
Step 1 — Push the activation branch The permanent workflow (.github/workflows/pr-validation.yml, AWS-credential-free: no id-token permission, no role assumption, no static keys, no deploy command) and a temporary OIDC smoke workflow (.github/workflows/pr-validation-oidc-smoke.yml, removed again before merge) are committed on a dedicated branch cut from the real origin/aws-deploy tip, then pushed:
git push -u origin <activation-branch> Step 2 — Open the pull request Base aws-deploy, compare the activation branch, title CI: activate PR validation.

title: CD pipeline activation
content:
5.4.12 activated CI only (PR validation, no AWS credentials). This step adds the CD half: giving GitHub Actions the ability to deploy code and infrastructure to the DEV AWS account through five gated workflows — dev-build, dev-deploy, chat-deploy, infra-plan, infra-deploy.
Step 1 — Review the five CD workflows Five workflows were designed in the planning phase under ci/drafts/github-actions/, each with the same safety discipline as the rest of this project:
dev-build.yml — builds and hashes the Lambda zips with zero AWS access (no id-token, no credentials). Runs automatically on every push to aws-deploy. dev-deploy.yml — manual (workflow_dispatch), dry_run: true by default, verifies artifact hashes against the build manifest before any AWS call, snapshots the EventBridge Scheduler state before and after to guarantee it is unchanged, and scans every command’s output for secret-shaped strings. chat-deploy.yml — manual; never changes the ECS service’s desiredCount unless force_on is explicitly passed, so a code deploy can never power Chat on or off by accident. infra-plan.yml — manual; creates a CloudFormation change set only. Its IAM role (GyminiDevInfraPlanRole) has an explicit Deny on cloudformation:ExecuteChangeSet, so the workflow cannot apply anything. infra-deploy.yml — manual; re-scans the named change set and binds it by SHA-256 digest to exactly what infra-plan.yml printed, so a change set modified after review cannot be executed. Step 2 — Create the three GitHub Environments The AWS-touching workflows declare environment: dev / dev-infra / dev-infra-plan, GitHub’s mechanism for requiring a human reviewer before a job runs. The three environments are created by hand in GitHub Settings → Environments (this needs repo-admin access).
For each environment: Required reviewers is set to the repo owner as the sole reviewer; “Allow administrators to bypass configured protection rules” is unchecked, because the owner is both administrator and reviewer and bypass would skip the approval click this gate exists for; Wait timer stays off, since the workflows are manual and reviewer-gated.
Verified through the API: total_count: 3, ["dev", "dev-infra", "dev-infra-plan"].
Step 3 — Restrict deployment to the aws-deploy branch The same rule (Ref type: Branch, name pattern aws-deploy) is added to all three environments.
Verified through the API (GET /environments/{name}/deployment-branch-policies): each environment returns total_count: 1, name: "aws-deploy".
Step 4 — Activate Gate 1 (dev-build.yml) The workflow is committed to .github/workflows/ on aws-deploy and triggers on the push, as designed:
Job Result impact success build skipped — only a workflow file changed, no Lambda service source No AWS calls are made: the workflow has no id-token permission and never configures AWS credentials.
Step 5 — Activate Gates 2 and 3 (dev-deploy.yml, chat-deploy.yml) Both workflows are committed to aws-deploy, and also to master. GitHub requires a workflow_dispatch workflow to exist on the repository’s default branch (master) before it can be dispatched, so the two files are copied there byte-identical. dev-build.yml stays on aws-deploy only, because it triggers on push. Both workflows then appear under their display names, DEV Application Deploy (Lambda code) and DEV Chat Deploy (ECS).
Step 6 — Activate Gates 4 and 5 (infra-plan.yml, infra-deploy.yml) Both workflows are active on aws-deploy and master, with these hardening features:
An unprivileged gate job in front of both workflows checks github.ref == refs/heads/aws-deploy and APIGW_ADOPTION_COMPLETE == true before any AWS credential is configured. TemplateSemanticGuard.psm1 runs after pnpm install, so its js-yaml dependency is present. Change-set creation passes the live template’s ChatAlbDnsName parameter. infra-deploy.yml validates the template bound to the named change set, not the file on disk. scripts/ci/infra-workflows.test.cjs runs the shipped gate logic in a disposable container for three scenarios: missing adoption, wrong branch, correct. Step 7 — Fresh adoption and drift certification Before the owner sets APIGW_ADOPTION_COMPLETE, the API Gateway stack is verified directly against AWS, read-only:
aws cloudformation list-stack-resources: 254/254 resources UPDATE_COMPLETE. A new detect-stack-drift call: StackDriftStatus: IN_SYNC, DriftedStackResourceCount: 0. Test-ApiRouteParity.ps1: 119/119 live routes match the source baseline, 0 MISMATCHED, 0 GATEWAY_ONLY. The owner then sets the repository variable APIGW_ADOPTION_COMPLETE=true.
Step 8 — dev-deploy.yml in use The owner runs Actions → DEV Application Deploy (Lambda code) against the auth service.
Dry run (dry_run: true). Succeeds; the AWS credential, identity and scheduler-snapshot steps are skipped by design and only the plan is printed.
Real deploy (dry_run: false). The environment: dev reviewer gate asks the owner to approve.
Deploy completes. Every step, including the read-only /health smoke check, passes.
aws lambda list-functions shows fitness-assistant-dev-auth with a new LastModified timestamp matching the run, which confirms the code was redeployed.
Step 9 — infra-plan.yml and infra-deploy.yml in use Plan. infra-plan.yml runs against aws-deploy and creates a change set. Template semantic diff: NO_SEMANTIC_CHANGE, Changes: [], and the change set carries the live stack’s current ChatAlbDnsName. Apply. infra-deploy.yml is dispatched with that change set and waits on the dev-infra reviewer gate. After approval, it binds the change set to the reviewed template, executes it, and runs the read-only post-apply checks. Result. The stack finishes UPDATE_COMPLETE. A follow-up infra-plan.yml run finds no differences, so the live stack and the template are in sync. The apply role GyminiDevInfraApplyRole carries cloudformation:GetTemplate, scoped to the single API Gateway stack ARN like every other statement in its policy. The post-apply route check runs with -AllowKnownSourceOnly: it still fails on any MISMATCHED route, and it treats the 10 known SOURCE_ONLY routes as a separately tracked backlog item, not an infrastructure regression.
Step 10 — Chat service deploy chat-deploy.yml builds and deploys a new chat image to ECS Fargate through the dev reviewer gate, without changing desiredCount. The chat service’s task definition is now at revision 9.
Step 11 — Make the live web app and chat work over HTTPS The frontend is served from CloudFront over HTTPS, so two settings point at it:
API Gateway CORS. AllowOrigins lists the CloudFront URL (https://d1ub83a48p566t.cloudfront.net) alongside the S3 origin, set with one additive update-api --cors-configuration call. Both the preflight and the real POST /auth/login carry access-control-allow-origin: https://d1ub83a48p566t.cloudfront.net. Chat over the same origin. A CloudFront origin (chat-alb-origin, OriginProtocolPolicy: http-only) and a behavior (/socket.io/*, CachingDisabled + AllViewer) route Socket.IO traffic to the chat ALB, so the browser never makes a mixed-content request. runtime-config.json sets chatWsUrl to the CloudFront domain. The ECS chat service runs with desiredCount: 1, and the target passes its health check. Verification: GET https://d1ub83a48p566t.cloudfront.net/socket.io/?EIO=4&transport=polling returns 200 OK with a genuine Engine.IO handshake (sid, upgrades: ["websocket"]).
Step 12 — Admin access A working ADMIN login is provisioned on the deployed app through a one-time, controlled password reset on the auth Lambda:
The auth Lambda is switched briefly to NODE_ENV=development with an empty SMTP_HOST, so the password-reset request returns its development link instead of sending email. The reset is completed by invoking the Lambda directly, because /auth/password-reset* is not exposed on API Gateway. The Lambda’s original environment is restored from a backup file and read back: NODE_ENV=production, SMTP_HOST=smtp.gmail.com, all 10 variables present. The account registered with the real email address (tranminhduy12a1@gmail.com) is used as the ADMIN login. A read-only query through the RDS Data API, enabled for a few minutes and then disabled again (HttpEndpointEnabled: False), confirmed which ADMIN rows exist. No data was modified. The owner changes the temporary password in the app after the first login.
Result Five CD workflows are active: dev-build, dev-deploy, chat-deploy, infra-plan, infra-deploy. Three GitHub Environments (dev, dev-infra, dev-infra-plan) require a human reviewer, have administrator bypass off, and allow deployment from aws-deploy only. dev-deploy.yml, chat-deploy.yml, infra-plan.yml and infra-deploy.yml have each run against the real DEV account through the reviewer gate. dev-build.yml runs automatically on push with no AWS access. The API Gateway stack is in sync with its template: 254/254 resources, no drift, 119/119 routes matching the baseline. The web app signs in and chat connects over HTTPS through CloudFront. An ADMIN login is available on the deployed app.

title: CloudFront, Aurora reader and CloudWatch alarm
content:
This step covers three parts of the architecture that the earlier steps only mention: the CloudFront distribution in front of the frontend and the chat, the Aurora reader in the second Availability Zone, and a CloudWatch alarm that notifies an SNS topic. For each part you see the finished result from the console and the form used to create it. In the screenshots, a red box with a number marks what to fill in or click, in order.
The screenshots of the creation forms were captured by opening each form and leaving it with Cancel: nothing was created while taking them, and the real resources were checked afterwards (still 12 alarms, 2 Aurora instances, 1 extra CloudFront behavior). The real resources are created by the CloudFormation stacks of the project, so the same result is reproducible without clicking.
Part A — CloudFront distribution The distribution serves the web app over HTTPS and forwards the chat traffic to the load balancer.
A.1 — Check the two origins. Open CloudFront → Distributions → E2MHD79JFC1700 → Origins. There must be two:
Origin name Type Access frontend-s3-origin S3 Origin Access Control, so the bucket is read only through CloudFront chat-alb-origin Elastic Load Balancing HTTP only towards the origin (the load balancer has no HTTPS listener) The Origins tab: the S3 origin uses Origin Access Control and the second origin is the chat load balancer.
A.2 — Check the two behaviors. Open the Behaviors tab. The /socket.io/* rule must come first, so the chat is matched before the default rule.
The Behaviors tab: /socket.io/* goes to the chat origin, everything else goes to S3.
A.3 — Create the chat behavior. Click Create behavior and fill in the form (numbers refer to the red boxes):
Path pattern: type the pattern below. Origin and origin groups: choose chat-alb-origin. Viewer protocol policy: choose HTTPS only. /socket.io/* The first half of the form: path pattern, origin and viewer protocol policy.
Then scroll down and set the cache and request policies:
Cache policy: CachingDisabled, because a WebSocket or long-polling connection must never be cached. Origin request policy: AllViewer, so every viewer header, including the upgrade headers, reaches the chat service. For Allowed HTTP methods choose all seven methods (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT, POST, PATCH, DELETE), because the Socket.IO polling transport uses POST. Click Create behavior to finish.
The second half: cache policy and origin request policy.
A.4 — Verify. After the distribution status is Deployed, this request must return 200 with an Engine.IO handshake (sid, upgrades: ["websocket"]) while the chat service is running:
curl "https://<distribution-domain>/socket.io/?EIO=4&transport=polling" If it returns 502, the load balancer behind chat-alb-origin was recreated with a new DNS name: edit the origin and enter the current load balancer DNS name.
Part B — Aurora reader in the second Availability Zone The cluster has one Writer and one Reader, so a read can continue if one instance or one Availability Zone has a problem.
B.1 — Check the result. Open Aurora and RDS → Databases. The cluster fitness-assistant-dev-aurora has two instances, both Available: one with the role Writer instance and one with the role Reader instance, both Aurora Serverless v2.
The cluster with its Writer and Reader instances.
B.2 — Add a reader. Open the cluster and use the Actions menu:
Click Actions at the top right of the cluster page. The cluster page, step 1: the Actions button.
Choose Add reader. The Actions menu, step 1: Add reader.
In the Add reader form, type a DB instance identifier (for example fitness-assistant-dev-aurora-instance-2) and keep DB instance class on Aurora serverless. The capacity range is inherited from the cluster: minimum 0.5 ACU, maximum 2 ACU. fitness-assistant-dev-aurora-instance-2 The Add reader form: instance identifier and Aurora serverless class.
Scroll down, keep the defaults for network, security and monitoring, and click Add reader. The reader is placed in a different Availability Zone from the writer, and its Promotion tier decides which reader becomes the writer first in a failover.
Part C — A CloudWatch alarm that sends an e-mail The project has 12 alarms, created by CloudFormation. This shows how one of them is built by hand: errors of the auth function above the threshold send a notification to the SNS topic.
C.1 — Check the notification target. Open SNS → Topics → fitness-assistant-dev-app-alerts. The Subscriptions tab must show one e-mail subscription with the status Confirmed.
The topic and its confirmed e-mail subscription.
C.2 — Create the alarm. Open CloudWatch → Alarms → Create alarm.
Click Select metric. Step 1 of the wizard: Select metric.
Choose Lambda → By Function Name, tick the Errors row of fitness-assistant-dev-auth, then click Select metric. The metric picker: the Errors metric of fitness-assistant-dev-auth.
Set Statistic to Sum and Period to 5 minutes. In Whenever Errors is… choose Greater/Equal, type the threshold below, then click Next. 5 The condition: greater than or equal to 5 errors in 5 minutes.
In Configure actions, keep In alarm as the trigger, choose Select an existing SNS topic, and pick fitness-assistant-dev-app-alerts. Add a second notification for OK with the same topic, so you also get a message when the alarm recovers. The actions step: choose the SNS topic.
Click Next, enter the name fitness-assistant-dev-auth-lambda-errors, click Next, review and click Create alarm. C.3 — Verify. The new alarm shows OK (or Insufficient data for a few minutes). The full list of the project’s alarms:
The 12 alarms of the project. The three NAT Gateway alarms show Insufficient data while the NAT Gateway is switched off.
Test the alert path without breaking anything by forcing the alarm into the alarm state, then wait for the e-mail and for the alarm to return to OK by itself:
aws cloudwatch set-alarm-state --alarm-name fitness-assistant-dev-auth-lambda-errors --state-value ALARM --state-reason "Alert path test" Result The CloudFront distribution has an S3 origin with Origin Access Control and a chat origin, with /socket.io/* matched first. The Aurora cluster has a Writer and a Reader in different Availability Zones. A CloudWatch alarm sends ALARM and OK messages to a confirmed e-mail through SNS.

title: Infrastructure as code with CloudFormation
content:
Most of the resources in the earlier steps were first created by hand in the console so that every setting could be explained. The parts that are cheap to describe and risky to click again are also kept as CloudFormation templates, so they can be recreated, reviewed and changed through a change set. This step lists the stacks, the files to download, and how to deploy one.
1. Stacks and attached files Stack in the account Template (download) What it creates fitness-assistant-dev-app-monitoring app-monitoring.yaml 9 CloudWatch alarms and the SNS topic fitness-assistant-dev-app-alerts (5.5.5) fitness-assistant-dev-frontend-cdn frontend-cdn.yaml The CloudFront distribution and its Origin Access Control for the frontend bucket gymini-dev-on-demand dev-on-demand.yaml The hourly-billed parts that are switched on and off per session: NAT Gateway, Chat load balancer, listener, target group and VPC endpoints fitness-assistant-dev-cicd-iam ci-cd-oidc.yaml The five least-privilege IAM roles that GitHub Actions assumes through OIDC fitness-assistant-dev-api-gateway managed by the infrastructure workflows The HTTP API with 254 resources (routes, integrations, stage); too large to attach, changed only through reviewed change sets (5.4.16) The attached copies replace the AWS account ID and the subnet IDs with placeholders (123456789012, subnet-0123456789abcdef0). Replace them with your own values before deploying. No password, key or e-mail address is stored in any template.
2. What the templates do and do not contain Parameters instead of hard-coded values. The templates reference existing resources (VPC, subnets, Aurora cluster, API ID, bucket name) through parameters, so the same template works in another account after the values are changed. No credentials. The monitoring template creates the SNS topic but no subscription. The e-mail is subscribed afterwards with the command shown in the stack output, so no address is committed anywhere. Least privilege by design. In the OIDC template each role trusts exactly one GitHub environment (dev, dev-infra, dev-infra-plan) and the plan role has an explicit deny on executing change sets. There is no static access key and no administrator access. Separation of lifetimes. The on-demand stack holds only what costs money while idle. The VPC, subnets, Aurora, Lambda functions and secrets live outside it, so switching the environment off never touches them. 3. Deploy one stack Example with the monitoring template. Replace the placeholders, then deploy through a change set so the result can be reviewed before it is applied:
aws cloudformation deploy \ --region ap-southeast-1 \ --stack-name fitness-assistant-dev-app-monitoring \ --template-file app-monitoring.yaml \ --parameter-overrides ApiId=<your-api-id> AuroraClusterIdentifier=<your-aurora-cluster> \ --no-execute-changeset Review the change set in the console (CloudFormation → Stacks → the stack → Change sets), then execute it. After the stack is created, subscribe your own e-mail address to the topic with the command in the Outputs tab (SubscribeCommand) and confirm the message you receive.
The OIDC template creates IAM roles with fixed names, so deploying it needs the capability flag:
aws cloudformation deploy --template-file ci-cd-oidc.yaml --stack-name fitness-assistant-dev-cicd-iam --capabilities CAPABILITY_NAMED_IAM --no-execute-changeset 4. Check the result Open CloudFormation → Stacks. Each stack must be CREATE_COMPLETE or UPDATE_COMPLETE. Open a stack and check three tabs: Resources (every resource in CREATE_COMPLETE), Outputs (the IDs and ARNs the other steps use) and Events (a clean history with no rollback).
To compare the live stack with the template, use Stack actions → Detect drift. A stack whose status is IN_SYNC has no change made outside CloudFormation. The API Gateway stack is checked this way before every infrastructure change (5.4.13).
Screens of the console The screens below were captured in the account. The Create stack wizard was walked through up to the final review and then cancelled, so no stack was created.
Open CloudFormation → Stacks and click the stack name (1). The account has 5 project stacks, all in CREATE_COMPLETE or UPDATE_COMPLETE.
Open the Resources tab (1). Every resource must show CREATE_COMPLETE (2). The 10 resources of the monitoring stack: 9 alarms and the SNS topic.
Open the Outputs tab (1) to read the values the other steps use, including the subscribe command. Outputs of the monitoring stack (account ID hidden).
To create a stack from a template file, click Create stack and choose With new resources (standard) (1). The Create stack menu.
In step 1 choose Upload a template file (1) and pick the YAML file downloaded above (2). The console uploads it and shows its address. Click Next (3). Step 1: the template file is uploaded.
In step 2 type the Stack name (1). The template parameters appear with their default values (2); keep them or change them. Click Next (3). Step 2: stack name and parameters.
Step 3 holds the optional settings (tags, service role, rollback behavior, notifications). Keep Roll back all resources (1) and click Next at the bottom of the page. Step 3: stack options.
Step 4 shows a summary: the template (1) and the stack name and parameters (2). Read it before submitting. Step 4: review.
At the bottom, Submit creates the stack and Cancel leaves without creating anything. The screenshots here end with Cancel (1) because the monitoring stack already exists in the account; to create it for real, click Submit (2) and watch the Events tab until the status is CREATE_COMPLETE. The Submit and Cancel buttons.
5. Clean-up Delete a stack with Delete, or run aws cloudformation delete-stack --stack-name <name>. Delete the on-demand stack first when shutting everything down, because the other stacks do not depend on it. The order for the whole environment is in 5.7.

title: GitHub Actions workflows
content:
This step collects the six GitHub Actions workflows of the project in one place, with the files to download. 5.4.12 and 5.4.13 show how they were activated; this page shows what each one does and how to use it.
1. The workflows Workflow (download) Trigger Who it acts as What it does pr-validation.yml Every pull request to master or aws-deploy No AWS access Install, lint, type-check, unit tests per service, IaC lint, Docker build of the chat image, and the PowerShell helper tests dev-build.yml Push to aws-deploy, or manual No AWS access Builds and hashes each changed Lambda zip and stores it as a workflow artifact dev-deploy.yml Manual, reviewer approval GyminiDevAppDeployRole through OIDC Deploys the Lambda code of the chosen services from a build, checks the artifact hashes first, then runs a /health smoke check; dry run by default chat-deploy.yml Manual, reviewer approval GyminiDevAppDeployRole Registers a new ECS task definition revision for the Chat service without changing the desired count infra-plan.yml Manual GyminiDevInfraPlanRole Creates a CloudFormation change set for the API Gateway stack, scans it, publishes a digest of the changes; cannot execute anything infra-deploy.yml Manual, reviewer approval GyminiDevInfraApplyRole Executes one reviewed change set, only if its digest matches what the plan printed, then runs read-only checks The attached copies replace the AWS account ID with the placeholder 123456789012. Replace it, and the role names and bucket names, with the values of your own account.
2. How the safety works No stored keys. The workflows that touch AWS use the aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials action with role-to-assume. GitHub issues a short-lived OIDC token, and each IAM role trusts exactly one GitHub environment. There is no access key in the repository or in the repository secrets. A human approves every change. Jobs that change AWS declare an environment (dev, dev-infra-plan, dev-infra). Each environment requires a reviewer, has administrator bypass turned off, and only allows deployment from the aws-deploy branch (5.4.13). Plan and apply are separate roles. The plan role has an explicit deny on executing a change set, so it cannot apply anything even if the file is edited. The apply role can execute but cannot create change sets. The reviewed change is the applied change. The apply workflow takes the digest that the plan printed and refuses to run if the change set no longer matches it. Dry run by default. The deploy workflows start with dry_run: true, so a first run only prints what would happen. 3. Use a workflow Open the repository on GitHub, then Actions, and choose the workflow in the left list. Click Run workflow, choose the branch aws-deploy and fill in the inputs. For a deploy workflow, leave dry_run checked on the first run and read the summary. Run again with it unchecked for the real deploy. When the job reaches the environment step it shows Waiting. Click Review deployments, tick the environment and click Approve and deploy. Inputs used in practice:
Workflow Input Example dev-deploy.yml build_run_id the run ID of the dev-build.yml run to deploy dev-deploy.yml services auth chat-deploy.yml force_on unchecked, so the Chat service stays on or off as it is infra-deploy.yml change_set_name, reviewed_digest both printed by infra-plan.yml 4. Check the result In Actions every job of the run must be green. A deploy run ends with a summary that lists the services, whether it was a dry run and the result. After a real Lambda deploy, LastModified of the function changes and the smoke check calls /health:
aws lambda get-function-configuration --function-name fitness-assistant-dev-auth --query LastModified Screens of GitHub Open the repository, then Actions. Choose a workflow in the left list (1); the runs appear on the right (2). The six workflows and the recent runs.
Open a run. A successful run shows the Success status (1), every job green (2) and a job summary (3) with the commit, the services, the dry-run flag, the result and the previous code hash kept as a rollback reference. A real deploy run of the Lambda code, finished with Success.
To start a deploy, open the workflow and click Run workflow. Choose the branch aws-deploy (1), enter the run ID of the build (2) and the services (3), and leave dry_run ticked (4) for the first run. Then click Run workflow in the form. The inputs of the deploy workflow.
The approval gate is a GitHub environment. In Settings → Environments → dev, Required reviewers is ticked with the reviewer (1), administrators cannot bypass the rules (2), and only the aws-deploy branch may deploy (3). The protection rules of the dev environment.
5. Requirements for a new repository The OIDC roles from 5.4.15 exist, with the GitHub repository name set in the GitHubRepository parameter. The three GitHub environments exist, each with a required reviewer and the aws-deploy deployment branch rule. The repository variable APIGW_ADOPTION_COMPLETE is set to true only after the API Gateway stack has been verified as managed and free of drift. Manual workflows exist on the default branch too, because GitHub can only dispatch a workflow that is on the default branch.
